  • Industry observers note that in a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission.
  • To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission. At bottom, she argues for implementing a version of the UK Takeover Panel to regulate procedural requirements for proposal submission while leaving decisions about content scope to shareholders. Along the way, she argues that The Heritage Foundation, including by way of its American Investor Initiative, “is having second thoughts” about prior positions Heritage has taken on the issue, and that Heritage “seems distinctly unhappy with the SEC’s direction of travel” and is thus left in “the strange position of defending the very mechanism it spent years arguing had made shareholder meetings too political.” These characterizations of Heritage warrant some clarification.To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time. Having said that, our current view of Rule 14a-8 is not nearly as conflicted as Wilson presents.For example, Wilson contrasts our past criticism of proxy advisers, ESG and “woke investment,” with our current position of cautioning against too hasty rescission of Rule 14a-8. Specifically, as we noted in a recent letter published in the Wall Street Journal, we believe the goal of depoliticizing corporate governance is best served by a “generous grace period” before rescission takes effect.The current mix of corporate commitments took shape over decades in which mainly one set of proponents used the proposal process. Proponents who favor corporate neutrality, Heritage among them, have only recently begun to use the process effectively. Ending it abruptly would freeze in place the results of that one-sided period. A transition period would also allow states to develop their own frameworks for shareholder proposals, give companies and investors time to adjust, and avoid entrenching a status quo that formed under proxy-advisory and asset-manager voting practices that are themselves only now being reformed.While our position may in some sense have shifted from “keep the rule” to “rescind the rule slowly,” the animating principle remains the same: The prosperity-generating power of free-market capitalism must be defended against the myriad conflicts of interest distorting relevant inputs from corporate leaders, asset managers, proxy advisors, activists, and others. Particularly with respect to ESG (including DEI, sustainability, and net zero, as well as the successor labels under which similar commitments are increasingly marketed), resisting the use of corporate and regulatory machinery to advance policy goals that could not be achieved through markets or legislatures is a consistent theme. As has been said: “Every great cause begins as a movement, becomes a business, and eventually degenerates into a racket.”>>> The Case of the Missing Heritage Foundation ProposalsTo illustrate, consider the four justifications most commonly offered for corporate sustainability commitments and investments, and why each, on closer examination, proves incomplete. First, sustainability commitments are often described as a matter of legal compliance. But the leading climate-disclosure mandates, such as California’s SB 253 and SB 261, require companies to report emissions and climate-related risks, not to adopt reduction targets. And when we have offered to withdraw shareholder proposals if a organization would state publicly that its sustainability commitments are legally required, companies have generally declined to do so. That reluctance suggests the commitments rest on something other than compliance.Second, sustainability commitments are frequently defended as risk management, a necessary cost of reducing exposure to climate-related harm. But according to the Global Carbon Budget 2025, the United States accounts for roughly 13 percent of global fossil CO₂ emissions, compared with about 32 percent for China and 8 percent for India. Even if every U.S. corporation reached net zero, the effect on global emissions, and so on the physical risks companies face, would be modest without comparable action elsewhere. Firm-level transition risks, such as regulatory and litigation exposure, may justify some measures. But those risks call for targeted, quantified responses, not open-ended commitments.Third, sustainability commitments are said to reflect client demand. BlackRock’s 2020 letter to clients, for example, justified its sustainability initiatives in part by noting that “more and more of our clients have focused on the impact of sustainability on their portfolios.” Client demand alone, however, does not show that a commitment creates value for shareholders. Demand for a product does not justify supplying it at any price, and sustainability commitments deserve the same discipline. Their costs and benefits should be fully disclosed so that clients and shareholders can make informed judgments.Finally, one would expect companies making substantial sustainability commitments to have done the relevant expected-value analysis and to track the returns. Yet even advocates of corporate sustainability acknowledge that this rarely happens. The director of NYU Stern’s Center for Sustainable Business has observed that “most companies are not monetizing the Return on Sustainability Investment,” and that financial benefits “are tracked differently (if at all) by different units and are not aggregated.” Without such measurement, it is difficult to assess whether these commitments serve shareholders’ interests.If these conventional justifications are incomplete, a further explanation lies in the incentives of the parties involved. Asset managers market ESG products and compete for mandates from clients who want them. Proxy advisors have offered ESG-related advisory services alongside their voting recommendations. And corporate managers benefit from the wide discretion that stakeholder-oriented commitments afford. Other incentives may reinforce these: avoiding confrontations with activist investors, the reputational benefits of visible sustainability commitments in settings such as the World Economic Forum, the social and professional norms within which many executives and directors operate, and bias against people of faith. Together, these incentives help explain why corporations would adopt net zero commitments without documented support for their returns, despite well-documented concerns about affordability, national security, and energy independence.>>> More Than Ever, It’s Time for Economic Freedom, Not DEI or ESGAll the foregoing also helps explain low vote counts on anti-ESG proposals. Once you’ve accounted for the influence of conflicted asset managers, proxy advisors, and corporate insiders—and public pension funds whose voting policies may weigh collateral policy objectives alongside beneficiaries’ financial interests—there aren’t many votes left that can reflect the views of the “true owners.” As Jerry Bowyer, also mentioned in Wilson’s article, has essentially noted, if a foreign country’s national election returned 2% or less of the votes in favor of a candidate widely known to only have 50% of the support, all the defenders of democracy would be calling the election corrupt and illegitimate.Yet this is basically what we see in proxy voting every season when it comes to conservative anti-ESG and anti-DEI proposals. Vote totals can also be misread in the other direction. When an anti-DEI proposal receives 2% support, the result is sometimes reported as showing that 98 percent of shareholders ‘support DEI.’ Yet comparable pro-DEI proposals have recently drawn similarly low support, particularly since asset managers revised their voting policies and proxy advisors came under regulatory scrutiny. That pattern suggests low totals often reflect reluctance to support prescriptive proposals of either kind, not an endorsement of the underlying policy.All the foregoing helps explain why Heritage believes rescinding Rule 14a-8 too rapidly would turn laudable federalism into problematic favoritism by sealing in conflicted gains just when free-market proponents have started making material gains getting corporations back to neutral. And that position can be completely consistent with also supporting the ultimate rescission of the rule due to it being unauthorized and undermining proper federalism.Much more can, should, and will be said about the proper balance of state oversight of proposal submission and scope requirements, as well as federal oversight of related corporate disclosures in interstate commerce. But for now, it is worth noting that a consistent theme animates Heritage’s past and present positions on Rule 14a-8. Heritage certainly appreciates the ways we are witnessing private ordering, federalism, and the marketplace of ideas operating in response to the proposed rescission of the rule, but we are in fact happy “with the SEC’s direction of travel.”.

Industry observers note that in a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission. At bottom, she argues for implementing a version of the UK Takeover Panel to regulate procedural requirements for proposal submission while leaving decisions about content scope to shareholders. Along the way, she argues that The Heritage Foundation, including by way of its American Investor Initiative, “is having second thoughts” about prior positions Heritage has taken on the issue, and that Heritage “seems distinctly unhappy with the SEC’s direction of travel” and is thus left in “the strange position of defending the very mechanism it spent years arguing had made shareholder meetings too political.” These characterizations of Heritage warrant some clarification.

To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time. Having said that, our current view of Rule 14a-8 is not nearly as conflicted as Wilson presents.

It has been revealed that for example, Wilson contrasts our past criticism of proxy advisers, ESG and “woke investment,” with our current position of cautioning against too hasty rescission of Rule 14a-8. Specifically, as we noted in a recent letter published in the Wall Street Journal, we believe the goal of depoliticizing corporate governance is best served by a “generous grace period” before rescission takes effect.

Industry observers note that the current mix of corporate commitments took shape over decades in which mainly one set of proponents used the proposal process. Proponents who favor corporate neutrality, Heritage among them, have only recently begun to use the process effectively. Ending it abruptly would freeze in place the results of that one-sided period. A transition period would also allow states to develop their own frameworks for shareholder proposals, give companies and investors time to adjust, and avoid entrenching a status quo that formed under proxy-advisory and asset-manager voting practices that are themselves only now being reformed.

While our position may in some sense have shifted from “keep the rule” to “rescind the rule slowly,” the animating principle remains the same: The prosperity-generating power of free-market capitalism must be defended against the myriad conflicts of interest distorting relevant inputs from corporate leaders, asset managers, proxy advisors, activists, and others. Particularly with respect to ESG (including DEI, sustainability, and net zero, as well as the successor labels under which similar commitments are increasingly marketed), resisting the use of corporate and regulatory machinery to advance policy goals that could not be achieved through markets or legislatures is a consistent theme. As has been said: “Every great cause begins as a movement, becomes a business, and eventually degenerates into a racket.”.

>>> The Case of the Missing Heritage Foundation Proposals.

It has been revealed that to illustrate, consider the four justifications most commonly offered for corporate sustainability commitments and investments, and why each, on closer examination, proves incomplete. First, sustainability commitments are often described as a matter of legal compliance. But the leading climate-disclosure mandates, such as California’s SB 253 and SB 261, require companies to report emissions and climate-related risks, not to adopt reduction targets. And when we have offered to withdraw shareholder proposals if a manufacturer would state publicly that its sustainability commitments are legally required, companies have generally declined to do so. That reluctance suggests the commitments rest on something other than compliance.

Second, sustainability commitments are frequently defended as risk management, a necessary cost of reducing exposure to climate-related harm. But according to the Global Carbon Budget 2025, the United States accounts for roughly 13 percent of global fossil CO₂ emissions, compared with about 32 percent for China and 8 percent for India. Even if every U.S. corporation reached net zero, the effect on global emissions, and so on the physical risks companies face, would be modest without comparable action elsewhere. Firm-level transition risks, such as regulatory and litigation exposure, may justify some measures. But those risks call for targeted, quantified responses, not open-ended commitments.

In a recent development, third, sustainability commitments are stated to reflect client demand. BlackRock’s 2020 letter to clients, for example, justified its sustainability initiatives in part by noting that “more and more of our clients have focused on the impact of sustainability on their portfolios.” Client demand alone, however, does not show that a commitment creates value for shareholders. Demand for a product does not justify supplying it at any price, and sustainability commitments deserve the same discipline. Their costs and benefits should be fully disclosed so that clients and shareholders can make informed judgments.

Industry observers note that finally, one would expect companies making substantial sustainability commitments to have done the relevant expected-value analysis and to track the returns. Yet even advocates of corporate sustainability acknowledge that this rarely happens. The director of NYU Stern’s Center for Sustainable Business has observed that “most companies are not monetizing the Return on Sustainability Investment,” and that financial benefits “are tracked differently (if at all) by different units and are not aggregated.” Without such measurement, it is difficult to assess whether these commitments serve shareholders’ interests.

According to recent reports, if these conventional justifications are incomplete, a further explanation lies in the incentives of the parties involved. Asset managers market ESG products and compete for mandates from clients who want them. Proxy advisors have offered ESG-related advisory services alongside their voting recommendations. And corporate managers benefit from the wide discretion that stakeholder-oriented commitments afford. Other incentives may reinforce these: avoiding confrontations with activist investors, the reputational benefits of visible sustainability commitments in settings such as the World Economic Forum, the social and professional norms within which many executives and directors operate, and bias against people of faith. Together, these incentives help explain why corporations would adopt net zero commitments without documented support for their returns, despite well-documented concerns about affordability, national security, and energy independence.

Recent findings suggest that all the foregoing also helps explain low vote counts on anti-ESG proposals. Once you’ve accounted for the influence of conflicted asset managers, proxy advisors, and corporate insiders—and public pension funds whose voting policies may weigh collateral policy objectives alongside beneficiaries’ financial interests—there aren’t many votes left that can reflect the views of the “true owners.” As Jerry Bowyer, also mentioned in Wilson’s article, has essentially noted, if a foreign country’s national election returned 2% or less of the votes in favor of a candidate widely known to only have 50% of the support, all the defenders of democracy would be calling the election corrupt and illegitimate.

Industry observers note that yet this is basically what we see in proxy voting every season when it comes to conservative anti-ESG and anti-DEI proposals. Vote totals can also be misread in the other direction. When an anti-DEI proposal receives 2% support, the result is sometimes reported as showing that 98 percent of shareholders ‘support DEI.’ Yet comparable pro-DEI proposals have recently drawn similarly low support, particularly since asset managers revised their voting policies and proxy advisors came under regulatory scrutiny. That pattern suggests low totals often reflect reluctance to support prescriptive proposals of either kind, not an endorsement of the underlying policy.

Industry observers note that all the foregoing helps explain why Heritage believes rescinding Rule 14a-8 too rapidly would turn laudable federalism into problematic favoritism by sealing in conflicted gains just when free-market proponents have started making material gains getting corporations back to neutral. And that position can be completely consistent with also supporting the ultimate rescission of the rule due to it being unauthorized and undermining proper federalism.

Much more can, should, and will be mentioned about the proper balance of state oversight of proposal submission and scope requirements, as well as federal oversight of related corporate disclosures in interstate commerce. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on October 12, 2026, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gave a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland in which he outlined NATO’s newly introduced theory of victory to deter and, if necessary, defeat Russian aggression.[REF] This theory of victory, called “Block, Blunt, Break,” centers on employing combined arms and maneuver to block initial enemy assaults on Alliance territory, blunt follow-on offensives, and, if necessary, break the enemy’s ability to sustain combat operations. SACEUR’s speech comes at a time of considerable consternation in Eastern European capitals after months of suspected Russian hybrid activities including drone incursions and sabotage. General Grynkewich’s deterrence-focused theory of victory struck the right tone, reassuring worried allies and signaling to Moscow that the United States and its NATO allies are confident of their ability to defeat a Russian incursion into a NATO state and that Russia would do well not to consider one. The speech and the strategy itself also appear wisely designed to avoid unnecessary escalation with Russia as SACEUR made clear throughout that NATO is a defensive Alliance.Block, Blunt, BreakGeneral Grynkewich mentioned that a classified version of this new NATO strategy had been agreed on by all 32 members of the Alliance about three months before his October 12 speech.[REF] He explained his decision to present Block, Blunt, Break in public as a helpful measure to assuage increasingly anxious NATO populations vulnerable to evolving security threats.[REF] General Grynkewich summarized his theory of victory as follows: “We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”[REF]Block. NATO land forces will meet any enemy assault with preponderant force at the point of contact and not trade territory for time. As these forces prevent adversaries from seizing Alliance territory, air and sea forces will gain superiority before aggressively supporting NATO forces on the ground. Space and cyber forces will be employed, creating a lattice of forces meant to prevent the enemy from holding its ground.Blunt. Following the block phase, NATO forces will focus on denying the enemy’s ability to generate offensive momentum. This effort will include expanded deployments of manned and autonomous forces across domains to maintain operational advantage. The mass employment of effects in the forward battlespace will overwhelm enemy formations, thereby disrupting any continued advance.Break. If the enemy continues its attack or employs reserves, NATO forces will expand operations to break the enemy’s broader warfighting system. NATO will apply mass pressure through all domains to break down the enemy’s ability to sustain its forces. A major contributing factor to this pressure campaign will be the pairing of precision munitions with sweeping volumes of attritable and affordable effects. These efforts will isolate enemy formations from replenishment and paralyze the command and control of the opposing force.[REF]Strategic ContextThis theory of victory is a marked shift from earlier NATO theories of victory, which focused on trading space for time—that is, allowing Russian forces to move into NATO territory, while NATO forces harass and slow Russian advances until decisive force can be brought to bear to destroy and then expel all Russian forces from NATO territory.Block, Blunt, Break is a significant change from NATO Cold War strategy.During the Cold War, West Germany was the NATO state considered most likely to be attacked by massive numbers of Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, and the Fulda Gap was often identified as the most likely attack route. The geographic size of West Germany meant that NATO forces could fall back tens or hundreds of kilometers before they could generate enough combat mass to begin a counteroffensive against Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces and then expel them from NATO soil. In this sense, NATO planned to trade territory for time, during which it would seize the conventional advantage.Today, the Suwalki Gap between Lithuania and Poland is often cited as the modern equivalent of the Fulda Gap, especially because it separates Russian-allied Belarus from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.[REF] The three Baltic States of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are for numerous reasons the NATO states against which full-scale Russian aggression is most likely; for example, Russian revanchists claim the existence of Russian-speaking minorities in Estonia and Latvia as a potential pretext, and Russian military planners could seek to connect the Russian exclave by land to either Belarus or Russia, and Lithuania is in their way. In the Baltic States, Block, Blunt, Break makes sense as the strategy for deterring or defending against Russian aggression from both a military planning and a political perspective.From a military planning perspective, the lack of strategic depth in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania was likely a major factor in the change in strategy. Blocking the Russian advance from the outset prevents the Russians from gaining a foothold that may prove difficult to dislodge once fortified and reinforced.From a political perspective, Block, Blunt, Break reinforces allied cohesion in the face of Russian aggression against a Baltic state or some other frontline state. Should Russia rapidly gain lodgment within Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, it could then sue for peace before NATO could dislodge Russian forces and liberate those three NATO members. This could well create real political divisions within the North Atlantic Council, in which some countries would press for the liberation of the Baltic States, while others may seek to accept the peace proposal. It is not inconceivable that such a development could lead to the fracturing and potential breakup of NATO—long a goal of Moscow. This new strategy articulated by SACEUR could be a way to defend every inch of NATO soil from the outset and prevent this difficult scenario.Strategic SignalsGeneral Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to demonstrate how NATO allies intend to prevent conflict and defeat aggression if needed. He stressed that NATO’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy is defensive and seeks to prevent enemies from achieving their offensive objectives. While detailing this theory of victory, General Grynkewich provided a vision for a future NATO with enhanced military strength, operational readiness, and a unified commitment to the defense of all the Alliance’s territory.This speech landed amid persistent suspected Russian gray-zone warfare against European NATO member states. On October 13, Bulgaria’s government summoned the Russian ambassador after two ships were hit by drones near its territorial waters.[REF] Two additional merchant ships were struck by drones near Bulgaria’s coast the week before, attacks that followed a strike on a civilian ship off Romania,[REF] and Romania has faced repeated Russian drone incursions over the past year.[REF]While not mentioning these and other similar events directly, General Grynkewich stated that threats and intimidation against Alliance members will only bind NATO closer together. He noted that this unity is enhanced by the Alliance’s confidence in its ability to move up the escalation ladder if needed. General Grynkewich identified NATO’s strength, cohesion, and readiness as key factors that should significantly complicate an adversary’s military calculus of escalation. SACEUR also exhorted European NATO allies not to shy away from identifying the source of gray-zone provocations when they occur.The United States’ ongoing European force posture review and discussions of a likely reduction in U.S. troop levels in Europe as part of the necessary rebalancing of forces to the Indo-Pacific have led to uncertainty among NATO allies regarding America’s contributions to the Alliance.[REF] General Grynkewich’s speech reaffirmed the United States’ commitment to European security, albeit within the larger framework of increased burden sharing promoted by the Trump Administration.NATO’s theory of victory relies on aggressive, forward resistance to enemy advances. Implementing this operational concept will require the Alliance to bring substantial force to bear within a constrained timeline. While General Grynkewich’s speech serves as an overt commitment to a continued American presence in NATO, European states will likely have to shoulder a significant burden as part of the rapid joint response to an attack on the Alliance. To ensure NATO’s ability to execute this proposal, European states should continue expanding their defense spending to improve their warfighting capabilities, forward-deploy certain capabilities, and substantially improve military mobility.General Grynkewich prefaced his explanation of NATO’s theory of victory with a frank assessment of NATO’s security environment. He held that conflict is neither imminent nor inevitable. This status quo, he said, can be sustained by clearly articulating NATO’s intentions, maintaining open lines of communication with external states, and maintaining deterrence by denial through military capacity.Commenting on the character of NATO, General Grynkewich stressed that the Alliance is defensive and has “no looks, no intentions, and no ambitions” other than the protection of NATO peoples and territories. SACEUR nevertheless cautioned potential adversaries not to mistake NATO’s defensive nature for a lack of resolve and emphasized that member states will ensure any attack on Alliance territory will prove futile.[REF]This point was underlined by additional commentary regarding NATO’s deterrence posture. General Grynkewich drew attention to the Alliance’s “decision advantage.” He asserted that NATO will not be caught by surprise thanks to an immense intelligence footprint encompassing a vast network of sensors and sources. General Grynkewich framed NATO’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capability as a key enabler of the Alliance’s theory of victory. By rapidly assessing an opposing force’s presence and intent, NATO forces will have time to mobilize in the numbers required to deny attackers at the point of contact, especially because these troops will be reinforcing significant numbers of NATO troops forward positioned within NATO’s easternmost states.Because of NATO’s doctrine, character, and posture, General Grynkewich remarked that the burden of escalation will always lie upon NATO’s aggressors. NATO’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy seeks only to prevent an enemy from realizing its revisionist aspirations. He plainly asserted that such states will “bear the full moral, political, and strategic weight” of initiating and expanding conflict with the Alliance.[REF]General Grynkewich included within this posture of deterrence and denial an explicit characterization of NATO’s intentions after the outbreak of conflict. He emphasized that the Alliance’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy does not seek at the outset to impose a strategic defeat upon its adversaries. Instead, NATO seeks simply to employ its theory of victory to maintain the Alliance’s territorial integrity by tactically defeating its attackers.In sum, General Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to communicate fundamental Alliance convictions to audiences both within and outside NATO. He articulated how NATO is not simply relying on decades-old defense strategies but adopting new means to meet emerging security threats. He delineated an internal Alliance dynamic defined by cohesion anchored in a collective determination to defend Alliance territory from opportunistic adversaries. He portrayed to external audiences a NATO whose mandate is limited to protecting its citizens and territory but that is also unified and firm in its willingness to fight and to defeat an aggressor if needed. General Grynkewich confidently messaged to Russia that he wants to assure those who “might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”[REF]Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation.

He emphasized that the Alliance’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy does not seek at the outset to impose a strategic defeat upon its adversaries. Instead, NATO seeks simply to employ its theory of victory to maintain the Alliance’s territorial integrity by tactically defeating its attackers.

Recent findings suggest that in sum, General Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to communicate fundamental Alliance convictions to audiences both within and outside NATO. He articulated how NATO is not simply relying on decades-old defense strategies but adopting fresh means to meet emerging security threats. He delineated an internal Alliance dynamic defined by cohesion anchored in a collective determination to defend Alliance territory from opportunistic adversaries. He portrayed to external audiences a NATO whose mandate is limited to protecting its citizens and territory but that is also unified and firm in its willingness to fight and to defeat an aggressor if needed. General Grynkewich confidently messaged to Russia that he wants to assure those who “might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”[REF].

Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation.

Does Board and Management Diversity Improve Financial Performance? The Evidence Is Weak

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3434 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history.
  • Industry observers note that in 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history.
  • Especially in the wake of a latest report, Capturing the Diversity Benefit, which claims that companies with more racially diverse management teams perform better financially.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history. Huff’s central insight—that correlation dressed in the vestments of causation can seduce even careful readers—has aged better than most mid-century paperbacks. It’s due for a revival.Especially in the wake of a upcoming report, Capturing the Diversity Benefit, which claims that companies with more racially diverse management teams perform better financially.The report is not without ambition. It draws on federal EEO-1 workforce filings matched to financial data for 1,482 publicly traded companies between 2016 and 2024, and it contains some genuine quantitative analysis.But its empirical research design is deeply flawed, and in ways Huff would have recognized instantly. The analysis may document correlations inside a selected dataset, but it does not establish that management diversity improves corporate performance, that DEI programs create shareholder value, or that companies incur financial risk by scaling those programs back.Consider, first, the sample, always the place a skeptical reader should look, and always the place such reports hope one will not. The number of observed companies changes substantially by year, reaching 1,059 workforce observations in 2020 and falling to 523 in 2024. Earlier data combine voluntary disclosures with records obtained through a Department of Labor Freedom of Information Act release. Later data rely heavily on voluntary disclosure alone, a shift roughly analogous to switching, mid-poll, from a mandatory census to a call for volunteers.>>> DEI’s Days in the Corporate World Are NumberedThe report itself concedes the consequence: companies choosing to disclose had 4.5 percentage points more BIPOC management representation than companies that never disclosed. Selection into the sample is therefore entangled with the very variable under study, which is a polite way of saying the study measures, in part, itself.Nor does the report tell readers how its companies compare with the Russell 3000 or the CRSP-Compustat universe, the benchmarks against which any claim to represent “corporate America” must be tested. Readers do not learn whether the sample differs in size, industry, age, profitability, exchange listing, geographic exposure, or prior stock performance.These are not incidental details; they are precisely the characteristics that predict both workforce composition and financial outcomes. Pooling a large technology organization with a small regional manufacturer and regressing profits on a single demographic measure does not make those differences disappear. It merely makes them invisible.The changing sample, moreover, weakens whatever trends the report reports. An average can move for two quite different reasons: because the same firms changed, or because different firms wandered into and out of the dataset. To its credit, the report acknowledges that sample composition may explain part of the sharp decline in female representation it reports for financial services between 2020 and 2021.That caveat, once granted, applies throughout the time series, a fact the report is less eager to grant. A balanced panel and a decomposition of within-firm change from sample entry and exit are prerequisites, not refinements, for interpreting these averages as corporate trends rather than statistical artifacts of who happened to show up.Measurement supplies a second problem, and a subtler one. EEO-1 filings are more standardized than ordinary ESG ratings, which is a modest compliment, but they still require decisions about establishments, corporate ownership, mergers, missing filings, and the aggregation of executive, senior, first-line, and mid-level managers. The report provides too little information to reproduce those choices. Its Racial Justice Initiative score is even less transparent. It combines 27 indicators—ranging from promotion data and EEO-1 disclosure to public statements, donations, and references to political movements—with some categories assigned five times the weight of others. One is invited to trust the recipe without seeing the kitchen.The ESG measurement literature explains, with some precision, why these choices matter. Florian Berg, Julian Kölbel, and Roberto Rigobon compared six major ESG rating systems and found correlations ranging from 0.38 to 0.71, hardly the tight clustering one would expect if these systems were measuring the same underlying reality. They attribute 56% of rating divergence to measurement, 38% to scope, and 6% to weighting.Any claimed DEI-performance relationship therefore raises a prior question, one the report never quite gets around to asking: What DEI score is being used, which indicators enter it, and how are they weighted? A composite social score cannot be treated as an objective corporate trait without its coding rules, missing-data procedures, reliability checks, and sensitivity to alternative weights. Put simply, DEI and ESG scores vary so markedly across providers that they have largely lost their meaning as fixed facts about a company.Related research by Christos Makridis and Majeed Simaan demonstrates that this measurement noise is not merely an academic nuisance; it has real consequences for actual investment decisions. Using more than 22,000 firm-year observations and 21 years of out-of-sample portfolio tests, they find that portfolios incorporating Refinitiv ESG scores do not consistently outperform return-based strategies on a risk-adjusted basis. ESG-only rules can produce higher average returns in some specifications, true enough, but they also generate greater volatility and downside risk (the fine print investors are seldom shown).Return-based factor models achieve comparable or better ex-post ESG standing without using ESG ratings directly at all. Their panel analysis also finds that market volatility predicts later ESG ratings, while ESG ratings do not predict later volatility, suggesting the ratings absorb information the market already knew rather than furnishing anything so useful as foresight.Capturing the Diversity Benefit then commits its largest error, and here Huff would surely have reached for his red pen: it estimates simple bivariate regressions. Financial performance depends on firm size, book-to-market ratios, profitability, investment, leverage, industry, firm age, prior performance, and macroeconomic conditions. The main analysis controls for none of them. This omission is especially damaging because the report’s own tables show sharply different results across market-capitalization groups. The authors call firm size “almost certainly” a confound—then proceed, undeterred, to present unadjusted aggregate estimates anyway.Income after tax, measured in dollars, illustrates the difficulty. Large companies generally earn more dollars and may also employ more diverse managers. A positive coefficient can therefore capture company scale rather than operating performance—correlation masquerading, once again, as insight.Raw multiyear stock-price appreciation is similarly inadequate to the task. Finance researchers evaluate abnormal returns only after accounting for established sources of risk and return. The Fama-French five-factor model incorporates market exposure, size, value, profitability, and investment; cross-sectional work commonly employs the Fama-MacBeth method to test whether a given characteristic predicts returns after competing explanations have had their say. The report employs none of this.Timing presents yet another serious obstacle. Matching workforce composition in a given year with performance measured in that same year does not reveal which came first. Strong companies may simply have more resources to recruit broadly, invest in management systems, and publish workforce data in the first place. Both diversity and performance may reflect nothing more exotic than management quality itself. Showing that a correlation existed before 2020 does not resolve the question of reverse causality. It merely pushes it back a few years. At a minimum, the analysis should use lagged representation to predict future outcomes, control for prior performance, and account for the swath of unobserved differences across firms over time.The report also runs hundreds of statistical tests across demographic groups—approximately 15 outcomes, 11 sectors, three size categories, and nine years. At a 5% significance threshold, false positives become not merely possible but inevitable when researchers search across that many combinations. It would be more surprising if nothing turned up significant by chance alone. Yet the tables display only plus signs, minus signs, and blanks. They omit coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and economic magnitudes—the very information a reader would need to judge whether “significant” means “large” or merely “detectable.” The analysis should identify a small set of primary outcomes and adjust for multiple testing accordingly.Prior research illustrates why this quantitative discipline matters so greatly. Jeremiah Green and John Hand attempted to reproduce McKinsey’s influential diversity-performance findings using observable S&P 500 data and found no statistically reliable relationship between executive racial and ethnic diversity and industry-adjusted profitability, sales growth, return on assets, return on equity, or total shareholder return. Their critique also identifies reverse causality in relating later diversity measures to earlier performance—the chicken-and-egg problem dressed in academic clothing.>>> The Myth of “Voluntary” ESGAlex Edmans, Caroline Flammer, and Simon Glossner draw an equally key conceptual distinction. Their employee-survey measure of DEI has little correlation with demographic representation as such. It is associated with stronger future accounting performance, earnings surprises, and valuation ratios while demographic diversity, on its own, is not. The DEI measure also does not predict future stock returns. Representation, inclusion, and corporate programs are, in short, different constructs measuring different things, and the report moves among them with a freedom the evidence does not license.Which raises the damning question: if DEI scores do not reliably reflect a company’s actual demographic composition, doesn’t the entire argument collapse under its own premise?None of this forecloses the possibility that a serious analysis might yet find that management diversity contains financially relevant information. The current report has simply not demonstrated it. The authors should compare their sample with the public-company universe, publish their data construction and coding rules, use a balanced panel, estimate models with firm and year fixed effects, control for standard company characteristics, evaluate factor-adjusted returns, lag the workforce variables, and correct for multiple testing. They should also report effect sizes rather than colored symbols, which are decorative rather than dispositive.Until then, the defensible conclusion is a modest one: among the company-years observed in this selectively disclosed dataset, some measures of management representation correlate with some financial outcomes. That could well be the case. But it does not establish a “diversity benefit,” and the distance between those two claims is the whole of the matter. Corporate leaders should demand better evidence before accepting a financial claim simply because it supports a preferred social or political conclusion. The same standard, it hardly needs saying, should apply when the conclusion cuts in the opposite direction. Huff, one suspects, would have appreciated the symmetry.

One is invited to trust the recipe without seeing the kitchen.

Privacy Act Claim Against U.S. Over Release of Victims' Names in Epstein Files Can Go Forward

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From Magistrate Judge Virginia DeMarchi (N.D.
  • Plaintiffs … filed this action against the United States, Google LLC ("Google"), and X.AI Corp.
  • Industry observers note that plaintiffs allege that in "late 2025 and early 2026, the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Magistrate Judge Virginia DeMarchi (N.D. Cal.) today in Doe 1 v. U.S.:.

Plaintiffs … filed this action against the United States, Google LLC ("Google"), and X.AI Corp. ("X.AI"). Plaintiffs sue for themselves and on behalf of a proposed class of "[a]ll Jeffrey Epstein victims whose private information, including their name, photographic image, telephone number, email address, physical address, or place of residence, was disclosed without their consent in unredacted documents released by the United States between December 2025 and the present." Plaintiffs also sue on behalf of an injunctive relief subclass of "[a]ll Class members whose disclosed private information is indexed, cached, hosted, or otherwise made available to the public through any service operated by the United States, Google, or [X.AI]." The subclass "seeks injunctive relief under Rules 23(b)(2) only.".

Industry observers note that plaintiffs allege that in "late 2025 and early 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice ('DOJ') outed approximately 100 victims of the convicted sexual predator, publishing their private information and identifying them to the world." Plaintiffs further allege that "[e]ven after the government acknowledged the disclosure violated the rights of the victims and withdrew most of the information, artificial intelligence products like Google's AI Mode and [X.]AI's Grok, continue to republish it, refusing victims' pleas to take it down." Plaintiffs' sole claim against the United States is for violation of the Privacy Act of 1974 ("Privacy Act"), 5 U.S.C. § 552a(b) and § 552(g)(1)(D). Plaintiffs assert several claims under California law and common law against both Google and X.AI for violation of California's Unfair Competition Law (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200, et seq.), invasion of privacy, negligence, and negligent infliction of emotional distress. Plaintiffs seek injunctive relief, compensatory damages, statutory damages, punitive damages, reasonable attorneys' fees and costs, as well as pre- and post-judgment interest.

The Court rejected the federal government's motion to dismiss (Google and X.AI's motion to dismiss will be considered later):.

"The Privacy Act prohibits a federal agency from disclosing a record contained in a system of records pertaining to an individual unless the individual requests the information or consents to the disclosure in writing." To state a claim for wrongful disclosure under the Privacy Act, a plaintiff must allege facts showing that (1) the information disclosed is contained in a system of records; (2) the agency improperly disclosed the information; (3) the disclosure had an adverse effect on the plaintiff; (3) the disclosure was willful or intentional; and (4) the plaintiff suffered actual damages. The Privacy Act "provides for damages only where 'the court determines that the agency acted in a manner which was intentional or willful.'".

It has been revealed that for the present purpose of resolving the United States' motion to dismiss, only the third element regarding "willful or intentional" disclosure is at issue. Under the Privacy Act, willful or intentional conduct is "only somewhat greater than gross negligence," and "the Privacy Act 'imposes liability only when the agency acts in violation of the Act in a willful or intentional manner, either by committing the act without grounds for believing it to be lawful, or flagrantly disregarding others' rights under the Act.'" ….

Industry observers note that the United States notes that the disclosures in question were made pursuant to the Epstein Files Transparency Act ("EFTA"), which required the DOJ to release, within a 30-day period, millions of pages of documents from the DOJ's investigation of Mr. Epstein. While acknowledging that DOJ "admittedly made some mistakes, including inadvertent disclosures of victim information," the United States says that in enacting the EFTA, Congress imposed an "unprecedented" and "herculean task" upon the DOJ.

Additionally, the United States says that the DOJ made remedial efforts by, for example, establishing "a website through which victims could confidentially notify the [DOJ] of information that required additional redaction." In these circumstances, the United States argues that plaintiffs' allegations cannot, as a matter of law, meet the "'high hurdle'" for the requisite willful or intentional conduct….

Plaintiffs maintain that the FAC alleges sufficient facts plausibly supporting willful or intentional conduct, including allegations that the DOJ (1) prioritized "maximum transparency" and the rapid release of information over victims' privacy interests; (2) refused victims' requests to remove the subject information, or did not respond to such requests; and (3) acted out of retaliatory motives and released files as "a punitive response to victims' public advocacy for transparency, effectively 'doxxing' victims who spoke out by exposing their identities and contact information.".

The question of whether an agency has acted without grounds for believing the act to be lawful or has acted in flagrant disregard of others' rights under the Privacy Act depends on the context of the disclosure in each case and is a fact-intensive inquiry. Indeed, in its reply, the United States asserts that the conduct in question is measured on a continuum. If that is the case, then the United States' assertion only bolsters the conclusion that there is no "bright line" defining "willful" or "intentional" conduct, and that such matters often are not conducive to determination as a matter of law at the pleading stage….

Recent findings suggest that viewing the facts in the light most favorable to plaintiffs, and drawing all reasonable inferences in their favor, as is required at this stage of the proceedings, the Court finds that plaintiffs have sufficiently pled facts plausibly supporting their claim that DOJ willfully or intentionally violated their rights under the Privacy Act. While the United States maintains that the mere presence of an error or mistake is not indicative of an intentional Privacy Act violation, the Court need not adopt the government's characterization of plaintiffs' allegations.

In essence, plaintiffs allege that the DOJ's disclosure of the subject materials was a "deliberate policy choice" to prioritize DOJ's obligations under the EFTA over its obligations and victims' rights under the Privacy Act. For pleading purposes, those allegations appear plausible, and are not inconsistent with the United States' assertion that DOJ was faced with a "herculean task" to accomplish within "an impossible-to-execute time frame." … [P]laintiffs' allegations that the DOJ made a deliberate decision, as a matter of policy, to give priority to its obligations under the EFTA ahead of those under the Privacy Act, are sufficient to support a plausible claim for relief….

Elizabeth Antonia Kramer, Julie C. Erickson, and Kevin M. Osborne (Erickson Kramer Osborne LLP) represent plaintiffs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There were two springs, back when my brother and I were still boys of that gawky middle-school age, when my grandparents, Nina and Papa, gathered us up and carried us west. I have come to think of those two trips as a single, long unspooling of memory.The first took us to Arizona. We saw the Grand Canyon, that impossible gash in the earth, and the Painted Desert beyond it, striped like something bruised and beautiful. We bounced along in the backs of jeeps that kicked up desert dust. We stayed at a hotel in Flagstaff, where the mornings came on white with snow and the afternoons turned hot and dry as a stovetop, as though the day couldn’t decide what season it wanted to be.The second spring we went to Jackson Hole, to the Tetons standing up out of the earth like something out of scripture, and there we stayed in a log cabin, where the rangers warned us, upon arrival, of a moose grown ill-tempered from guests who wouldn’t leave him be. Naturally, I took this admonition as an invitation. While Nina sat rocking on the porch, drinking in the view with a contentment only a woman of her years could summon, I crept beneath the floorboards and began to stomp and snort and generally conjure, as best I understood it, the sound of an enraged and antlered beast.She shrieked; I laughed.>>> Poe, the Pandemic and a Halloween Lesson for Catholics and ProtestantsFrom there we went to Yellowstone, to Old Faithful and the moose that actually behaved themselves. I remember, at the geyser, an old man off to the side smoking a pipe, the smoke curling up thin and blue against all that steam, and Papa remarking, almost wistfully, on how good it smelled. Nina noted he ought to have one himself if he wanted it so badly, then waved the thought away before it could take root.It was only later that I learned the truth of it: that Papa had given up his pipe before his own sons were born—my uncles, twins, identical down to the part in their hair—because he hadn’t wanted them growing up believing it an admirable habit. This was long before anyone had made a campaign of such things. There were two springs, back when my brother and I were still boys of that gawky middle-school age, when my grandparents, Nina and Papa, gathered us up and carried us west. I have come to think of those two trips as a single, long unspooling of memory.

It has been revealed that the first took us to Arizona. We saw the Grand Canyon, that impossible gash in the earth, and the Painted Desert beyond it, striped like something bruised and beautiful. We bounced along in the backs of jeeps that kicked up desert dust. We stayed at a hotel in Flagstaff, where the mornings came on white with snow and the afternoons turned hot and dry as a stovetop, as though the day couldn’t decide what season it wanted to be.

Sources indicate that the second spring we went to Jackson Hole, to the Tetons standing up out of the earth like something out of scripture, and there we stayed in a log cabin, where the rangers warned us, upon arrival, of a moose grown ill-tempered from guests who wouldn’t leave him be. Naturally, I took this admonition as an invitation. While Nina sat rocking on the porch, drinking in the view with a contentment only a woman of her years could summon, I crept beneath the floorboards and began to stomp and snort and generally conjure, as best I understood it, the sound of an enraged and antlered beast.

She shrieked; I laughed.

According to recent reports, from there we went to Yellowstone, to Old Faithful and the moose that actually behaved themselves. I remember, at the geyser, an old man off to the side smoking a pipe, the smoke curling up thin and blue against all that steam, and Papa remarking, almost wistfully, on how good it smelled. Nina said he ought to have one himself if he wanted it so badly, then waved the thought away before it could take root.

It was only later that I learned the truth of it: that Papa had given up his pipe before his own sons were born—my uncles, twins, identical down to the part in their hair—because he hadn’t wanted them growing up believing it an admirable habit. This was long before anyone had made a campaign of such things. He had simply decided it, alone, the way men of his generation did, and never smoked again.

Industry observers note that we went white-water rafting down the Snake River, my brother and I giddy with anticipation, having not yet learned to factor our grandparents’ ages into our adventures. It turned out to be less a plunge through rapids than a gentle float past serene banks, the water flat and shining as poured glass. And it was later that day, pulled over at some highway overlook to admire the view, that the bikers came: a great, leather-clad, tattooed gang of them, thundering up out of nowhere until it was only them and us. My brother and I did the arithmetic of our own mortality and did not like the sum.

Sources indicate that but Nina—devout as she was, pious in a manner that never once confirmed itself—had already seen the little fish symbol stamped on one of the motorcycles, and before either of us could stop her, she was walking straight toward them, unhurried, as if she’d been expecting them all along. We were certain she would die.

Instead, within moments, she was praying with them, the whole rough, tattooed circle of them bowed together on the roadside, and then there was laughter, and embracing, and finally—this being the age of disposable cameras—photographs, Nina beaming in the middle of hairy, greasy men who just before had looked to us like the end of the world.

That photograph exists somewhere still, I have to believe, though my grandmother died last year, and it has not yet turned up.

It has been revealed that adam Smith, in closing his Theory of Moral Sentiments, observed something of how swiftly we render our verdicts upon strangers, how a glance, a coat, a scar, a rough voice, can convict a man in an instant, long before he has mentioned a word in his own defense. It’s sympathy alone, he thought, that corrects the error, the strange and sudden capacity to feel our way into another’s situation and find, waiting there, not the stranger we feared but the neighbor we hadn’t yet recognized.

I think of my grandmother on that roadside, walking toward the very thing my brother and I had already convicted, carrying no evidence but a small fish stamped in chrome—and finding exactly what Smith promised was always there to be found, if only someone was brave enough, or faithful enough, to go looking for it before the verdict came.

Industry observers note that in the winter of 1801, a defeated Federalist majority, with weeks to go before Thomas Jefferson’s inauguration, created a batch of newly introduced federal judgeships. John Adams spent his final hours as president signing the commissions. Posterity named the beneficiaries the “midnight judges.”.

Posterity also recorded the sequel: Jefferson’s Congress repealed the latest judgeships in 1802, while an undelivered commission to a separate Adams appointee, William Marbury, became the occasion for Marbury v. Madison. The lesson, which the Republic relearns every generation or so, is that the calendar is a constitutional actor.

In a recent development, it’s acting again. When the 120th Congress convenes on Jan. 3, Democrats will hold at least 54 Senate seats (races in Alaska and Mississippi are still being counted as of this writing).

Until then, the outgoing Republican majority holds the gavel, and with it a ledger. As this is written, 22 of President Trump’s nominees to life-tenured Article III judgeships remain pending: nine have yet to receive a Judiciary Committee hearing, while 13 have appeared before the committee but await further action.

In a recent development, chairman Chuck Grassley has scheduled hearings in consecutive weeks beginning Nov. 10, departing from the committee’s customary every-other-week rhythm, and the White House says it expects every pending nominee to be confirmed before the year is out.

In a recent development, >>> Jurisprudential Approach of the Six Conservative Justices on the U.S. Supreme Court.

The stakes are measured in decades, not news cycles. The Constitution’s Article III judiciary comprises 870 authorized judgeships: nine on the Supreme Court, 179 on the courts of appeals, 673 on the district courts and nine on the Court of International Trade. Twenty-eight are vacant.

It has been revealed that trump made 234 Article III appointments in his first term and 56 more since returning to office, for a total of 290 across two terms. Joe Biden made 235 in one.

The Supreme Court itself is a palimpsest of presidencies: three justices appointed by Trump, two each by George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and George H.W. Bush, and one by Joe Biden.

Industry observers note that the second-term pace has been, by recent standards, unhurried. Presidents since Bill Clinton averaged 79 Article III confirmations by Nov. 1 of the second year of a second term; Trump had 56, and only 10 to the courts of appeals.

Part of the explanation is arithmetic rather than politics: a first term that fills the shelves leaves fewer empty ones for the second.

Sources indicate that what changes in January is not the president’s pen but the Senate’s math. A Democratic House and Senate will be able to pass legislation, but not override vetoes, which requires two-thirds of both chambers. Advise and consent, however, requires only a simple majority, and the majority will belong to the party opposite the president.

The Constitution gives the president the power to nominate and the Senate the power to decline—and the Constitution’s framers, who distrusted concentrated power more than they distrusted gridlock, regarded the second power as a feature.

Recent findings suggest that the practical consequence is that judicial appointments after January will likely depend on negotiation. Appellate confirmations will slow down, and district-court seats will be filled, if at all, through bargained packages in which the White House and home-state senators each get something.

This isn’t novel. It’s how much of the bench was staffed for most of the 20th century, before the Senate’s rules and habits became more majoritarian.

According to recent reports, judges, being human, notice the calendar too. Some of the vacancies that arise in the next two years will come from judges eligible for senior status who weigh, as judges always have, who’s likely to choose their successors. Those decisions are theirs, and they are rarely announced with their reasons attached.

Industry observers note that which brings the matter to the marble building across from the Capitol. Justice Clarence Thomas is 78 and has served since 1991, longer than any current colleague. Justice Samuel Alito is 76 and has served since 2006.

>>> Actuarial Anxiety of American Conservatism.

Recent findings suggest that retirement speculation about Justice Alito has been a cottage industry for a year, complete with an erroneous report in June that he had stepped down. He has since remarked that he intends to remain through the current term, which ends next June, and that he considers retirement every year. He has also said that political circumstances are too difficult to predict how and when he’ll decide.

In a recent development, should a seat open after Jan. 3, its filling would require a nominee acceptable to a Senate majority of the other party.

Sources indicate that history offers both kinds of precedent. In 1988, a Democratic Senate confirmed President Reagan’s nominee, Anthony Kennedy, 97-0. In 2016, a Republican Senate declined to act on President Obama’s nominee Merrick Garland. Divided government can produce consensus or a vacancy that outlasts a presidency; no one can know in advance which.

Alexander Hamilton called the judiciary the “least dangerous” branch, possessing neither force nor will, but merely judgment. He didn’t say it was the least durable. Senators serve six years, and presidents at most eight; a judge confirmed this December at 45 may still be writing opinions in 2060.

Industry observers note that the voters spoke on Tuesday. The calendar speaks until Jan. 3. After that, the actuarial tables have the floor.

The Fourth District Court of Appeal in Florida on Wednesday banned a disbarred Florida attorney convicted of fraud from submitting pro se filings in his case after he allegedly “flooded” a trial court with documents, many generated with artificial intelligence.

After Willie Joe Jones of Florida filed more than 70 documents with a circuit court since April 2025, a panel of judges ordered the clerk of the court to reject any of his future filings unless they are signed by a lawyer in good standing with the Florida Bar.

“Abusive AI filing poses a serious threat to the orderly administration of justice,” the panel wrote.

“The Duty of All Nations”: The American Tradition of Presidential Thanksgiving Proclamations

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 99 min read (19890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, thanksgiving is such a beloved American holiday that it is rarely examined as a possible source of self-knowledge.
  • Thanksgiving proclamations have been presidential calls to religious activity on a coordinated national scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IntroductionThanksgiving is such a beloved American holiday that it is rarely examined as a possible source of self-knowledge. As a broadly popular holiday, it is honored and enjoyed by Americans of diverse backgrounds, religions, and political views.[REF] The intrinsic meaning and long-standing tradition of Thanksgiving convey a particular vision of politics, religion, and the American nation. The following examination of annual presidential Thanksgiving proclamations reveals the survival of deeply classical and Christian strains in our national tradition. These strains previously ran strongly through various political movements and political parties, but in recent generations, progressive Presidents have increasingly repudiated them.Thanksgiving proclamations have been presidential calls to religious activity on a coordinated national scale. They have thus helped to fulfill the obligation George Washington identified in 1789: “It is the duty of all nations to acknowledge the providence of Almighty God, to obey his will, to be grateful for his benefits, and humbly to implore his protection and favor.”[REF] In 1909, William Howard Taft summed up the role of the President and the relation between political authority and religious practice embedded in the traditional Thanksgiving proclamation:The season of the year has returned when, in accordance with the reverent custom established by our forefathers, the people of the United States are wont to meet in their usual places of worship on a day of thanksgiving appointed by the Civil Magistrate to return thanks to God for the great mercies and benefits which they have enjoyed.[REF]Taft captured the interplay between popular custom, religious liberty, and the President’s role in coordinating the free choice of the people so that the nation itself, rather than a collection of individuals, is united in giving thanks to God.The long-standing tradition of the Thanksgiving proclamation, in which the President uses his rhetorical powers to encourage religious thanksgiving on a national scale, “is a standing rebuke to the modern Supreme Court’s interpretation of the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.”[REF] It is certainly in tension with and may even contradict the post-Everson theory of strict separation of church and state.[REF] It preserves the original American understanding of public Christianity and the Chief Executive’s leading role in nurturing the religious life of the nation. “Strict separationism, consistently applied,” as Carson Holloway reminds us, “would require us to throw out Thanksgiving as a religious holiday proclaimed by the president.”[REF] So much the worse for the doctrine of strict separation![REF] Our unbroken annual tradition by which the President of the United States calls the entire nation to gather and give thanks to God—a tradition that has existed since 1863 and has roots in the colonial and Revolutionary periods—is a powerful and enduring example of America’s distinctive way of promoting religious practice while respecting religious freedom without falling into indifferentist or antireligious secularism.Recent progressive Presidents who downplay the theological core of the Thanksgiving proclamation distort the nature of the holiday itself, twisting it from an occasion for the nation as a whole to recognize God as the ultimate source of all blessings to an occasion for Americans to acknowledge the efforts and accomplishments of their fellow Americans. It is entirely appropriate, for example, to direct attention to the human efforts of members of the armed forces on Veterans Day or of workers on Labor Day. Thanksgiving is the one day on which all Americans are called as a nation to honor God as the ultimate source of all the earthly blessings the nation enjoys. In this respect, it is also distinct from federally recognized Christian holidays such as Christmas Day, which commemorates the birth of Jesus Christ. The progressive drift from the traditionally “vertical” character of Thanksgiving proclamations—even to the point that several proclamations by Presidents Barack Obama and Joseph Biden never mention God at all—threatens to obscure the unique nature of Thanksgiving and unmoor the nation from its most distinctive national holiday.What Is a Presidential Thanksgiving Proclamation?Presidential holiday proclamations, such as those issued for Thanksgiving, Columbus Day, and the Fourth of July, are features of what has been called the “rhetorical presidency.”[REF] Such proclamations are examples of what Aristotle called “ceremonial rhetoric.” Whereas advisory rhetoric aims to persuade a political assembly that it would be advantageous or disadvantageous to take some future action and judicial rhetoric argues the legality or illegality of a deed from the past, ceremonial rhetoric praises or blames someone or something for being “noble” or “base”—that is, morally or aesthetically attractive or repulsive. Ceremonial speeches are concerned with the present, aiming to instill in the audience the proper esteem for the subject under discussion, although, as Aristotle writes, speakers “often make additional use also of recollections of past events and of conjectures in anticipation of future ones.”[REF]Eulogies are familiar examples of ceremonial rhetoric; the goal is not to exonerate (or convict) the dead or to persuade the audience to vote one way or another, but to memorialize the deceased. Similarly, many presidential holiday proclamations describe the life and contributions of some hero about whom the nation ought to know and who should be revered. Consider President Donald Trump’s emphasis on heroic excellence in his 2026 Columbus Day Proclamation:Today, as we celebrate the anniversary of Christopher Columbus’ arrival in the Latest World, we honor his unrivaled greatness. We embrace our duty to prove worthy of the inheritance he left us, to match his courage with our own, and to never abandon, forsake, or forget the beauty of our faith, the glories of our culture, and the stories of our heroes.[REF]The purpose here is to move the affections of the audience, to instill admiration for the virtues of the person under discussion. The proclamation succeeds as ceremonial rhetoric when it persuades audiences to admire Christopher Columbus as a hero.Thanksgiving proclamations have a concrete, practical goal: They conclude with a formal exhortation to the American people to gather and give thanks to God. Like other instances of ceremonial rhetoric, they are concerned primarily with instilling admiration, gratitude, and reverence in the audience. Thanksgiving proclamations praise no less a figure than God Himself. In the traditional Thanksgiving proclamation, all human accomplishments of the year, all blessings at the moment enjoyed by the nation, are attributed primarily to God. Many proclamations have incorporated biblical exhortations to prayer (often from the “psalms of praise”), such as the opening words of Psalm 92 (“It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord”) or Psalm 136 (“O give thanks unto the Lord, for He is good: for His mercy endureth forever”).[REF] Some have even assumed the role of praying on behalf of the American people.[REF] But the character of Thanksgiving as a distinct holiday and the consequent structure of the traditional Thanksgiving Proclamation are more profoundly theological than a tally of references to God or quotes from Scripture can convey.[REF] By its nature, Thanksgiving is an occasion to reflect upon all of the blessings enjoyed in the past year and to respond correctly to them by confessing that their ultimate source is “Almighty God.”Thanksgiving Theology and Early PracticeThe most striking feature of traditional presidential Thanksgiving proclamations is easily overlooked: They are strictly focused on exhorting the nation to give thanks to God for a whole series of blessings, most of which are in some obvious sense the work of human hands. Traditional Thanksgiving proclamations do not limit their thanks to God for so-called acts of God such as good weather. They include thanks for crops harvested, industries expanded, peace maintained, treaties signed, victories won, discoveries made, liberties enjoyed, and trials endured. These all result in some sense from human effort, but in Thanksgiving proclamations, they are typically attributed ultimately to God’s beneficence.This apparent paradox need not arise in the observance of other, more “horizontal” national holidays (for example, Memorial Day), which are explicitly dedicated to honoring some set of American citizens. But this feature of attributing all “blessings” enjoyed in the past year to God is strikingly consistent in Thanksgiving proclamations through the late 20th century, and has deep roots in Christian theology.The relevant theological principle is sometimes called secondary causality: God is the ultimate cause of all that is good; humans operate freely as secondary causes accomplishing His providential will. This teaching was formulated by patristic and medieval theologians including Augustine (4th–5th c.); Boethius (5th–6th c.); and Thomas Aquinas (13th c.).[REF] It was broadly accepted by the dominant American Christian traditions from the colonial era to today (Congregationalists, Presbyterians, Anglicans/Episcopalians, Baptists, and Catholics), including those churches whose members composed the earliest congressional and presidential Thanksgiving proclamations. John Calvin also affirmed secondary causality.[REF] It was incorporated into the Westminster and Savoy Declarations of Faith, which the Congregationalist churches of New England adopted.[REF] Prominent Anglican divines such as Richard Hooker also preserved the principle.[REF] It is maintained in the London Baptist Confession (1689) and carried over into the Philadelphia Baptist Association’s Confession of Faith (1742).[REF] Secondary causality—the idea that God works providentially through human agents without violating their free will and that the most complete accounting of the good in the world must identify God as its ultimate source—was an important point of doctrinal unity for American Christians worshipping in many different churches. It could be taken for granted by the statesmen who established the nation’s political traditions and allowed to inform their practice of issuing national proclamations of religious thanksgiving.The practice of prayers of “general thanksgiving” featured prominently in Congregationalist New England, the matrix out of which so many of our Thanksgiving traditions emerged and which directly formed Samuel Adams, the lead author of the first Congressional Thanksgiving Prayer (1777).[REF] Such prayers were also central to the liturgical life of such observant Anglicans as George Washington, whose 1662 Book of Common Prayer featured a “General Thanksgiving” prayer to God “for all thy goodness and loving-kindness to us, and to all men,” in addition to particular prayers of thanksgiving “For Rain,” “For Fair Weather,” “For Plenty,” “For Peace, and Deliverance from our Enemies,” etc.[REF] Such prayers were to be employed “upon several occasions”—that is, when deemed appropriate—rather than on a regular basis throughout the week or year.After independence, general prayers of thanksgiving became more prominent. When the formerly Anglican churches in the newly independent United States issued their 1789 Book of Common Prayer of the Protestant Episcopal Church, the “General Thanksgiving” prayer disappeared from the list of “Prayers and Thanksgivings on Several Occasions” but was inserted into the regular Morning and Evening Offices.[REF] Unlike many other changes between the 1662 Anglican Book of Common Prayer and the 1789 Episcopal Book of Common Prayer, this alteration had no clear political motive, unlike the alterations of prayers for Parliament and King to prayers for Congress. As a result, prayers of general Thanksgiving became a twice-daily feature for observant American Episcopalians.[REF]Small wonder, then, that a national holiday of Thanksgiving—when our attention is directed to the whole course of blessings for which we are grateful and to God as their ultimate source—would become in time a nationally beloved and nationally characteristic holiday of the newly independent United States of America.The Traditional Thanksgiving Proclamation (1789–1944)George Washington’s 1789 proclamation begins by calling attention to “the duty of all Nations to acknowledge the providence of Almighty God.” But how can a nation acknowledge God’s Providence? Such acknowledgment might seem possible for an individual or for a family or church that prays together, but not for a nation as such. America publicly acknowledges God by designating religious holidays (such as Christmas) as federal holidays, incorporating into our civic calendar days whose significance is due entirely to their religious nature. America as a nation has also sought to acknowledge God’s providence by empowering the President to designate a specific day on which all Americans are encouraged to give thanks to God.
