Veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service. It is also a reminder that freedom depends on citizens willing to serve something larger than themselves—and not just when they are in uniform.

Our service members do much more than most of us realize, and our society is the better for it.

It has been revealed that across generations, American veterans have answered the nation’s call in war and peace out of a commitment to duty, sacrifice and country. Their example demonstrates that citizenship carries responsibilities as well as rights, and that self-government endures only when citizens place the common good above personal interest.

Sources indicate that the freedoms that Americans enjoy today were secured by all veterans who served. They defended not merely our borders but also the principles upon which this nation was founded: liberty, representative government and the rule of law.

Sources indicate that by defending the constitutional order, veterans helped preserve a nation in which political differences are settled through lawful debate and elections rather than force. Veterans Day is an opportunity to recognize the men and women whose sacrifices have made that peaceful self-government possible.

>>> The Three Values That Are the Real Keys to America’s Greatness.

In a recent development, veterans have helped secure liberty against some of the most oppressive ideologies in human history, including communism and national socialism. American veterans were instrumental in defeating the Nazi regime during World War II, helping liberate Europe from a government built on tyranny, aggression and the systematic denial of human freedom.

During the Cold War, generations of American servicemen and women stood watch against the expansion of Soviet communism, preserving the security of the free world through deterrence and steadfast resolve. Their service helped create the conditions that led to the collapse of the Soviet Union and the liberation of millions of people in Central and Eastern Europe.

The freedom enjoyed today by nations once trapped behind the Iron Curtain is part of the legacy of those veterans who answered their country’s call.

Across these conflicts, American veterans served as guardians of the principle that free people have the right to govern themselves. Veterans Day also reminds us that liberty is never self-executing. The constitutional freedoms secured through military sacrifice endure only when citizens practice the discipline, responsibility and respect for law that self-government requires.

The veteran’s example therefore reaches beyond the battlefield, offering a model for preserving freedom in civic life.

Industry observers note that veterans also participate in freedom’s defense at home at some of the highest rates in American society. According to the 2025 Veterans Civic Health Index, 81% of veterans were registered to vote in the 2024 election, compared with 74% of nonveterans. Seventy-three percent of veterans cast ballots, compared with 66% of nonveterans.

Industry observers note that the index also reports stronger veteran participation in volunteering, in civic organizations and in engagement with public officials and community institutions. Together, these measures point to a broader pattern: For many veterans, military service becomes a lifelong commitment to citizenship, civic responsibility and the preservation of our constitutional republic.

Industry observers note that veterans continue to serve as teachers, business leaders, first responders, elected officials and civic volunteers, bringing military habits of integrity, discipline and teamwork into civilian life. At Military.com, Medal of Honor recipient Clint Romesha captures that enduring impulse, saying, “So many of us veterans just want to continue to serve after service.”.

Mr. Romesha identifies teamwork as one of the military’s greatest lessons—“It’s not about me; it’s about the team”—and as a principle that continues to guide veterans long after they leave the uniform behind.

The veteran profiles of “American Heroes: Stories of Service” and “Pledge to Patriots” show this continuing commitment in action. These stories feature veterans mentoring young people, supporting one another, leading nonprofits, responding to disasters and strengthening communities.

>>> Nina and the Bikers.

It has been revealed that thousands of veterans serve as poll workers, election officials and observers, helping to administer and safeguard elections. As a former election official and U.S. Navy veteran, I have seen them step forward when communities need poll workers. Through the nonpartisan Vet the Vote initiative, more than 163,000 veterans and military family members served as poll workers during the 2024 election cycle, up from approximately 63,500 during the 2022 midterms.

Recent findings suggest that national Guard members have supported election operations, security, coordination and emergency response at the request of state authorities. Their commitment to duty, adherence to procedures and record of public service can strengthen confidence in the electoral process they defended in uniform.

On Veterans Day, we honor those who wore the uniform in defense of our nation. We should also follow the example they continue to set—as citizens, poll workers, community leaders and public servants—reminding us that freedoms secured on far-off battlefields must be preserved through faithful participation in self-government at home.

Veterans Day recognizes a profound commitment to country, but it also challenges every American to accept the duties of citizenship.

Education policymakers around the world often overlook a simple formula: To increase educational opportunity, increase economic development.

Recent findings suggest that but to improve development, a country needs the institutions that promote it. That’s why nations that want to help more children succeed should pursue economic freedom.

Recent findings suggest that the latest Economic Freedom of the World report from the Fraser Institute tells the story clearly. The highest-ranked 25% of countries for economic freedom dramatically outperform the lowest-ranked 25%. Incomes are seven times greater, while people work six fewer hours per week. People live 14 years longer. Fewer children die in infancy, and environments are cleaner.

Economic freedom translates into education and economic opportunity. Fewer students in developing nations will drop out in middle school to go to work. More families will be able to afford transportation to school. There will be more opportunities for graduates to get more productive, higher-paying jobs.

>>> Latin America Shifts Toward Market-Oriented Conservatism.

Industry observers note that take, for instance, Kurdistan in Iraq, which is focusing more on education now. Iraq ranks 159 out of 165 countries for its legal system and property rights, 152 for size of government, 141 for sound money, 149 for regulation of the economy, and 129 for freedom to trade internationally.

Imagine how many more students in Kurdistan could finish school with a great education if incomes were seven times higher. Imagine the hard trade-offs today that would not be necessary if Iraq were richer.

In a recent development, this point holds worldwide. What would best help a country’s children receive a strong education in the long run? Focus first of all on the country’s economic and legal institutions.

In a recent development, education is about making plans for society’s future. That means a small government with reliable courts, sound money, secure property rights, and free competition.

It has been revealed that economic development doesn’t automatically mean more government funding for government schools. In many countries, it can mean trusting families with education dollars to choose what is best for their own children.

Industry observers note that indeed, parents are a great education resource. They are the first line of influence to keep their children on track for success, and you don’t even have to pay them a salary.

Recent findings suggest that governments can do more to consider how to empower parents and teachers. Families know their own children the best. Teachers know their own students as individuals far better than a national government or the United Nations or UNICEF could ever know them.

Using international aid to push an ideological agenda is the wrong policy. Education policy choices should emphasize local knowledge rather than national and international one-size-fits-all, top-down impositions.

>>> Stablecoins Strengthen the Dollar and Empower the Developing World.

Educators also should teach economic and financial literacy. The scientific evidence is decisive that socialism fails and market economies succeed. We mark Nov. 7 each year as Victims of Communism Day in the United States by remembering the more than 100 million people who died of starvation or were killed under communist and socialist regimes in the 20th century.

On an individual level, each student should be taught the basics of economics and entrepreneurship. These lessons include the fundamentals of human action and incentives, supply and demand, and the invisible hand of Adam Smith. This also includes learning how to be alert to opportunities to create value for others in society while improving one’s own life.

In a recent development, this education means respecting and admiring entrepreneurs. Students should understand why people should be allowed to keep the fruit of their own labor. Students also should understand the value of building capital rather than consumption if they want to prosper.

To prepare students for employment and participation in society, teach economics and inspire entrepreneurship and an entrepreneurial mindset. Then the next generation will better understand the institutional reforms needed to help their country thrive.

In a recent development, given the results of the latest U.S. election, now that latest policymakers with socialist leanings (and actual socialists) will govern in states such as Michigan, New York, California, and elsewhere starting next year, this advice is not just for other countries. It’s also for us. Will we listen?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits. (Photo by Userba011d64_201/Getty Images).

New research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.

According to the report, which was released by the university’s researchers Thursday, more than a third of civil suits filed in Santa Clara County, California, and San Francisco County this year show signs of AI use. The researchers noted that this doesn’t include debt collection cases.

Among other findings, Stanford’s researchers noted that pro se litigants had higher AI adoption rates. In Santa Clara County, the share of self-represented complaints that highlighted signs of AI use increased from 19% in 2024 to 72% in 2026. Meanwhile, the share of attorney-filed complaints increased from 5% to 34% during this period.

Researchers also found that the use of AI varies by case type, with employment and business complaints in California showing the highest rates. They said AI use also varies throughout court filings, with more appearances in the statement of facts and causes of actions sections.

“The sharp rise we document here corroborates that AI in the law is a question of how, not whether,” Stanford’s researchers wrote in the report.

The ongoing riots in France have once again brought the world’s attention to large enclaves of Muslim immigrants in and around the country’s overcrowded housing projects. But foreign observers may be surprised to learn how many of the most recent arrivals came in through the tiny Balkan nation of Slovenia, which enabled a mass migration in 2022-2024. According to recent reports, in 2023, I spent four weeks visiting eight of the countries involved in the transit routes to learn why they had come back to life. Recent findings suggest that the Slovenia gap, as I’ll call it, helped flood France with at least 466,000 first-time foreign national asylum and refugee claimants from mostly Muslim-majority nations in 2022-23 alone. A Breach in the Defenses.

According to recent reports, the Balkan routes generally run northwest from Turkey through countries like Greece, Macedonia, Serbia, Bosnia, and Croatia. Migrants know that once they penetrate into the periphery of the E.U., a borderless inter-nation agreement (the Schengen Zone) enables inspection-free travel to rich and desirable interior countries like France.

A decade ago, ISIS fed its terrorist operatives into the migrant flows. They went on to kill and wound hundreds of French and Belgian citizens in 2015 and 2016, while dozens of other border-crossing migrants committed small terror attacks throughout Europe. Because of this mayhem, the E.U.’s external countries buttoned up their borders with stout fences and instant-expulsion policies backed by rigorous patrolling.

In a recent development, E.U. member Hungary started it off in 2015 with an electrified barbed wire double fence, which immediately choked off the main channel through Croatia and Serbia. When migrants diverted west to avoid it, Austria built another, forcing Slovenia to build a razor-wire fence along the border with Croatia to head off further spillover.

By 2016, the Balkan routes were considered effectively closed. It also helped that the E.U. paid Turkey and some proxy North African nations (and violent militias) billions of euros to stop and block emigration from their territories.

So how did another mass migration start in 2022 that would flood France with tens of thousands more?

In June 2022, Slovenian voters threw out the center-right Slovenian Democratic Party that had built that fence. They elected the center-left Freedom Movement and installed Prime Minister Robert Golob, who had campaigned to tear down Slovenia’s fence and immediately set about doing so.

Word spread that a gap in Slovenia’s Balkan route had just opened, so migrants came pouring through it. And there they were, inside the E.U. with no opposition, free to travel to France.

Recent findings suggest that E.U. governments pleaded with Croatia to police the territory. But with no wall and a porous border, Croatia was effectively unable to oblige. Immigrants on the Bosnia side told me they planned to push for the Slovenia gap and go on to France.

On the U.N.’s Camp Lipa in northwest Bosnia, for instance, nine young men from Morocco and Algeria were hardly worried about Croatian police catching them as they prepared for the short trek across Croatia to the Slovenia border.

“No problem!!!” almost everyone shouted, laughing as they turned and disappeared into the dark forest, chanting, “Inshallah! Inshallah!”—if God wills it.

These are powerful lures.

In 2023, immigrants told me they knew France and other destination countries wouldn’t—or couldn’t—deport them. One France-bound Algerian I encountered in northwest Bosnia answered this way when I asked how important the low probability of deportation was to him: “It’s 90 percent important,” he immediately responded. “If you do all the trip and they catch you and deport you, it’s very, very difficult. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At problem in Viramontes (now Khaya) v. Cook County in the Supreme Court is the difference between fully automatic firearms such as the M-16 and semiautomatic rifles including the AR-15 platform. The following are a few excerpts from four amicus briefs establishing that the difference is fundamental.

In a recent development, "But the M16 is capable of burst or fully automatic fire, meaning that a shooter can fire multiple rounds with a single function of the trigger. See Staples, 511 U.S. at 603. Fully automatic firearms 'were never in widespread civilian use' and have 'traditionally been banned' in the United States. Heller II, 670 F.3d at 1287 (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting). The AR-15, by contrast, is a semiautomatic firearm, meaning that it fires only one shot with each function of the trigger. See Cargill, 602 U.S. at 410–411, 416."  U.S. Br. 28.

"Semiautomatic rifles are in common use among law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes. 'The first commercially available semi-automatic rifles * * * entered the market between 1903 and 1906.' Heller II, 670 F.3d at 1287 (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting). Semiautomatic rifles 'have not traditionally been banned,' or even subjected to heavy regulation. Id. at 1269. Instead, they 'traditionally have been widely accepted as lawful possessions.' Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600, 612 (1994)." U.S. Br. 19–20.

Sources indicate that "A semiautomatic firearm fires one bullet for each trigger pull, while an automatic weapon (machine gun) fires continuously until the ammunition supply is exhausted, so long as the shooter presses and holds the trigger. See Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600, 602 n.1 (1994). 'The AR-15 is the civilian version of the military's M-16 rifle, and is…a semiautomatic weapon. The M-16, in contrast, is a selective fire rifle that allows the operator…to choose semiautomatic or automatic fire.' Id. at 603." Ballistic Experts Br. 6.

"Nor is an AR-15 'almost the same gun' as the military's M16 in the critical respect identified by federal law. Bevis, 85 F.4th at 1195. An ordinary AR-15 is semiautomatic: each trigger pull fires one round. A machinegun, by contrast, 'shoots, is designed to shoot, or can be readily restored to shoot, automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger.' 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b). That operational difference—not appearance or lineage—separates an ordinary semiautomatic AR-15 from an automatic machinegun." Cruz Br. 21.

"In 1963, Colt submitted to the predecessor agency of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) two firearms for evaluation: a semiautomatic 'AR-15 Sports Version Rifle' and an 'AR-15 automatic rifle' (later renamed the M16). The agency found that modifications to the automatic version that made it into the Sports Version 'have changed the weapon in basic design to the extent that it is not a "firearm" in the machine gun category' as defined in the National Firearms Act." Second Amendment Law Center Br. 3.

It has been revealed that the amicus briefs in Khaya v. Cook County that best explain the critical distinction between a fully automatic machine gun like an M16 and a semiautomatic AR-15 are these:.

Brief of United States at 19–20, 28–29.

Brief of Ballistic Experts and Second Amendment Law Professors at 6–8.

Brief of Second Amendment Law Center at 3–6.

Brief of Senator Ted Cruz at 21.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The median American read only two books in 2025, and 40% of us read not a single book all year. The French are more literary; they read an average of 18 books a year. They venerate authors—the more intellectual, controversial, and impenetrable the better.But that doesn’t mean authors are beyond criticism in France. The work of Michel Houellebecq, for example, has long been controversial. In 2002, he was charged with inciting racism for calling Islam “the stupidest religion.” Mosques in Paris and Lyon joined with the World Islamic League to bring the charges against him. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that consumers are justifiably angry about persistent inflation, interest rates, and a frozen housing market. High fuel prices were one of the most cited motivations in the midterm election’s exit polls. But politicians can’t address all these factors of the affordability crisis, without understanding one of its largest contributors.The Iran war obviously caused serious disruptions to global energy markets, and the resultant shortfall in supply drove up prices. Even with some oil and natural gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz, the cost to move that product is up dramatically as expenses like insurance have exploded.Since energy affects the price of everything we do and buy, more expensive energy pushes up prices throughout the economy. This occurs not only because of things like higher transportation costs, but also because energy is used to make many products too.Virtually all plastic in our lives is synthesized from either oil or natural gas. This includes countless products from automotive parts to polyester clothing, but also cosmetics to pharmaceuticals. Almost all fertilizer is also made from oil and gas.>>> Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy ShockSince energy is an input for so many products sold to consumers and industry alike, the effects of price changes are far-reaching, though it takes time for consumers to feel the full effect.For example, consumers are only recently experiencing the higher food prices stemming from energy market disruptions that started eight months ago. As farmers paid more for diesel and fertilizer, they began passing those costs on through supply chains via distributors, wholesalers, and grocers.But the cost of the war goes beyond consumer prices, as evidenced by the monthly Treasury statement for October. Spending on national defense last month spiked, hitting $129 billion—up 44.9 percent from September. That was a key contributor to the worst deficit ever for October: $404 billion. And military spending for this fiscal year is projected to exceed $1.1 trillion.All that additional spending and borrowing is adding to the national debt and costing taxpayers, both today and in the future. The cost to service the $41 trillion debt has become genuinely massive. Gross interest on the debt equaled 32.3 percent of all tax receipts in October, a figure projected to worsen.Excessive government spending and borrowing is further fueling inflation, a tax on today’s savers and wage earners that has also robbed more than 30 percent of the dollar’s value since the start of 2020.But the flood of debt issuance has also greatly increased the demand for loanable funds, or savings. That increased demand puts upward pressure on the price for loanable funds, which is the interest rate. The government is borrowing so much money that its crowding out the private sector and increasing interest rates on everything from mortgages to auto loans.>>> Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only TemporaryThat’s a key reason why homeownership affordability, which had improved to a three-year high in February, has fallen each month since the Iran war started as interest rates marched relentlessly higher. Those higher interest rates also stem from inflation expectations rising due to the war’s energy market disruptions.That’s created a deadly combination for the housing market where both home prices and interest rates have risen dramatically in recent years. That one-two punch has made housing unaffordable and cratered home sales.It now takes more than half of the median household’s after-tax income to afford the monthly mortgage payment on a median price home. For families whose budgets are already strapped from high consumer prices, homeownership is simply out of reach.Unfortunately, there’s more pain to come from what’s already working its way through supply chains. According to the producer price index, annual inflation rates hit 16.9 percent for unprocessed products that businesses sold to each other, while processed products hit 14.6 percent. Those price increases will eventually work their way to consumer prices too.To be clear, the affordability crisis started five years ago during the Biden administration, not with the Iran war. But the conflict was fuel on the fire and reversed the good progress made in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration. Solving the problem requires removing its causes, and the war is low-hanging fruit.

Consumers are justifiably angry about persistent inflation, interest rates, and a frozen housing market. High fuel prices were one of the most cited motivations in the midterm election’s exit polls. But politicians can’t address all these factors of the affordability crisis, without understanding one of its largest contributors.

Recent findings suggest that the Iran war obviously caused serious disruptions to global energy markets, and the resultant shortfall in supply drove up prices. Even with some oil and natural gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz, the cost to move that product is up dramatically as expenses like insurance have exploded.

Since energy affects the price of everything we do and buy, more expensive energy pushes up prices throughout the economy. This occurs not only because of things like higher transportation costs, but also because energy is used to make many products too.

Virtually all plastic in our lives is synthesized from either oil or natural gas. This includes countless products from automotive parts to polyester clothing, but also cosmetics to pharmaceuticals. Almost all fertilizer is also made from oil and gas.

>>> Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy Shock.

Since energy is an input for so many products sold to consumers and industry alike, the effects of price changes are far-reaching, though it takes time for consumers to feel the full effect.

For example, consumers are only recently experiencing the higher food prices stemming from energy market disruptions that started eight months ago. As farmers paid more for diesel and fertilizer, they began passing those costs on through supply chains via distributors, wholesalers, and grocers.

But the cost of the war goes beyond consumer prices, as evidenced by the monthly Treasury statement for October. Spending on national defense last month spiked, hitting $129 billion—up 44.9 percent from September. That was a key contributor to the worst deficit ever for October: $404 billion. And military spending for this fiscal year is projected to exceed $1.1 trillion.

It has been revealed that all that additional spending and borrowing is adding to the national debt and costing taxpayers, both today and in the future. The cost to service the $41 trillion debt has become genuinely massive. Gross interest on the debt equaled 32.3 percent of all tax receipts in October, a figure projected to worsen.

Excessive government spending and borrowing is further fueling inflation, a tax on today’s savers and wage earners that has also robbed more than 30 percent of the dollar’s value since the start of 2020.

But the flood of debt issuance has also greatly increased the demand for loanable funds, or savings. That increased demand puts upward pressure on the price for loanable funds, which is the interest rate. The government is borrowing so much money that its crowding out the private sector and increasing interest rates on everything from mortgages to auto loans.

>>> Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only Temporary.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a key reason why homeownership affordability, which had improved to a three-year high in February, has fallen each month since the Iran war started as interest rates marched relentlessly higher. Those higher interest rates also stem from inflation expectations rising due to the war’s energy market disruptions.

It has been revealed that that’s created a deadly combination for the housing market where both home prices and interest rates have risen dramatically in recent years. That one-two punch has made housing unaffordable and cratered home sales.

It now takes more than half of the median household’s after-tax income to afford the monthly mortgage payment on a median price home. For families whose budgets are already strapped from high consumer prices, homeownership is simply out of reach.

Unfortunately, there’s more pain to come from what’s already working its way through supply chains. According to the producer price index, annual inflation rates hit 16.9 percent for unprocessed products that businesses sold to each other, while processed products hit 14.6 percent. Those price increases will eventually work their way to consumer prices too.

To be clear, the affordability crisis started five years ago during the Biden administration, not with the Iran war. But the conflict was fuel on the fire and reversed the good progress made in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration. Solving the problem requires removing its causes, and the war is low-hanging fruit.

Yet the authors of the Latest Jersey bill explicitly admit they took their cue from the United Kingdom, writing that their definitions were “modeled in part after the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG), which is composed of British Parliament Members.”.

The All-Party Parliamentary Group’s 2018 report defining Islamophobia was adopted by several political parties and institutions, despite its potential infringement on free speech.

As our paper made clear, “Britain provides a warning of what happens when a Western state lacks the courage to prevent fully parallel Islamic structures that ultimately compete with, if not displace, civil law.”.

The APPG report was strongly influenced by the Muslim Council of Britain—which, according to another of the papers we published last week, was established and is run by the Muslim Brotherhood.

The Brotherhood, writes French anthropologist Florence Bergeaud-Blackler in that other paper, “has engaged in a century-old project to ‘Islamify modernity’ through gradual, lawful, multisector action” and it is doing so “across Europe, and now across the United States.”.

Which makes CAIR’s involvement with the New Jersey bill all the more attention-grabbing, given its links with the Brotherhood.

>>> Europe Wants To Be the World’s Speech Police.

Founded in Cairo, Egypt, in 1928, the Muslim Brotherhood is a transnational Islamist terrorist group that is banned in its home country as well as others throughout the Middle East.

In 1987, the Brotherhood created as its Palestinian branch the terrorist group Hamas. The Brotherhood also has ties to the Lebanese terrorist group Hezbollah.

How is CAIR tied to the Brotherhood? In 2007, the U.S. Justice Department named CAIR “an unindicted co-conspirator” in the Holy Land Foundation terrorism financing case.

Recent findings suggest that two CAIR co-founders, Omar Ahmad and Nihad Awad, were respectively the president and public relations director of the Islamic Association of Palestine, the public-relations arm of a Palestinian committee founded by the Brotherhood. Another co-founder, Rafeeq Jabar, was IAP president at one point.

All of this would be very difficult to discuss in the Garden State if the bill becomes law. “If this law passes, accusations of Islamophobia could be used to equate any criticism of Islam or Islamism with an attack on Muslims,” Bergeaud-Blackler texted me. “Fear of being accused of Islamophobia could lead journalists, researchers, and anyone who speaks critically about Islam in public debate to censor themselves.”.

Yes, we can expect that A1146, if passed, will face First Amendment challenges in the courts, but these are not sure to succeed.

Recent findings suggest that becoming a teacher is no way to get rich, but becoming the head of a teachers union? That’s a different story.

Take Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, who received $546,158 in total compensation last year, according to the union’s latest financial disclosure.

That’s over seven times the $74,495 average salary earned by public-school teachers nationwide.

And the newly introduced documents, recently filed with the federal Labor Department, show that an AFT president’s cronies can profit handsomely, too.

Outside consultants, a Newly introduced York law firm, a public-relations firm and others appear to have raked in more than $2.2 million from AFT coffers to help Weingarten produce her 2025 book “Why Fascists Fear Teachers”—up from the more than $1.4 million previously estimated by the Freedom Foundation and reported by The Post.

The payments break down across two filings, covering two separate fiscal years.

>>> Randi Weingarten’s Dirty Back-to-School War on Target.

The first, for a one-year period from 2024 to 2025, documented substantial costs connected to the book paid by the AFT—including payments to Weingarten’s literary agent Inkwell Management, to a fact-checker credited in her acknowledgments, and to a photographer for her author’s headshot.

The latest form adds further amounts apparently related to the same project.

On Sept. 25, 2025, nine days after the book’s release, the AFT paid Inkwell Management $28,125 for a “publication expense,” bringing combined payments to the agent across both filings to $92,215.

Separately, the union paid Feldman Strategies, a publicity firm, $202,500; shortly after the pub date, the PR group posted, “It has been a true honor for our entire team at Feldman Strategies to help promote” Weingarten’s book.

The latest filing also records an $80,000 “royalty payment” sent on Oct. 23, 2025, to a limited liability company controlled by Weingarten.

That sum follows a $125,000 royalty payment to the same entity disclosed in the union’s prior annual report, bringing the combined royalty transfers from AFT to the Weingarten-controlled tech giant to $205,000.

And in its 2026 filing, the union paid Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler LLP — the law firm credited in the book with reviewing Weingarten’s manuscript—another $591,174, bringing cumulative legal fees to the firm across both years to nearly $1.6 million.

The union indicates the firm toiled on the book “pro bono,” but the attorneys’ extensive financial ties to the AFT create an obvious incentive to characterize that work as such.

The royalty payments require additional explanation: Public filings show the AFT itself receiving publisher advances connected to the book, then disbursing a portion of those funds as a “royalty payment” to Teachers Want What Kids Need, LLC—an entity controlled by Weingarten.

The publisher did not pay royalties to Weingarten or her LLC directly; the money flowed through the union, in an arrangement that remains opaque.

Weingarten has stated that some of the book’s proceeds would go back to the AFT, the AFT Disaster Relief Fund, and the AFT Educational Foundation.

Even if that claim holds, dues-paying teachers shouldn’t be required to subsidize a book project that profits their union’s president.

In July, the GOP-led House Committee on Education and the Workforce opened a formal inquiry into the matter based on The Post’s initial report, requesting documents on the AFT’s book-related expenditures, contracts and royalty flows.

That inquiry is controlled by the committee majority, however—and once Democrats take control of the House in January, the probe is expected to stall or be closed.

The minority can still request materials and issue reports, but it cannot compel the same level of investigation.

Separately, the Department of Labor’s Inspector General has already opened its own review to probe whether union dues were improperly used for Weingarten’s book project.

That executive-branch inquiry can continue under President Donald Trump’s administration, regardless of which party controls Congress.

>>> Randi Weingarten’s Convention Exposes the Teachers’ Union as a Political Machine.

The latest 2026 filing supplies further evidence that any ongoing review should examine: The additional royalty payment, the fresh publication expense routed to the literary agent, the large PR contract and the further $591,174 to Patterson Belknap all post-date the period covered by the prior report.

Payments to the Weingarten-controlled entity, the literary agent, the PR firm and the consultants raise questions about whether dues money collected from teachers was used for the personal benefit of the union’s top officer.

Federal labor filings exist precisely so that members and the public can review such expenditures.

When these records show repeated transfers linked to an officer’s private project, the disclosures themselves supply the basis for scrutiny.

Teachers who don’t want their hard-earned paychecks to underwrite an officer’s vanity project have a practical alternative.

Organizations such as the Teacher Freedom Alliance offer membership—including free liability insurance—without routing teacher dues to electoral campaigns or left-wing causes.

If enough fed-up teachers leave the AFT, people like Randi Weingarten might think twice about wasting members’ money on personal and political pet projects.

The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.
  • Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.
  • Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I quickly moved into the world of e-discovery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 20, 2026, 10:47 am CST.

Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I quickly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

Satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software company, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each latest matter at the outset?

Industry observers note that chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of new datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material challenges in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or issue. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

Satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every newly introduced tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

In a recent development, ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

Chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our new law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

Recent findings suggest that satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

Sources indicate that chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same plan from the outset.

Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

It has been revealed that satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client claims it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”.

Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati noted earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

Industry observers note that satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

Recent findings suggest that chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely important, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

Satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be said in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

Industry observers note that chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that from Hines v. Stamos, decided yesterday by Judges W. Eugene Davis, Leslie Southwick, and Stuart Kyle Duncan:.

Industry observers note that jill Hines sued Stanford University, Alex Stamos, and others, alleging they conspired with the government to censor her online speech about COVID-19. The district court dismissed her suit without prejudice for lack of subject-matter and personal jurisdiction. Because Hines has not shown that her injury is fairly traceable to Stanford or Stamos, she lacks standing. We therefore AFFIRM without reaching personal jurisdiction….

According to recent reports, this case is closely related to Murthy v. Missouri, which guides our resolution of this appeal. In Murthy, Hines (along with others) sued federal officials and agencies, alleging the government censored her online speech against COVID-19 restrictions in violation of the First Amendment. Here, Hines challenges Defendants' participation in an academic project named the Election Integrity Partnership (EIP). She alleges the EIP and its participants aided the government's scheme to have Facebook suppress her online speech, also in violation of the First Amendment. {Our review is limited to Hines's claims against Stanford and Alex Stamos, the former director of the Stanford Internet Observatory, which was an EIP member.}.

According to recent reports, facebook began moderating COVID-19 content early in the pandemic, deleting or demoting posts it deemed false. In April 2020 alone, it labeled roughly 50 million pieces of content. That same month, Hines launched a grassroots campaign to challenge COVID-19 government restrictions and used Facebook to communicate with her supporters. She was aware of Facebook's moderation and took deliberate measures to circumvent it.

It has been revealed that the EIP, a consortium of researchers and institutions, was formed in July 2020. It sought to identify misinformation about elections and voting. For about three months in 2020, it monitored elections-related content on social media. EIP participants sometimes recommended actions to social-media platforms and logged their communications when they did. In most instances, the platforms took no detectable action on those recommendations….

To have standing, a "plaintiff must have (1) suffered an injury in fact, (2) that is fairly traceable to the challenged conduct of the defendant, and (3) that is likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision." For the claims before us, the second inquiry—traceability of Hines's past injuries—is "the whole ball game." ….

According to recent reports, there is one injury that Hines claims is traceable to Defendants: on September 9, 2020, Facebook removed a post from Hines's page that attached an article entitled Masks Don't Work. At the time, Facebook explained the post went "against our Community Standards." It also reduced distribution of Hines's page on COVID-19 restrictions for "repeated" violations of its standards on "Inauthentic Behavior" and for "repeated sharing of false news." Hines does not dispute that these restrictions fit Facebook's own content moderation….

Hines's traceability theory rests on an inference drawn from timing. On September 8, 2020, the EIP received a massive submission of over 200 webpages and social-media posts from the Democratic National Committee. Among those 200 webpages was a single post by Hines where she encouraged her followers to lobby their representatives to end the COVID-19 public-health emergency. In Hines's view, the one-day timing between the DNC's submission and Facebook's moderation of her page is evidence that EIP participants called Facebook's attention to her single post in the 200-webpage DNC submission.

We are not persuaded by her argument. Discovery revealed no communication between the EIP and Facebook about Hines, and Facebook did not remove or moderate the post that the EIP received. {Hines argues there may be evidence of Defendants' communications with Facebook in undiscovered Slack or Zoom messages. But Stanford produced "communications and other documents" mentioning Hines or her account, and Hines neither challenged that production nor moved to compel additional discovery, although the scheduling order allowed for that. The mere possibility of undiscovered communications that were not sought in the district court is not evidence.}.

Recent findings suggest that A notation in the EIP's records even claims Hines's COVID-19 posts were beyond the scope of the EIP's elections-oriented work. We conclude as a matter of law that timing alone is too attenuated to trace Hines's injury to Defendants.

According to recent reports, murthy also requires us to consider Facebook's own incentives to moderate content. Facebook gave its own reasons for acting when it removed Hines's post and demoted her page, and Hines does not dispute that that moderation aligned with Facebook's COVID-19 policies. We agree with the district court that there's no indication that Facebook, in moderating Hines's post, did anything other than follow its own moderation policy….

I am not at all involved with Stanford's defense of this lawsuit.

Recent findings suggest that elisabeth S. Theodore, John B. Bellinger, III, R. Stanton Jones, and Stephen K. Wirth (Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer, L.L.P.) and James A. Brown (Liskow & Lewis, A.P.L.C.) represent defendants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States has recently made a concerted effort to water down draft resolutions at the United Nations that reference the rights of women and girls, sexual orientation and gender identity, and the International Criminal Court (ICC).

The US efforts at the General Assembly’s Third Committee, which focuses on human rights, highlight the Trump administration’s positioning as an outlier among established democracies as it picks and chooses among universal human rights.

Unlike in the UN Security Council, where the US and the other four permanent members have a veto and the US has successfully struck out language on the ICC, gender, and other topics — no single country can block General Assembly resolutions.

In a recent development, at the Third Committee, the US targeted language in draft resolutions referencing sexual and reproductive rights for women and girls. For resolutions on violence against women and girls and trafficking in women and girls, the US proposed adding “in accordance with national laws” after such references. The proposed amendments reflect the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle internationally protected reproductive rights.

Industry observers note that the US has not been acting alone. Russia proposed deleting an ICC reference from the resolution on trafficking in women and girls. Egypt submitted similar amendments to the resolution on violence against women and girls and sought to remove a reference to “sexual orientation and gender identity” from a resolution on extrajudicial executions.

UN member countries rejected the amendments and adopted the resolutions.

Industry observers note that the US also voted against a resolution supporting human rights defenders because it included references to gender and reproductive rights. It abstained on human rights resolutions it traditionally supports on North Korea, Myanmar, and Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia because of ICC references. Those resolutions also passed.

The Trump administration’s assault on the international human rights system has not been limited to UN resolutions. It has imposed sanctions on ICC judges, prosecutors, nongovernmental groups, a UN human rights expert, and the court itself. It has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick” to prevent investigations of US and Israeli officials.

It’s heartening that these attempts by the US and others to undermine human rights and international accountability have failed so far. But UN member countries need to work together to resist future efforts to weaken human rights norms and international justice.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Sydney) – Australian officials should press the Vietnamese government to release political prisoners and reverse its intensifying repression of human rights during the upcoming 21st Australia-Vietnam Human Rights Dialogue, Human Rights Watch said today. The case of an Australian national Tran Hiep, a democracy and human rights activist, is of particular concern. He has been detained in Vietnam since he was reported missing in Cambodia in September 2026.

Human Rights Watch urged Australia, in a submission to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, to seek clear, concrete, and measurable progress from Vietnam on complications including political prisoners, labor rights, transnational repression, and freedom of religion and belief.

Recent findings suggest that “Since Australia’s last dialogue, Vietnam has sharply intensified human rights abuses both inside and outside the country,” said Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at Human Rights Watch. “Australia needs to make it clear to Vietnam that merely holding another meeting is not itself a measure of progress.”.

In a recent development, vietnamese authorities have stepped up transnational repression, reaching beyond the country’s borders to suppress dissent by targeting human rights activists, government critics, and others in violation of their human rights. In late September, the overseas political organization Viet Tan alleged that Vietnamese police had detained three of its members in Cambodia, including Tran Hiep, and transferred them to Vietnam.

The Vietnamese government right now holds more than 160 political prisoners for exercising their rights to free expression or for peacefully advocating human rights and democracy. Dozens more are detained and awaiting trial. During the first nine months of 2026, Vietnamese courts convicted and sentenced at least 31 activists to lengthy prison terms, including the prominent bloggers Hoang Thi Hong Thai and Huynh Ngoc Tuan. During this period, the police arrested at least 46 other people for criticizing the government.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming dialogue should also focus on Vietnam’s suppression of independent labor organizing. Both Australia and Vietnam are parties to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, which contains provisions obligating Vietnam to carry out reforms and to allow the creation of independent trade unions. However, as Human Rights Watch recently documented, the Vietnamese government has not actually reformed its policies and practices, and prevents workers from forming and operating genuinely independent unions.

It has been revealed that the Australian government should communicate concerns about these violations. It should also outline how Vietnam’s failures to reform will affect Australia-Vietnam relations and implementation of trade and tariff provisions in the partnership.

“The Australia-Vietnam human rights dialogue will accomplish little so long as concrete outcomes aren’t formalized,” Gavshon noted. “A human rights dialogue shouldn’t be a box-ticking exercise but instead a diplomatic exchange with real-world implications.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 20, 2026, 11:10 am CST.

Consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both noted they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that fresh candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock).

The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both remarked they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that newly introduced candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

“Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”.

“A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

“The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s vital to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith said to Law.com.

In a recent development, smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

Sources indicate that “We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith stated. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s crucial to look at their options early.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that my latest essay in Civitas Outlook combines much of my recent thinking about Justice Kagan. She has shifted to different modalities of persuasion over her career on the bench. The latest front is to preemptively blame the Court for destroying democracy and then complain how the Court's legitimacy is being wounded. She is like the arsonist who seeks mercy for burning down her own house. The bigger problem is her predictions are simply wrong. Kagan has some serious crow to eat after the blue tsunami. An entire jurisprudence based on consequentialism fails if the consequences never happen.

Here is the introduction of Justice Kagan Cries Wolf:.

Industry observers note that justice Elena Kagan recently confessed, "I'm much better in print than I am in person." She's right. Through a series of carefully coordinated public appearances, Justice Kagan has attempted to influence how her colleagues vote and how the public perceives the Court. Worse still, Kagan made dire predictions about how the Court has wounded democracy and its own legitimacy. But in short order, the midterm elections refuted her consequentialism. Elena Kagan is the Justice who cries wolf. Justices should speak through their judicial writings, not try to distort the process from the sidelines. . . .

According to recent reports, this sort of consequentialist judging carries a distinct risk: what if the consequences never manifest? In other words, a jurisprudence based on predicting certain outcomes fails if the predictions are wrong. Kagan did not just try to predict the outcome of the midterm election; she proclaimed she could divine the future of our republic. Alas, in short order, Justice Kagan has proven herself to be less Cook Report and more Miss Cleo.

Kagan's point seems to be that ruling against the President who appoints you is proof you're a fair justice. That premise holds only if the law does not support the appointing President's policy. If a Justice simply rules against the President who appoints him, then the Justice is no longer a judge. In his new book So Ordered, Justice Alito chides so-called "insecure originalists" who favor outcomes that yield results they dislike to bolster a reputation of independence. Alito, "Twenty-first-century originalists should shed this insecure mindset." Yet Kagan intentionally feeds into this insecurity.

Justice Kagan, and all Justices, cannot predict the consequences of their decisions. Australia confirmed on November 18 further targeted sanctions on three individuals and four entities involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank. Although these sanctions are a welcome step, they are long overdue and don’t go far enough.

In a recent development, the situation in the West Bank is dire. State-backed settler violence has risen to all-time highs. Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been displaced and 1,394 killed by settlers or soldiers in the West Bank since the start of 2023. The number of illegal Israeli settlements has nearly doubled, including the E1 settlement project, which even Israel’s allies have called a “red line,” and which Israeli ministers openly boast is intended to erase any possibility of a future Palestinian state.

Industry observers note that on the same day as Australia’s announcement, the United Kingdom announced sanctions against eight construction companies and property development firms that have not, until now, been sanctioned by any government. The individuals and companies sanctioned by Australia, however, have previously been sanctioned by the United Kingdom and other states.

When the United Kingdom, France, and Canada confirmed a ban on Israel’s illegal settlements in September, Australia did not join. Instead, at the time, Foreign Minister Wong promised further sanctions to deter illegal settlement, which are the ones just announced.

Israel’s settlements are illegal. In its 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found that all states have an obligation to “take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assist in the maintenance of the illegal situation created by Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.” Banning trade with illegal settlements isn’t optional. It’s required by international law.

In a recent development, australia says it is genuinely committed to upholding international law while continuing to trade with unlawful settlements that rob Palestinians of their land and livelihoods. Recent reporting suggested that the majority of agricultural shipments coming to Australia marked as “products of Israel” are from illegal settlements.

It’s past time for Australia to do everything in its power to stop the expansion of settlements, both through a trade ban and targeted sanctions on construction companies engaged in illegal settlement expansion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since early November, many rural communities in the Catatumbo region, near the Colombia-Venezuela border, have suffered violent abuses and forced displacement as the 33rd Front, a dissident group of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), has clashed with the National Liberation Army (ELN) over control of the territory.

During a field visit from November 9 to 12, Human Rights Watch interviewed community members, representatives of civil society organizations, humanitarian workers, and local authorities, who mentioned these groups have continued to kill civilians, recruit children, plant antipersonnel mines, carry out drone attacks, and impose strict social control over communities.

People told us that on November 8 in Caño Salado, a rural community in Tibú, members of the 33rd Front threatened residents and accused them of collaborating with the ELN. Two community leaders were killed. “They told people to leave, or they would kill anyone who was involved with the ELN,” a civil society member told Human Rights Watch.

Dozens of families have also been displaced from Bocas de San Miguel and El Diamante, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

According to media reports, armed groups have also carried out six attacks using drones armed with explosives in Catatumbo in the first half of November, killing at least five people, including one civilian, and injuring 14 civilians.

The situation in Catatumbo has been critical since early 2025, when Human Rights Watch documented that armed groups killed, assaulted, kidnapped, disappeared civilians and caused the displacement of more than 100,000 people.

In a recent development, according to official announcements, since President De la Espriella took office in August, the government has carried out three airstrikes in Catatumbo, resulting in 10 deaths. The strikes were followed by Colombian army ground operations that resulted in six arrests, and the recovery of two children who had been recruited by armed groups. Community members told us these actions have done little to reduce armed groups’ violence and control over communities.

Recent findings suggest that the government should urgently protect civilians, by ensuring that its security strategy goes beyond military operations. It should include effective law enforcement and criminal prosecutions, a stronger humanitarian response, support for affected communities, and targeted social and economic policies to reduce the high levels of poverty that fuel the strength of armed groups in the region.
