    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that from today's decision by Judge Loren Alikhan (D.D.C.) in ABC, Inc.
    • Plaintiffs assert that Defendants violated their First Amendment rights by designating their broadcast licenses for early renewal as retaliation for Plaintiffs' broadcasting unfavorable speech about President Donald J.
    • According to recent reports, because broadcast media requires access to radio spectrum to operate, and because radio spectrum is a finite public resource, the FCC is responsible for granting and renewing broadcast licenses….
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that from today's decision by Judge Loren Alikhan (D.D.C.) in ABC, Inc. v. FCC:.

    Plaintiffs assert that Defendants violated their First Amendment rights by designating their broadcast licenses for early renewal as retaliation for Plaintiffs' broadcasting unfavorable speech about President Donald J. Trump and the Republican Party….

    According to recent reports, because broadcast media requires access to radio spectrum to operate, and because radio spectrum is a finite public resource, the FCC is responsible for granting and renewing broadcast licenses…. The FCC may grant an initial license or a license renewal for a term of no more than eight years, and it "ordinarily" grants licenses for eight-year terms, with term dates staggered by the geographic location of each station. "However, if the FCC finds that the public interest, convenience and necessity will be served thereby, it may concern either an initial license or a renewal thereof for a lesser term." ….

    The FCC argued that the ABC licenses were being designated for early review because the FCC was investigating the possibility that Disney and ABC were discriminating in employment for "DEI" reasons. But Judge Alikhan concluded that this was likely a pretext, and the likely real reason for the FCC's action was unconstitutional Administration retaliation against ABC's speech:.

    "Courts have recognized that [] circumstantial evidence, including proximity in time between the protected speech and government's adverse actions, the defendant's expression of hostility to the protected speech, and the absence of a proffered legitimate alternative explanation for the action[,] can support a finding that protected speech caused the agency's response.".

    It has been revealed that here, robust circumstantial evidence strongly supports Plaintiffs' theory of causation. Although Defendants proffer a legitimate alternative explanation, the court does not find that explanation to be credible on the record before the court. Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now. What started in 2020 as questions about how ABC "can keep getting a license" if it "report[s] fake news" has crescendoed into repeated calls for the Commission to strip ABC's broadcast licenses for their editorial decisions.

    Industry observers note that the court counts eleven such calls made by President Trump over the past two years—the most recent being in July 2026. See ECF No. 1 ("When you have a network and you have evening shows, and all they do is hit Trump[,] … I think maybe their license should be taken away. It will be up to [Chairman] Carr."); ECF No. 2-3, at 109-10 ("[T]hey ought to take away [ABC's] license."); id. at 157 ("ABC's license should be TERMINATED."); id. at 166 ("CBS should lose its license, and it should be bid out to the Highest Bidder, as should all other Broadcast Licenses, because they are just as corrupt as CBS—and maybe even WORSE!"); id. at 252 ("I think ABC should lose its license."); id. at 303 ("ABC & NBC FAKE NEWS … SHOULD, ACCORDING TO MANY, HAVE THEIR LICENSES REVOKED BY THE FCC."); id. at 306 ("ABC and NBC FAKE NEWS … should lose their Licenses."); id. at 321 ("[T]he Federal Communications Commission should look into the license of … ABC Fake News."); id. at 340 ("I think the license should be taken away from ABC because your news is so fake and it's so wrong. And we have a great commissioner, the chairman, who should look at that."); ECF No. 2-4, at 13 ("If Network NEWSCASTS, and their Late Night Shows, are almost 100% Negative to President Donald J. Trump, MAGA, and the Republican Party, shouldn't their very valuable Broadcast Licenses be terminated? I say, YES!"); id. at 99 ("ABC fake news ha[s] [] said that [it] would not cover this speech…. Fraud like this should mean a revocation of their licenses.").

    To be sure, President Trump is within his rights "to persuade Americans, including by speaking forcefully or critically, in ways that [he] believes would advance the public interest." Here, however, the President's persistent "rhetoric demonstrates that [he] harbored animosity" toward Plaintiffs because of their protected speech, specifically—to quote the President—their "negative" and "unfair coverage" of him and the Republican Party.

    What is more, Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders. The same week he was tapped to be President Trump's FCC chair, following months of President Trump's calling for "ABC [to] lose its license" for how it covered the presidential campaign, then-Commissioner Carr lauded "license revocation" as a "remedy" to "deter this kind of conduct." Then, early in his tenure as chairman and after committing himself to President Trump's agenda, Chairman Carr ordered the Enforcement Bureau to investigate Disney's employment practices, and soon ordered another investigation into The View.

    In a recent development, when President Trump first called for Mr. Kimmel to be fired—as well as for ABC's license to be "taken away"—Chairman Carr vowed to intervene if Plaintiffs did not "take action on Kimmel." Months later, when President Trump decried Mr. Kimmel's skit about the First Lady, the Commission, at Chairman Carr's behest, initiated early license renewal proceedings the next day. Chairman Carr mentioned of the move, "If you didn't take us seriously, now you should.".

    Industry observers note that most recently, when President Trump touted that Plaintiffs' not broadcasting his address justifies "revocation of their licenses," Chairman Carr announced that the Commission was "looking into" Plaintiffs' decision, and that he expected it to come up during the early license renewal proceedings. This conduct and rhetoric are "powerful evidence of [Defendants'] retaliatory motive.".

    Sources indicate that in response, Defendants point to Chairman Carr's assurances that the Commission "has not singled out any one manufacturer for special treatment," and will remain "open-minded" throughout the early license renewal proceedings. But these assurances fall flat when Chairman Carr is simultaneously making comments that the Commission is "looking into" Plaintiffs' "decision [not] to air" a presidential address as part of the proceedings, especially given that Chairman Carr has mentioned that this specific presidential address is "something that broadcasters should be carrying.".

    Recent findings suggest that turning to temporal proximity, against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr's call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel's skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings. Indeed, in the wake of Mr. Kimmel's September 2025 comments about President Trump and his supporters, Chairman Carr stated, "We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.".

    According to recent reports, chairman Carr made this promise at the same time that President Trump said of the situation: "When you have a network and you have evening indicates, and all they do is hit Trump[,] … I think maybe their license should be taken away. It will be up to [Chairman] Carr." Chairman Carr's "fast-moving" inquest into Plaintiffs' business operations and editorial decisions from the moment he was appointed as chairman and seemingly at the President's direction further "indicates [Defendants'] retaliatory animus." ….

    The court therefore enjoined the FCC from "from taking any continuing or further action against Plaintiffs in relation to the early license renewal proceedings before the Federal Communications Commission, including issuing a Hearing Designation Order;".

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that (Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch said today with the release of the “Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that (Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch said today with the release of the “Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines. Human Rights Watch is a founding member of the campaign and contributed to the report.

    The 200-page report examines global compliance with the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty and the challenges facing the treaty nearly three decades after its adoption. The treaty comprehensively bans antipersonnel mines and commits countries to eliminate stockpiled weapons, clear contaminated land, and assist mine victims and affected communities.

    “At a time when civilian casualties are rising and new technologies make mines easier to deploy, supporting the Mine Ban Treaty is more important than ever,” stated Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “All countries should join the treaty, and members should fully uphold its obligations.”.

    Recent findings suggest that antipersonnel mines continue to kill and maim civilians long after fighting moves elsewhere. Whether they are placed by soldiers on the ground or delivered remotely by weapons systems and drones, the mines contaminate land, roads, and communities for years. Their presence can prevent displaced families from returning home, obstruct humanitarian operations, and undermine efforts to rebuild livelihoods and food production.

    A total of 162 countries are now bound by the Mine Ban Treaty. Three countries joined during the reporting period: Lebanon, Marshall Islands, and Tonga. Five other countries withdrew from the treaty in 2025 and 2026: Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland.

    In a recent development, ukraine confirmed on July 18, 2025, that it would “suspend the operation” of the treaty while engaged in armed conflict with Russia, citing Russia’s extensive use of landmines. Suspensions, however, are unlawful under the treaty, notably during armed conflict, and Ukraine remains fully bound by all the treaty’s obligations. During the reporting period, Ukraine has acquired, produced, and used newly assembled antipersonnel mines, including types that are delivered by drone, in violation of the treaty.

    In addition to Ukraine’s use of antipersonnel mines, states not party to the treaty used them, including Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, and Russia.

    Industry observers note that antipersonnel mines were increasingly used in border conflicts, involving Cambodia and Thailand, Bangladesh and Myanmar, and in Thailand along the borders with Myanmar and Malaysia. Non-state armed groups also used antipersonnel mines, in many cases improvised, in Colombia, India, Myanmar, Pakistan, Sudan, and in locations in Western and Central Africa, including in the Chad Basin, Burkina Faso, and Mali.

    The Landmine Monitor reported that 15 states not party to the treaty either presently produce antipersonnel mines or maintain the option to produce them in the future. Of these, India, Myanmar, Poland, Russia, and South Korea appear to be actively producing or developing antipersonnel mines. Finland, Latvia, and Lithuania—all of which withdrew from the treaty in 2025—have indicated their intent to develop or acquire antipersonnel mines. Non-state armed groups have produced improvised mines that explode due to the presence, proximity, or contact of a person in Colombia, India, Africa’s Sahel region, and sporadically in Thailand.

    According to recent reports, in 2025, casualties from antipersonnel landmines and explosive remnants of war occurred in at least 54 countries and areas. Of these, 39 are party to the Mine Ban Treaty. Myanmar, which is not a party, recorded the highest number of annual casualties (1,891) for the third consecutive year, and Syria recorded 1,602 casualties. Civilians made up at least 84 percent (5,078) of all recorded casualties, while children accounted for 50 percent (1,690) of civilian casualties where the age group was known.

    According to recent reports, even as renewed mine use is contaminating upcoming territory, progress remains possible. Croatia declared completion of its mine clearance obligations in March 2026, following Oman in 2025. Since the Mine Ban Treaty entered into force in 1999, 32 states parties have successfully cleared all known antipersonnel mine contamination from their territory.

    In a recent development, the near elimination of government stockpiles remains one of the treaty’s greatest achievements. Of the 162 states parties, 157 report that they do not possess stockpiled antipersonnel mines. Ninety-four countries have finished destroying their stocks, a total of more than 55 million mines. As during previous reporting periods, Greece and Ukraine continue to possess stockpiles of antipersonnel mines, in violation of article 4 of the treaty.

    Industry observers note that “The world should be moving closer to ending the suffering caused by antipersonnel mines, not witnessing a resurgence in their use,” Coyle noted. “Governments should be seeking global adoption of the ban treaty and reinforcing compliance, not stepping away from one of the world’s most successful humanitarian disarmament treaties.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the “Landmine Monitor 2026” is the 28th annual publication by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, the global coalition of nongovernmental organizations that received the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize. Human Rights Watch co-founded the campaign in 1992 and contributes to its Landmine Monitor reporting initiative.

    In an effort to help overburdened federal courts, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators reintroduced a bill Friday that would add 71 fresh federal judgeships in phases over several presidential administrations.

    Congress last enacted a significant expansion of the federal courts in 1990, according to a story by Law360.

    The federal courts currently have 677 district judgeships and 179 appellate judgeships. Under the bill, judgeships would be added in a number of states, including Arizona, California, Iowa, New Jersey and New York.

    According to recent reports, the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate passed a version of the bill in 2024, but then-President Joe Biden vetoed it during his last few weeks in office.

    EU: Forced Labor Remedies Should Center on Workers

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions noted in a report released today.

    In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

    Industry observers note that “Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” said Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”.

    The groups propose concrete steps for companies to prepare, deliver and assess their remediation obligations. The report comes as the European Union prepares to enforce its Forced Labour Regulation, which will ban products made with forced labor from the EU market across all sectors and stages of production beginning on December 14, 2027. Under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, companies in its scope will also have a legal duty to remedy harm they cause, completely or in part.

    Recent findings suggest that an estimated 17.3 million people were in situations of forced labor in the private economy in 2022, according to global estimates by the International Labour Organization (ILO), Walk Free, and the International Organization for Migration. The number of victims increased by 8 percent between 2016 and 2021. The ILO estimates that forced labor in the private economy generates US$63.9 billion in illegal profits every year.

    Recent findings suggest that academics and experts found that forced labor is rarely only the result of a few bad actors, but is rooted in poverty, discrimination, weak labor protections, and restrictive migration regimes. Migrant workers face heightened risks, including recruitment fees that lead to debt bondage, deceptive recruitment practices, and visas tied to a single employer. Fear of deportation and retaliation often keeps victims from seeking redress.

    The civil society groups said that companies should put in place remediation measures that restore as much as possible the situation for workers if the abuse had not occurred. This would require the cessation of the abuse, restitution, rehabilitation, compensation, apologies, and guarantees of non-repetition. Companies should also ensure that workers and their representatives can identify abuses through grievance mechanisms they trust, define remedies, and assess whether they have been delivered to their satisfaction, the groups said. At all times, affected workers should be protected from retaliation.

    Recent findings suggest that companies should treat remediation as part of their human rights due diligence, not as a one-off response to a scandal, the groups said. Their responsibility should reflect their involvement in failing to prevent or meaningfully address the harm. Companies should not “cut and run” from suppliers when and where labor abuses, including forced labor, is found, as this can leave workers worse off. Instead, the groups said, companies should fairly agree on how to address and share remediation costs.

    Recent findings suggest that to prevent forced labor from occurring and recurring, companies should examine structural causes such as poverty, discrimination and impairments to freedom of association but also how their own purchasing practices may drive it. They should pay to cover the cost of decent working conditions and living wages. The groups point to worker-driven models, such as the Fair Food Program in US agriculture and the Dindigul Agreement in India’s textile sector, as evidence of good practices.

    Recent findings suggest that the EU and its member states should ensure that the competent authorities empowered to enforce the Forced Labour Regulation assess whether effective remediation has actually delivered for workers, including through workers’ own accounts and evidence of compensation paid. They should also ensure that, regardless of their migration status, workers can at least access support, file complaints, and recover unpaid wages.

    According to recent reports, “Workers know best what they have lost and what it will take to rebuild their lives,” de Rengervé remarked. “Companies and EU authorities should listen to affected workers and measure the efficiency of remediation by what workers receive and whether they completely remediate the harm suffered.”.

    #135973. Pakistani Prisoners Face Poor Access to Health Care

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (439 w)

    Pakistani Prisoners Face Poor Access to Health Care

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (439 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.
    • Recent findings suggest that human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care.
    • After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.

    Recent findings suggest that human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care. Many inmates who fall ill in custody fail to receive prompt or decent care at all.

    After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.

    Industry observers note that colonial-era laws have long-enabled Pakistani officials and powerful people to interfere in prison operations, sometimes making use of poor conditions to harass jailed political opponents. In a November 16 letter released by his lawyer, former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed for urgent medical care for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, citing his high blood pressure and her need for eye surgery. Khan’s appeal echoes complaints about medical care in custody from former President Asif Ali Zardari and former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. All have alleged that prison services denied access to medical care as a form of punishment.

    Federal and provincial governments in Pakistan should bring health care in jails and prisons in line with international standards, notably the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Mandela Rules), which require that prisoners receive necessary free medical care to the same standard available in the community, with prompt attention in emergencies. In October, Justice Project Pakistan called for common standards across provinces so prisoners can see medical specialists when needed and continue treatment after release.

    Pakistan’s federal and provincial governments should provide prescribed medicines free of charge and require prisons to record how long patients wait for care. When care requires an urgent hospital transfer, prison authorities should promptly facilitate transport. Authorities should ensure all prisoners, regardless of political affiliation or status, receive timely and adequate medical care, with continuity of treatment.

    #135971. Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3202 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hrw ↗ Open Full Page

    Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • Industry observers note that president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts.
    • It has been revealed that “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch said today. The ICC trial in The Hague against Duterte for crimes against humanity is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.

    Industry observers note that president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts. Families of victims seeking to file latest cases face significant barriers. Meanwhile, government records and human rights group reports show that drug-war abuses continue, with police harassing, arbitrarily arresting, and at times killing suspected drug dealers and owners.

    It has been revealed that “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.”.

    In a recent development, between September and November 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed 13 people, including 7 drug-war victims and their families both under Duterte and Marcos, 4 human rights defenders, and 2 government officials; reviewed recent data and reporting on drug-related killings; and analyzed a database of local government Peace and Order and Public Safety Intends. Human Rights Watch also requested and received information from the Philippine Justice Department and Commission on Human Rights on drug-war cases before the courts.

    Relatives of drug-war victims described a justice system in which the burden of uncovering evidence of an unlawful killing fell mostly on them instead of government prosecutors. “It’s so hard to prove that you’re telling the truth,” mentioned a woman whose husband was killed in 2016 in a police “buy-bust” drug sting operation. “It’s tiring pursuing a case here—it’s as if we can never pass the tests.”.

    In a recent development, some facing obstacles to justice have pinned their hopes on the ICC. “In the Philippines, what was our chance, given how the government works,” mentioned another woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants in 2016. “In the ICC they are impartial, that’s where our hope is.”.

    During the Duterte presidency from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine National Police reported 6,200 deaths during anti-drug operations, although United Nations agencies, the Philippine Commission on Human Rights, the Supreme Court, and domestic human rights groups put the number of killings by police and unidentified assailants at between 20,000 and 30,000.

    Only five cases of Duterte-era “drug war” killings, involving nine police officers, have resulted in convictions. Government prosecutors initiated the first three cases, following the successive murders of three teenage boys in Caloocan in August 2017, which sparked public outrage. The fourth and fifth cases—for killings in 2016—were filed through the efforts of nongovernmental legal groups and led to convictions in 2024 and 2025.

    In November 2024, the Justice Department created a task force to investigate and prosecute extrajudicial killings during Duterte’s “war on drugs” but only four cases it identified have advanced to trial, with three others under preliminary investigation, based on Justice Department data.

    Recent findings suggest that the Marcos administration, after arresting and surrendering Duterte to the ICC in March 2025, confirmed renewed efforts to advance domestic accountability for the “drug war.” But families and human rights groups who met with Justice Department officials said that they were concerned the government’s witness protection program would not keep their families safe if they pursued charges against police officers. Meetings between victims’ groups and the Justice Department tapered off.

    Duterte will stand trial at the ICC for three counts of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder allegedly committed when he was mayor of Davao City, and then president between November 2011 and March 2019. The prosecution’s case focuses on a non-exhaustive list of 56 specific incidents and 87 victims, while noting that “[its] evidence demonstrates that the attack [against a civilian population] was broader than this representative sample of incidents.”.

    The ICC is a court of last resort, only stepping in when domestic authorities are unwilling or unable to investigate and prosecute crimes under its jurisdiction. In November 2021, the Duterte government asked the ICC prosecutor to defer his investigation, opened in September 2021, claiming that national authorities had begun their own drug-war investigations of extrajudicial killings.

    In a recent development, in January 2023, ICC judges ruled that the Philippine government had failed to demonstrate that it took sufficient action to investigate and prosecute Duterte-era killings and authorized the resumption of the ICC prosecutor’s investigation. The decision was upheld on appeal.

    Recent findings suggest that the ICC trial against Duterte begins as the court is under growing pressure from the US government, which has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick.” On October 9, the Trump administration sanctioned the ICC, escalating its attack on the court and adding to existing sanctions on ICC judges and prosecutors, three Palestinian groups, and a UN human rights expert. The Trump administration sanctions reaffirm the ICC’s critical role as a court of last resort, Human Rights Watch remarked.

    Marcos has never repudiated the “war on drugs” as a government policy and has yet to rescind the orders and other policy statements Duterte issued that underpinned the anti-drug campaign. In its review of a database of 2023-2025 local government budgets, Human Rights Watch found that 77 municipalities had allocated funds for anti-drug campaign awards and rewards, or for financial support to informants, police officials, and other local officials. Two of those municipalities, and another eight municipalities specifically referred to “neutralization” or “negation” of suspects; terms used as euphemisms for “killing” in 2016 police circular that set out the “war on drugs.” While such incentives are not necessarily unlawful, those linked to enforcement goals or operational results can create pressure to meet targets and encourage abusive practices, including extrajudicial killings.

    Recent findings suggest that despite a significant decline in drug-related extrajudicial killings during the Marcos administration, such killings and other abuses continue, particularly in low-income urban areas where they remain routine. As of November 7, there have been at least 1,342 public reports of drug-related killings under Marcos, according to the independent monitoring of the Dahas project. These reports identified uniformed officers as responsible for 486 of those deaths.

    Recent findings suggest that the Philippine government’s failure to hold those responsible to account perpetuates a climate of impunity. Families of drug-war victims under the Marcos administration encounter many of the same past obstacles when seeking justice, but the Justice Department has no task force or special mechanism to investigate post-Duterte cases, Human Rights Watch said.

    Industry observers note that “Even if killings are down from the ghastly Duterte years, President Marcos’ pledged ‘bloodless campaign’ against drugs has been anything but bloodless,” Buan said. “To end these abuses, Marcos needs to stop the brutal ‘drug war’ and put in place a robust and impartial law enforcement and judicial system.”Elusive Justice for Killings during Duterte and Marcos Administrations.

    Under the Duterte administration in 2020, the Justice Department opened an inter-agency panel to “reinvestigate” drug-war killings by the police. The panel identified 52 cases in which the Philippine National Police carried out internalinvestigations. However, by 2024, when Marcos was in office, the panel had only filed six cases in court. In November 2024, the Justice Department created a fresh task force on Duterte-era drug war killings. It began investigations anew and worked mainly with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI)—the Justice Department’s investigative arm—instead of with the police to avoid conflicts of interest when developing cases implicating police officers.

    Despite renewed Justice Department efforts, victims’ families still struggled to file charges. Many victims’ families who wanted to pursue charges could not do so because their relative’s death certificate declared an illness as the cause of death, even though they were found with gunshot wounds to their heads and bodies. During the height of Duterte’s “drug war,” police pressured families to sign waivers stating that they did not want to conduct autopsies or pursue charges, in exchange for faster retrievals of the bodies from funeral homes. Many families could not afford the autopsy fees, and without accurate government death records, they could not pursue charges.

    The woman whose husband was killed in a police operation in 2016 decided in 2022 to retrieve documents about his killing from the police because she believed the climate of fear had lifted under Marcos. “They were not really helping us,” she said. “They just left us there to search their logbooks.” Police officials had named the woman’s husband as a drug suspect killed in an “armed encounter” in a news report that featured her children wailing for their dead father. Yet she never found a police report of the operation, only a record of bystanders injured. She was unable to prove he was shot dead, because his death certificate lists the cause of death as pneumonia and his body was cremated. Government investigators have not pursued a case. The woman recalled the one conversation with the Justice Department: “They said, ‘If you have no document like police report or autopsy, it’s hard to file a case.’ So, what about me? I had no documents.”.

    In a recent development, the woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants did not know for years the circumstances under which her husband was killed. She found his body with gunshot wounds at a funeral home in 2016 and signed a waiver not to conduct an autopsy. His death certificate listed pneumonia as cause of death. After Marcos became president, the woman sought help from a nonprofit law group. In 2023, she had her husband’s body exhumed and examined by a forensic pathologist, Raquel Fortun. The autopsy demonstrated that he died from gunshot wounds to the head.

    According to recent reports, that year, she finally found the police report from the night her husband died. It stated that police responding to reports of gunshots found him dead with three sachets of crystal meth, and a piece of cardboard that read “I’m a drug pusher, don’t be like me.” She had an interview with the NBI, who told her they had also summoned local officials and the funeral home. But nothing further happened in the investigation. “No one has followed up with me, I still wonder what happened to that NBI case,” she remarked.

    Industry observers note that fortun became a commissioner of the Philippine Truth Commission, a civil society initiative working closely with the Catholic Church to investigate Duterte-era drug war crimes. She has recorded 13 cases in which people were shot and killed but whose death certificates cite illnesses such as heart attack, pneumonia, and high blood pressure as causes of death. Fortun stated during a Truth Commission briefing that government prosecutors have pushed back when presented with evidence of falsified death certificates in court. In one case, the government prosecutor acted on behalf of the defendant, instead of the victim: “I was grilled in cross-examination, and I was surprised that it was the prosecutor. I don’t understand it. So if you’re a poor family with a similar case, would you still have it corrected. It’s so hard.”.

    According to recent reports, the Commission on Human Rights told Human Rights Watch that its investigations of Duterte-era drug-war killings have resulted in cases moving through the justice system. Between 2016 and 2023, 25 cases were filed in court, 37 cases at the Office of the Ombudsman, and 42 with the Justice Department. No further progress was reported by the commission on the cases filed. The commission has no prosecutorial power and can only file cases in a manner similar to private complainants.

    Despite the Commission on Human Right’s limited powers, families seek confirmation from the commission that they have been victims of rights violations, which entitles them to limited financial assistance under the commission’s internal rules of procedure. Yet the commission denied assistance for lack of evidence to two women whose husbands were fatally shot in 2016.

    Only the woman who exhumed her husband’s body was able to challenge the decision; after she submitted the postmortem examination report in August 2026, the commission told her to file a petition for reinvestigation. “I just want to prove that what I’m saying is the truth,” she said.

    The commission told Human Rights Watch that it created its own task force, which is right now reinvestigating 493 cases of Duterte-era drug-war killings, with the goal of resolving 140 before the end of 2026.

    Duterte-Era Drug-War Policy Persists.

    In a recent development, the mother of a man killed by police in Central Luzon in 2022—after Marcos became president—noted that she tried to pursue murder charges. She cited a witness who told her that her son was lured to the location the night of the killing, and an autopsy report that indicated he had been shot execution-style and not during an armed encounter as police had claimed. The witness has since gone missing. Prosecutors dismissed her case twice, most recently in 2025, because a medical expert’s testimony was required. The mother said that she was working on finding a medical expert to testify, but even just the cost of reproducing copies of documents was weighing on her.

    No special task force has been created to investigate alleged drug-war crimes under the Marcos government. The government has claimed that its anti-drug campaign is “bloodless” and that “rather than resorting to violence, it focuses on strengthening prevention and rehabilitation efforts.” But Human Rights Watch found that disturbing Duterte-era language, such as “neutralization,” remains in intends for current anti-drugs campaigns.

    There is no legal definition of “neutralization,” but on July 1, 2016, Duterte’s police chief, Ronald Dela Rosa, issued Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, the operational document for the anti-drug campaign, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals.

    In 2017, two human rights groups, the Center for International Law (CenterLaw) and the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), filed petitions before the Supreme Court seeking to declare the anti-drug campaign unconstitutional, citing the use of the word “neutralization” in the circular. The Supreme Court has yet to rule on the case. ICC prosecutors have accused Duterte of developing “a State policy to ‘neutralize’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines who were perceived or alleged to be involved in drug-related and other crimes,” noting the language in the circular.

    Sources indicate that in November 2025, the ICC issued a sealed arrest warrant for Dela Rosa. He is alleged to be responsible for the crime against humanity of murder as part of a common plan together with other co-perpetrators—including Duterte—with the aim of killing drug suspects between 2011 and 2019. This included issuing the Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals. The ICC unsealed the warrant in May 2026; Dela Rosa has since gone into hiding.

    The Marcos government has not rescinded that circular, but in 2024 the Philippine National Police told lawmakers that they were actually following a newly introduced circular without the word “neutralize.” The Marcos government also committed todrug policy reform as part of a US$4 million joint human rights program with the United Nations.

    According to recent reports, A 2026 study by two organizations, No Box Philippines and Harm Reduction International, found that the Philippine government was still allocating millions of US dollars for local anti-drug campaigns whose policy documents retained similar language to the original circular, such as “neutralization” and “negation.” Their findings were based on an analysis of 2023-2025 local government “Peace and Order and Public Safety” budgets. Local governments are supervised by the Department of Interior and Local Government, the executive department that also supervises the police.

    Human Rights Watch analyzed local government plans obtained by the two groups, and found that 85 towns, municipalities, and cities allocated funds for rewards, awards, and incentives for successful anti-drug operations, including 10 municipalities where the funds were specifically for “conducting negation operations” or “neutralizing drug personalities.”.

    During the Duterte presidency, for an area to declare itself “drug-free,” local councils had to monitor, surveil, and compile a drug “watch list.” Human rights groups frequently alleged the lists determined who would be killed, whether the assailants were police officers or masked police agents.

    Under public safety intends in effect under Marcos, local governments still offer financial rewards for making their areas “drug-free,” by giving “incentives to assets,” or “awards/rewards for significant illegal drugs accomplishment” or “neutralization of drug personalities.” ICC prosecutors alleged in their case against Duterte that “law enforcement personnel knew that extrajudicial killings would result in them being financially rewarded.” There have been fewer drug-related killings under Marcos, but human rights defenders who live in drug-war hotspots in Metro Manila and neighboring provinces mentioned abuses continued.

    It has been revealed that “Their raids are not as brazen, but they still plant evidence,” one rights defender noted. The quota system—the number of arrests and kills under Duterte to qualify for rewards—“was still alive.”.

    According to recent reports, under Marcos, human rights defenders monitoring drug-war abuses in their communities have observed that the police are more likely to extort victims than to kill them, targeting many of the same people who were on drug “watch lists.” They stated police still arbitrarily arrest people, threaten them with drug charges, and then detain them on criminal anti-street-gambling charges with lighter penalties. The Philippine organization PhilRights has documented that “police officers offer to cover the victims’ release costs in exchange for repayment with interest, effectively profiting from the arrest.”.

    Industry observers note that in 2025, a man came home one night to find police officers in the vicinity, his sister remarked. “They patted him down and found nothing,” she said. “But a police informant handed sachets of crystal meth and forced him to admit it was his.” The police arrested the man and took his bicycle. She said she made several visits to the police station where her brother had been detained. The police officials told her he had been charged with gambling. “I told them, ‘You said you found drugs, now the charge is gambling. How long are you detaining him?’” she said. “They told us we can ‘just pay P10,000 [$160].’ But we had no money at all at the time.”.

    According to recent reports, the sister took a month processing documents in several police stations before her brother was released. He was detained for a month without being brought before a judge in violation of his rights. “We can still see them surveilling our area from time to time,” the sister said.

    This publication has been updated to attribute the source of the data for drug-related killings under the Marcos administration.

    Philippine Police Killings in Duterte’s “War on Drugs”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 23, 2026, 10:36 am CST.

    In a recent development, then-White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images).

    A former White House press secretary for President Donald Trump—whose tenure lasted five days in October—is facing an investigation by the State Bar of California after describing herself as a lawyer without being licensed to practice law.

    In a recent development, katie Zacharia, who graduated with a JD from the Pepperdine University Rick J. Caruso School of Law in 2011, never passed the bar but has repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer. A California code says a candidate must have passed the bar exam to be called a lawyer.

    Zacharia has stated she worked as the outside counsel to the World Bank, an international financial institution, and as the general counsel for a conservative California nonprofit, according the Campaign for Accountability, a nonprofit government watchdog group.

    The Campaign for Accountability received a notice of the probe in a Thursday letter from the state bar and told the nonprofit that its complaint was assigned to an investigator and legal adviser.

    “Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” said Michelle Kuppersmith, the executive director of the Campaign for Accountability, in a statement Thursday.

    Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary.

    Is she or isn’t she? Trump’s latest press secretary claims she took the bar—in China.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every year during the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence women’s rights defenders come together to remember women facing violence—including those we have lost—and to renew the struggle for gender equality.

    Sources indicate that this year we face growing gender inequality, as the rights of women and girls are rolled back and threatened by authoritarianism and conflict in many countries. Across all regions, governments and powerful anti-rights movements seek to dismantle hard-won rights for women and girls. Technology is adding newly introduced dimensions to abuse, from online harassment and surveillance to digitally enabled threats, violence, and sexualized deepfake images;  women politicians are often targeted.

    In the United States and Russia, authorities are dismantling reproductive rights. In Africa, lawmakers, with support from foreign conservative groups, are promoting a charter aiming to roll back women’s rights across the continent. In Argentina, funding for preventing GBV has been scrapped.

    As armed conflict increases across the globe, more women and girls are living in proximity to fighting. During conflict, women and girls face heightened risks of sexual and gender-based violence, displacement, and economic insecurity, often with little access to protection or justice. In Sudan and Democratic Republic of Congo, sexual violence is a common feature of ongoing conflict with survivors facing significant barriers to obtaining protection, services, and justice. In Myanmar, women political prisoners are tortured. Reproductive rights are a casualty of Israel’s closures in the West Bank, its ongoing blockade of the Gaza Strip, and its continued attacks on Palestinian health facilities.

    But activists refuse to accept erosion of women’s rights.

    In March, the Commission on the Status of Women called for strengthening access to justice for all women and girls. In April, the European Parliament passed a resolution calling for consent to be the determining factor in rape legislation across the EU. In November, Hungary declared it would ratify the Istanbul Convention, strengthening women’s rights protections. Activists from Afghanistan are fighting to have gender apartheid recognized as an international crime.

    Activists are also pushing back against technology-facilitated abuse, demanding that companies protect, rather than endanger, women and girls. In different countries young women are leading protest movements to challenge corruption and authoritarianism.

    Rights defenders will not lose hope.

    Violence Against Lesbian, Bisexual, and Queer Women and Non-Binary People.

    Accelerating Supply Chain Transparency in the Apparel and Footwear Industry.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A federal grand jury has indicted Igor D’iu, a Russian national, on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notice to the Attorney General, interstate stalking, and fraud in connection with identification documents, all in connection with an alleged scheme to conduct surveillance and gather information about employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense tech giant.

    According to recent reports, “The Americans who build our defense technology help keep this country safe by arming our warfighters with the tools and weapons they need to prevail against our adversaries and enemies,” noted Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “As alleged, D’iu entered our country illegally at the direction of foreign handlers to surveil, follow, and gather information about some of those who work in this vital industry. Such conduct, if proven, is a flagrant violation of U.S. sovereignty and an unacceptable attempt at intimidation. We will use every tool at our disposal to find, prosecute, and punish such conduct, wherever and whenever it happens.”.

    “The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense organization because of that company’s assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia,” said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California. “We will not tolerate any efforts — by foreign governments or otherwise — to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations. And my office, working in concert with our law enforcement partners, will aggressively pursue and prosecute those who seek to carry out such illegal operations on American soil.”.

    It has been revealed that “Igor D’iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major U.S. technology firm, using physical surveillance, electronic tracking devices, and fraudulent identities to gather intelligence,” mentioned Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “Russia may rely on covert operatives and criminal intermediaries as it attempts to gain an edge in its war against Ukraine, but those tactics do not place its government or its collaborators beyond the reach of the law. This indictment should serve as a warning to anyone looking to undermine U.S. interests or threaten our national security: No matter where you are or who you’re working for, justice will find you.”.

    D’iu had his initial appearance in federal court on Nov. 2, and has remained in federal custody since then. He is next scheduled to appear in federal court on Nov. 24. According to the indictment and affidavit supporting the criminal complaint filed in the case, D’iu entered the United States unlawfully in the summer of 2026 after being recruited by co-conspirators through the messaging platform Telegram, to carry out clandestine assignments targeting employees of a large technology and defense company with an office in Palo Alto, California. According to the affidavit and indictment, D’iu received instructions, equipment, and financial support from co-conspirators communicating with him through Telegram, who told D’iu his work was for “the Motherland” and directed D’iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine.

    The affidavit and indictment allege that D’iu traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, to Mexico City, Mexico, in June 2026, where his co-conspirators connected him with an individual who helped him cross the United States and Mexico border. After D’iu entered the United States, co-conspirators allegedly instructed D’iu to purchase laptops, cell phones, wireless networking equipment, and remote access software, all of which he did, to facilitate his assignments. According to the affidavit, D’iu’s co-conspirators directed him to visit a coffee shop near the firm’s Palo Alto office, identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens while they worked. His co-conspirators also allegedly instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity.

    It has been revealed that according to the affidavit, D’iu’s assignments expanded to include surveillance of company employees and their residences. D’iu conducted online searches for several employees’ home addresses, including the residence of a senior company executive. On or about Sept. 3, D’iu allegedly followed a female employee in a silver Lexus SUV for nearly 30 miles as she drove from the company’s Palo Alto office toward San Francisco. The employee attempted to evade D’iu by making irregular turns, taking back roads, and entering a grocery store parking lot. D’iu allegedly aggressively continued following her, including through U-turns and illegal left turns, and ran a red light to remain behind her vehicle. Fearing for her safety, the employee called 911 and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department’s Mission Station. D’iu allegedly abandoned his pursuit after the employee contacted a police officer. Investigators also obtained evidence that D’iu had followed other company employees on preceding days.

    According to recent reports, the affidavit further alleges that D’iu obtained fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity and continue his activities. Investigators intercepted two international packages shipped from overseas that contained in them concealed identification documents, including a falsified California ID card, an altered U.S. passport, and a Social Security card bearing the assumed name of “Hugo Landry Johns.” According to the affidavit, the passport was an authentic U.S. passport originally issued to an individual elsewhere in the country that had been modified to display the defendant’s photograph and assumed identity.

    In a recent development, after Palo Alto police contacted D’iu regarding the Sept. 3 stalking incident, he allegedly changed vehicles, obtained a fresh phone number, and traveled to Reno, Nevada, at the direction of his co-conspirators on Telegram. According to the affidavit, D’iu subsequently returned to the Bay Area to continue carrying out his assignments.

    In a recent development, in October, FBI agents executed search warrants on D’iu and at his residence in East Palo Alto, recovering approximately $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, two Russian passports, wireless networking equipment, and the fraudulent identification documents. Agents also recovered a notebook containing 10 handwritten addresses, numerous of which corresponded to the residences of tech giant employees, and detailed profiles of at least three employees containing personal information, family members’ names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses.

    D’iu is charged by indictment with one count of conspiracy to act as an agent of a foreign government,; one count of acting as an agent of a foreign government without notice to the Attorney General, one count of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud in connection with identification documents.

    If convicted, D’iu faces the following maximum penalties:.

    The maximum penalties are prescribed by Congress and are provided for informational purposes only. Any sentence would be determined by the court after consideration of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

    The FBI is investigating the case, with assistance from the Palo Alto and San Francisco Police Departments.

    This case is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorneys Office for Northern District of California and the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (London) – The Hong Kong government should ensure meaningful accountability for the devastating fire that killed 168 people one year ago and end its suppression of peaceful criticism, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • Recent findings suggest that on November 26, 2025, Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades engulfed seven residential high-rise buildings at Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po.
    • Industry observers note that “The Hong Kong government responded to the horrific Wang Fuk Court fire by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability,” stated Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (London) – The Hong Kong government should ensure meaningful accountability for the devastating fire that killed 168 people one year ago and end its suppression of peaceful criticism, Human Rights Watch said today.

    Recent findings suggest that on November 26, 2025, Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades engulfed seven residential high-rise buildings at Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po. The authorities initiated an independent investigation and arrested three dozen people implicated in crimes. The Housing Minister resigned. But the authorities have also threatened and arbitrarily arrested those engaging in criticism and activism concerning the fire.

    Industry observers note that “The Hong Kong government responded to the horrific Wang Fuk Court fire by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability,” stated Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities need to recognize that the only way to prevent similar tragedies in the future is to allow people to speak out safely and hold those responsible fully accountable.”.

    The authorities have engaged in apparent acts of repression of free expression in the weeks ahead of the anniversary:.

    Police Commissioner Joe Chow said police routinely asked organizers about upcoming public events, while decisions on whether to proceed “rested with the organizers themselves.”.

    Amid continued restrictions on freedom of expression and peaceful assembly in Hong Kong, Hong Kong communities around the world have planned commemorations of the fire.

    In a recent development, deep concerns surrounding the 2026 anniversary follow a year-long government crackdown on criticism, reporting, and civil society-organizing related to the fire. Immediately following the fire, hundreds of people gathered near Wang Fuk Court to donate and distribute supplies to victims, but as the volunteer effort grew, police told them to leave and government workers took over the site.

    It has been revealed that authorities targeted people calling for accountability. Just four days after the fire, national security police reportedly arrested a university student, Miles Kwan, for “seditious intent” after he initiated an online petition calling for an independent investigation into the fire, and two others on suspicion of “inciting hatred against the government.”.

    Hong Kong and Beijing authorities subsequently accused “foreign forces” and “anti-China destabilizing forces” of using the fire to “incite hatred against the government.” Within hours of these announcements, two prominent online commentators, Ellie Yuen and Hailey Cheng, who had been frequently quoted in foreign media, said they would stop reporting on the fire.

    National security police also arrested the online commentator Wong On-yin in December after he planned to hold a news conference about the Wang Fuk Court fire and discussed on YouTube his subsequent questioning by police. The authorities prosecuted him for allegedly obstructing a national security investigation and publishing “seditious material.” He remains in custody awaiting a verdict in January 2027.

    Between April and May 2026, the authorities barred Wang Fuk Court residents from displaying banners from their homes or being accompanied by journalists as they were briefly permitted to return to their apartments to retrieve belongings.

    Also in May, the authorities arrested the former Wang Fuk Court owners’ committee member Kong Cheung-fat and his wife on allegations of fraud and money laundering. Kong had joined other owners in seeking a meeting to discuss insurance and other post-fire issues. While out on bail, he mentioned he would no longer give interviews or comment publicly. Some residents said his arrest made them more cautious about speaking publicly.

    Sources indicate that an independent committee, set up by Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee, published a report on October 29 that found wide-ranging regulatory failures across four government bodies, including inadequate oversight of renovation work and fire safety, weaknesses in building maintenance regulation, and supervisory failures by contractors and other professionals. That day, Lee and senior officials formally apologized to the victims of the fire and their families while promising to implement “systemic reforms.” Housing Secretary Winnie Ho later stepped down from office while the authorities arrested 35 people in connection with the fire and possible corruption in the renovation project.

    Sources indicate that “An apology and promises of reform are no substitute for ensuring that people can freely question and criticize the authorities,” Pearson mentioned. “The Hong Kong government should act on the independent committee’s recommendations and provide adequate compensation and other support for victims and their families.”.

    Academic Freedom in Hong Kong Under the National Security Law.
