    Nepal: Predatory Lending Abuses Exacerbated by Conflict in the Gulf

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2956 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, (Tokyo) – Authorities in Nepal should hold illegal moneylenders accountable for abuses against borrowers, including unlawful land dispossession, arbitrary eviction, threats and acts of violence, and sexual exploitation, Human Rights Watch remarked today.
    • “Despite government commitments to protect borrowers, illegal practices are rife in Nepal’s informal credit sector, leaving those with the fewest resources dependent on moneylenders who can take everything they own,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, Asia deputy director at Human Rights Watch.
    • Human Rights Watch interviewed 18 borrowers, as well as local government officials, lawyers, and activists from six districts in the Terai region where informal money lending is rampant, reviewed government reports, and examined over 50 cases in Nawalparasi district.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, (Tokyo) – Authorities in Nepal should hold illegal moneylenders accountable for abuses against borrowers, including unlawful land dispossession, arbitrary eviction, threats and acts of violence, and sexual exploitation, Human Rights Watch remarked today. Conflicts in the Gulf region, where many Nepalis are migrant workers facing exorbitant recruitment fees, have made more people vulnerable to extortion by illegal lenders.

    “Despite government commitments to protect borrowers, illegal practices are rife in Nepal’s informal credit sector, leaving those with the fewest resources dependent on moneylenders who can take everything they own,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, Asia deputy director at Human Rights Watch. “The government of Prime Minister Balendra Shah should carry out the government’s commitments to ensure that the law against fraudulent and abusive lending is consistently enforced.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed 18 borrowers, as well as local government officials, lawyers, and activists from six districts in the Terai region where informal money lending is rampant, reviewed government reports, and examined over 50 cases in Nawalparasi district.

    Human Rights Watch found that many families are struggling with unmanageable debt particularly as migrant workers in the Gulf States during 2026 have faced reduced incomes or involuntary travel delays ahead of starting jobs due to the conflict between the US, Israel, and Iran. War-induced disruption amplified pre-existing abuses, including reliance on unauthorized individual agents and unreasonable recruitment fees. Human Rights Watch previously found that companies in Gulf states play a critical role in driving these illegal costs by refusing to cover costs and fees to recruiters that they know will be borne by workers.

    Government investigations have shown that, under Nepal’s informal credit practices, a borrower signs or thumbprints an unsecured personal loan contract, known locally as kapali tamasuk, which can falsely list a principal amount three to ten times more than the cash received. These loans, known as meter byaj, in some cases compound at annual rates ranging from 36 percent to 60 percent or more, compared with less than 10 percent charged by banks.

    As low-income households that had relied on remittances disrupted by the war have shifted their limited resources toward expenses for food, fuel, and healthcare, they have been increasingly unable to repay their loans, leading to a surge in defaults. In response, some moneylenders are forcing evictions or land transfers, including through violence, in the worst cases tying people into generational debt. Nepal authorities are not pushing for effective long term solutions beyond encouraging and facilitating debtors and creditors to enter pre-court settlements.

    Following the outbreak of conflict in the Persian Gulf, in March 2026, the Nepal government suspended both institutional and individual labor permits to protect its citizens, including to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Kuwait, with an estimated 2,000 Nepalis denied labor permits daily. Thousands were stopped from travelling at the international airport despite possessing valid medical clearances, verified visas, and binding employment contracts, while administrative delays also led foreign firms to cancel labor contracts. However, the authorities failed to step in to protect aspiring migrant laborers who still had to service their high interest meter byaj loans, leaving them exposed to violent enforcement by loan sharks.

    Sources indicate that “They did not just hit my father to get the money,” said one victim. “They beat him in the middle of the road during the day so that everyone else in the village would see what happens when you cannot pay the meter byaj. The local goons told us, ‘If you don’t sign over the land title today, your family will receive a corpse tomorrow.’”.

    Recent findings suggest that while abuses, including violent attacks and forced evictions, appear to be increasing due to conflict related disruptions, many moneylenders have long wielded political and economic power over borrowers. Claiming that the justice system routinely favors the moneylenders, borrowers have staged three extended protests in Kathmandu over the last four years—the longest for 442 days—and three long marches. Each time, the government agreed to resolve debt complications but failed to honor its commitments to protect victims. Consequently, the borrowers have regularly protested at district and provincial levels as well.

    In a recent development, although government has criminalized such loans, borrowers and activists in Madhesh Province stated that police have repeatedly refused to file reports when victims seek protection. Instead, they said, the police typically dismiss abuses and intimidation by moneylenders as “private civil disputes.”.

    “When the moneylender came to break our door, we ran to the police, but the officers told us to go home and settle personal transactional disputes ourselves,” noted a Rautahat district migrant worker.

    According to recent reports, the police also back moneylenders when they use signed blank checks and banking laws to threaten defaulters with arrest, or use informal deeds as the basis to seize land and evict families. “The lender made me sign a blank check when he gave me a loan, and later on he filled it for 10 lakhs (US$6,500) and sent the police to threaten me with jail when the check bounced,” said a Siraha district farmer.

    Borrowers also cite cases in which the authorities do not intervene even when lenders use patently unlawful loan agreements to obtain asset foreclosure orders. “The lender told me openly that he owns the courts and the administration,” remarked Shiv Shanker from Gaur, Rautahat district, who after facing abuses from a moneylender, is leading protests. “When the state shuts its doors on a poor farmer, death feels like the only place left to hide from this meter byaj.”.

    On May 5, 2023, the government criminalized informal loans as an “improper transaction,” and declared that forging loan contracts, threatening borrowers, or fabricating loan amounts, are punishable by up to seven years in prison. However, enforcement remains weak. Successive governments have established inquiry commissions to address the crisis, but over 65,000 complaints registered with inquiry commissions remain unresolved due to a lack of legal provisions and administrative bottlenecks.

    These failures have contributed to deadly outcomes including suicide. Santidevi Mahato from Biratnagar died by suicide on June 21, following threats from a moneylender because she could not service her debt, people interviewed stated. After borrowing 150,000 Nepali rupees (US$975) in October 2015, she had repaid 400,000 Nepali rupees (US$2,600) in installments. Yet, violating their agreement, the moneylender seized her land and threatened to evict her from her house.

    Under international human rights law and standards, governments have the obligation to take steps to protect people from serious rights abuses caused by private actors, such as moneylenders, including through investigating and prosecuting serious crimes.

    It has been revealed that on July 17, the government led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah concluded a nine-point pact with protest leaders to eliminate predatory lending, after debt victims began a march to Kathmandu. The government should take immediate legal and policy steps to institutionalize its commitment, Human Rights Watch remarked. Nepal’s donors and international partners should assist the government to establish systematic debt relief, and grievance mechanisms that can support debt restructuring.

    Sources indicate that “The Balendra Shah government was elected with the promise of change, to overturn existing oppressive structures,” Ganguly stated. “More closely regulating moneylenders and ending their chokehold on farmers and laborers is a crucial step in ensuring lasting social justice.”.

    Nepal’s informal credit system is rooted in its feudal history, where local elites used predatory debt to trap peasants in tenancy and systems of generational servitude such as Kamaiya, Haliya, and Haruwa-Charuwa.

    Recent findings suggest that the present-day meter byaj system evolved around a spurt in labor migration during the decade-long civil war in Nepal, from 1996 to 2006, and rapidly spread after the 2007 political unrest in the Terai region. An estimated 7 million Nepalis work abroad, about half in India and a majority of the rest in Gulf countries, contributing a third of the national GDP. For many households, migration became one of the few viable ways to earn a living, while the absence of accessible and affordable institutional credit left them dependent on informal lenders to finance the costs of securing employment abroad.

    Some local moneylenders and corrupt agents demanded exorbitant fees to help rural youth find jobs abroad, particularly in the Gulf States and Malaysia. Land or property was borrowers’ main collateral, but they often later discovered that their contracts were fraudulent, including falsified sums and forged documents. The schemes exploited bureaucratic complicity at government land offices to transfer property titles despite contracts being illegal, and borrowers lost their assets due to a lack of protection from the government.

    In interviews, debt victims described devastating cycles in which migrant workers are forever bound to serving a predatory moneylender, while the authorities fail to intervene. Ramnath Musahar from Susta, Nawalparasi district, said the family borrowed to send two of his brothers to work in the Gulf States in 2015, but despite servicing the loan, their debt had grown enormously:.

    Sources indicate that my brothers sent back Rs. 1,200,000 (US$8,000) from their wages, and we sold our plots [of land] to pay an extra Rs. 1,800,000 (US$11,000). But the lender went to the district court with a fake contract and claimed we still owe him Rs. 5,000,000 (US$33,000). The court looked only at the paper and our thumbprints; it did not look at our tears. The police came and threw our belongings into the dirt. We went from being independent farmers to beggars overnight.

    Since the US and Israel began their assault on Iran on February 28, 2026, and Iran subsequently blocked and attacked ships traveling through the Strait of Hormuz and attacked sites across the Gulf States, the fallout is being felt far beyond the region.

    It has been revealed that in Nepal, UN agencies warned that “rising fuel prices, closure of shipping routes, and growing financial uncertainty are placing mounting pressure on economies, labor markets and vulnerable households.” According to the World Bank, Nepal’s real GDP growth could fall from 3.67 percent in 2024 to 2.3 percent in 2026 due to reduced tourism, higher transport costs, and supply chain snags. Rising inflation, a weakening currency leading to a rise in import costs, a spike in fuel costs, and stalled fertilizer supply have placed additional pressure on low-income households, and increased demands for overseas employment.

    Hoping to seek jobs to support their families, many rural youths have taken loans from loan sharks, who have responded by raising rates. Many families were stuck servicing those loans, even as people were unable to travel because of conflict-related disruptions.

    Workers already employed in the Gulf States are facing job losses, unpaid leave, wage reductions, and other disruptions that have reduced their ability to keep sending remittances. Compared with the same period the previous year, Gulf-bound labor approvals plummeted by 52 percent—from 228,165 down to 109,249—between the outbreak of the war in late February and mid-September, according to Department of Foreign Employment data. At least two Nepali workers have been killed due to the conflict, and 15 injured.

    Many are returning to Nepal stripped of their anticipated income, and unable to service their loans. The authorities have failed to act as moneylenders crack down on defaulters, beating them, evicting them, and forcing land or asset transfers. The lenders are also seeking court-ordered asset foreclosures and even arrest warrants based on the loan contracts, including contracts that borrowers alleged contained fabricated loan amounts. As a Mahotari district borrower observed, “The law says meter byaj is a crime, but police demanded receipts I never got, so the thief walks free, and I am made the criminal.”.

    It has been revealed that women-led households, Dalits (considered an “untouchable” caste), and Indigenous ethnic communities have even fewer protections from violence such as beatings and sexual violence due to their caste, gender, and discrimination. One woman from Dhanusha district noted she was raped by a moneylender under threat of eviction.

    My husband was trapped in a labor camp abroad and couldn’t send money. The lender came to my house with the contract and mentioned he would evict my children the next morning unless I “compromised” with him. He held our roof over my head like a weapon. I had to endure his abuse in silence because a poor woman in this village has no voice against a powerful man who holds her land paper.

    Industry observers note that while the conflict has exacerbated the crisis, debt-ridden families had already proliferated in Nepal, particularly in Terai districts. The authorities have failed to protect these families.

    In a recent development, chirai Chamar, a widowed Dalit worker in Paklihawa, Nawalparasi district, while struggling to gain control of her inherited family land, had borrowed 20,000 Nepali rupees (US$130). A moneylender offered to help with the legalities in exchange for a portion of that land. “A moneylender, from whom I had borrowed Rs. 20,000, came to me saying he will help me to acquire all the papers required to own my family land, and in return I need to give him two katthas (650 square meters) of land,” she said.

    He then grabbed an additional four katthas (1336 square meters), paying Chamar a grossly undervalued sum of Rs. 150,000 (US$970). When rights activists intervened to reclaim Chamar’s land and restore her livelihood, local thugs threatened them and destroyed Chamar’s crops. Despite complaints, the police and the local officials failed to assist her.

    Ashamaya (name changed), a resident of Thecho, Lalitpur, supported her family by running a small tea shop. However, when her father-in-law fell ill, she had to close the business to care for him. Left without income as the medical expenses mounted, she borrowed money from a moneylender, who charged an extortionate annual interest rate of 120 percent, which she could not pay. Under pressure, she took on another usurious loan simply to pay off the old one.

    Although she settled that debt by selling a piece of land, she had to borrow again, this time to cover her husband’s medical costs, but she no longer had enough land for collateral. The moneylender coerced her into sex with multiple men after he forced her to sign a fresh contact for Rs. 2500,000 (UDS$16,167), amounting to five times her initial debt.

    Industry observers note that debt victims have started to organize under various banners and groups, demanding that the government protect them from abusive loan sharks. In 2022, after hundreds walked barefoot for weeks from districts including Siraha, Dhanusha, Mahottari, Sarlahi, Kapilvastu, and Nawalparasi to stage protests in Kathmandu, the government at that time establisheda three-member Commission for the Investigation of Loan Sharking (CILS) in April 2023, to collect complaints, study structural issues, and resolve loan-sharking disputes.

    It has been revealed that by May 21, 2023, when the District Administration Offices stopped accepting these complaints, over 28,000 had been filed across 67 districts, with an alarming 21,552 cases concentrated in Madhesh Province. However, the commission only resolved and closed 5,115 loan disputes. Several victims reported abuses by district offices. “We went to the Chief District Officer expecting justice, but instead, the police and the lender ganged up on us, warned us that going to court would mean total land auction, and scared us into signing an agreement to pay half the inflated sum,” noted a woman from Siraha.

    Sources indicate that as complaints persisted, including of violent encounters in which the police failed to intervene, the authorities largely resorted to symbolic agreements with the victims, followed by the repeated formation of upcoming commissions. A commission was set up in March 2024, led by former high court judge Tej Bahadur Karki, and another in March 2025, led by Baburam Regmi. In November 2025, the Regmi Commission reported a total of 41,409 complaints registered in 43 districts. Of these, 6,393 cases had been resolved, while 35,016 complaints remain pending.

    According to recent reports, each commission exposed the vast scale of the crisis but political commitments to break the stranglehold of moneylenders remain unfulfilled. Nawalparasi’s Deputy Chief District Officer Poshan Raj Bhandari told Human Rights Watch that, “The existing law will not be enough to resolve this problem; the government needs to think of a separate legal process to resolve this.”.

    When Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s government was elected in March 2026 with a large majority, victims had cause for hope. However, instead of the government ensuring a collective debt moratorium, victims say that moneylenders have convinced the police to issue a surge of arrest warrants against debtors.

    Recent findings suggest that in response, victims have organized upcoming protests. Nigra Nabin, a leader of the protest movement, said that based on “past experiences” the victims “had three long-standing demands” including the nullification of all illegal agreements and the underlying loan contracts that support them; a new law to institutionalize these actions and establish special legal procedures; and a separate entity dedicated to ensuring justice for the victims.

    On July 9, the anti-loan shark movement began an 11-day justice march from Janakpur to Kathmandu. On the sixth day of the march, Home Affairs Minister Sudhan Gurung traveled to Nijgadh to hold direct talks with the protesters. Following three days of negotiations, the government accepted the three core demands and signed an updated nine-point deal, leading the protesters to call off the march.

    The victims are waiting. One of them, Sobita Devi Mahato, mentioned: “If this is not resolved, the only resort I have is to go to the Home Ministry and hang myself there.”.

    Second District Court Rules Against Trump's Newly introduced Birthright Citizenship Executive Order

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, yesterday, in the case of Nathan v.
    • Recent findings suggest that I previously  wrote about Trump's fresh executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it.
    • Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the latest order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, yesterday, in the case of Nathan v. Trump, federal district Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of DC issued a ruling against Trump's new executive order restricting birthright citizenship. The ruling is very similar to an earlier September decision by Judge Boardman of the District of Maryland. The one difference is that the class action injunction in Nathan covers a class that literally consists of all children illegally deprived of birthright citizenship under the new order, whereas the class in the Maryland case is slightly narrower.

    Recent findings suggest that I previously  wrote about Trump's fresh executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it. As I pointed out then, almost every part of the new order is at odds with the Supreme Court's recent ruling in Trump v. Barbara, which struck down Trump's executive order denying birthright citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States, and those born to non-citizen parents here on temporary visas. The Fourteenth Amendment guarantees citizenship to all children "born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof." In Barbara, the Supreme Court majority made clear that "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" includes children of all persons who are subject to and required to obey US law.

    Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the latest order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:.

    Industry observers note that earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's Executive Order 14160, which purported to deny citizenship to children born to parents temporarily or unlawfully present in the country. Those children, like "nearly all children born in the United States," the Court explained, are "citizens at birth" because they are born "subject to American law." Trump v. Barbara, 609 U.S. 719, 734–37, 740–41 (2026). Barbara reaffirmed that birthright citizenship extends to all but three narrow categories of children, each long understood to be beyond the Nation's governing authority at birth: children of foreign officials enjoying full diplomatic immunity, children of enemy forces in hostile occupation of U.S. territory, and children born aboard foreign public ships.

    Yet Barbara's ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents. Among those now targeted are children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organizations but lack diplomatic immunity, children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements, and children with a parent suspected of membership in certain gangs or terrorist organizations. As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws. The Court will therefore certify a class consisting of children who are or will be unlawfully denied citizenship under the Order. And it will preliminarily enjoin the Government from enforcing the Order against members of that class.

    As explained in my original August post on the fresh executive order, that order covers four groups almost all of whose members are clearly subject to US law:.

    Children of "alien enemies," defined as those where at least one of two non-citizen parents is a "designated Foreign Terrorist Organization under 8 U.S.C. 1189 or Specially Designated Global Terrorist, consistent with the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq., and Executive Order 13224 of September 23, 2001 (Blocking Property and Prohibiting Transactions With Persons Who Commit, Threaten to Commit, or Support Terrorism).".

    Children born to at least one non-citizen parent who is a "foreign government employee" or employed by an "international organization that possess[es] international-organization immunity.".

    Children where "either parent" has engaged in "birth tourist" transactions of various kinds (deliberately seeking to give birth in the US so the child would get birthright citizenship).

    Children "born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute." …[T]his only applies to children born in American Samoa, the one populated overseas US territory to whose residents Congress has not conferred citizenship by statute….

    As I explained more fully in my August post, all of the children in these four categories are obviously subject to US law, with the exception of those born to foreign diplomats who have diplomatic immunity. This latter group is already excluded from birthright citizenship. In that post, I also explained why the analogy between "alien enemies" (as defined in the order) and children of members of an invading army occupying US territory fails.

    Judge Cooper's opinion analyzes all four categories thoroughly and effectively. He's particularly strong on the case of children of "alien enemies," a category which - he explains - the Trump order defines far more broadly than is justified by legal precedent, and which in any case does not include anyone not "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States, because all such people are under US control and required to obey US law when on American soil. That differentiates them from the historically recognized exception for children of enemy troops in "hostile occupation" of US territory during a war. The US does not have effective jurisdiction over territory occupied by a hostile enemy army. But the last time any such thing occurred was during World War II, when the Japanese occupied a number of US island possessions in the Pacific.

    I noted some additional problems with Trump's "alien enemies" carveout in my August post about the second birthright citizenship order:.

    Sources indicate that finally, the [order is wrong about] children of "alien enemies," defined…. as members of various designated "terrorist" entities. If they enter the United States, they are subject to US law. That's why they can be prosecuted for any crimes they commit on US soil - including acts of terrorism!

    Members of these groups may be bad people. Some have committed horrendous crimes. But that is no reason to visit the sins of the parents upon the children. If a murderer or a rapist has a child born on US soil, the child is entitled to birthright citizenship, notwithstanding the reprehensible behavior of the parents. The same logic applies here.

    It is also worth noting that the "foreign terrorist organization" (FTO) designation has been slapped onto various groups that are not actually terrorists in the ordinary meaning of the word, most notably groups engaged in smuggling illegal drugs.

    Recent findings suggest that trump may be trying to use the "alien enemy" designation here to analogize these children to children of members of an invading army, born  at a time and place where the invaders have seized control of US territory, thereby preventing the exercise of US "jurisdiction." Trump v. Barbara reaffirms the longstanding view that such children are excluded from birthright citizenship, because born in an area where US jurisdiction does not (at the time) meaningfully apply.

    Industry observers note that but FTOs have not, in fact, "invaded" or occupied any part of the United States. Thus, US jurisdiction still applies. Therefore, children of members these organizations are not analogous to children born to members of an occupying foreign army. No part of the United States has actually been invaded and occupied since the Japanese seized various US territories in the Pacific during World War II.

    In my article, "Immigration is Not Invasion….," I explain in much more detail why the activities of drug dealers do not qualify as an "invasion," why an FTO designation cannot change that reality, and why courts should not defer to the president's claims that an "invasion" has occurred.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as “Chapo Isidro,” an alleged leader of the Sinaloa Cartel, has been captured by the Mexican military following a Homeland Security Task Force Investigation.

    In a recent development, “We commend Mexico’s military and special forces on last night’s capture of Sinaloa Cartel senior leader ‘Chapo Isidro,’ said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “A combined interagency effort, including the Homeland Security Task Force, supported this Mexican operation to remove a leader of one of the most dangerous drug cartels in Mexico. This successful operation is the result of a bilateral effort to eliminate terrorists in Mexico. We extend our condolences to the families of the elite soldiers who were killed and our gratitude to the Mexican government.”.

    According to recent reports, “The arrest of Chapo Isidro demonstrates the outstanding strength and reach of the Homeland Security Task Force,” stated Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. “Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and our HSTF partners relentlessly pursued one of the world’s most dangerous cartel leaders, whose organization is alleged to have flooded our communities with deadly narcotics and terrorized communities through extreme violence. This operation sends an unmistakable message, cartel leaders cannot hide behind borders, money, or brutality. The Homeland Security Task Force will continue its work to dismantle these criminal and terrorist networks, hold their leaders accountable, and protect the American people.”.

    Meza Flores was captured on November 20 in a spectacular military operation in Guasave, Sinaloa, Mexico, that also resulted in the arrest of alleged cartel leader German Rolando Galvez Meza, also known as “El Serafin.”.

    Industry observers note that A federal grand jury in the District of Columbia returned a second superseding indictment on September 25 charging Meza-Flores, 44, of Sonora, Mexico, with conspiracy to provide material support to a terrorist organization, narcoterrorism, conducting a continuing criminal enterprise, money laundering and firearms related charges. The case is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California and the Justice Department’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section.

    The Sinaloa Cartel is one of the most prolific and dangerous drug cartels in Mexico, known for its widespread use of corruption and violence to further its drug trafficking activities. On February 20, 2025, the U.S. Secretary of State designated the Cartel de Sinaloa as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) under Section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act and as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist under Executive Order 13224. The Secretary of State has also listed the following aliases for the Cartel de Sinaloa: Sinaloa Cartel, Mexican Federation, and Guadalajara Cartel.

    According to court documents, under Meza Flores’s leadership, the Sinaloa Cartel produced and trafficked multi-tonnage quantities of drugs, including cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and fentanyl into the United States, and used extreme violence to further its operations. Meza Flores commanded a large contingent of gunmen to control significant territory in the Guasave, Los Mochis, and remote Sinaloa mountains. The cartel uses this territory to manufacture and distribute illicit controlled substances, transporting them north to the United States. It is further alleged that Meza Flores has engaged in continual and extreme violence, including (1) murdering rival cartel members in public; (2) kidnapping, torturing, and murdering rival cartel members at camps and elsewhere; (3) kidnapping, torturing, and murdering members of the Mexican police; and (4) terrorizing the people of Mexico.

    It has been revealed that “Meza Flores is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives List for a reason; he is the most dangerous man in Mexico,” noted Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa Cartel, promoting unparalleled violence throughout southern Mexico and flooding the United States with deadly substances all in the name of profit. With this indictment made possible by the Homeland Security Task Force, subsequent arrest and the continued support of our Mexican partners, we aim to bring him to justice and fully dismantle this cartel.”.

    According to recent reports, “Chapo Isidro built an empire in the shadows. Today’s sunrise was his sunset,” stated U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon for the Southern District of California.

    It has been revealed that “Another FBI Ten Most Wanted fugitive is off the board,” remarked FBI Director Kash Patel. “Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” has been captured by Mexican forces with U.S. assistance. This alleged cartel leader is accused of flooding American communities with deadly drugs, including fentanyl. This is the 11th Ten Most Wanted fugitive captured under the Trump Administration. Outstanding work by our law enforcement partners in Mexico and everyone involved in this operation. Under President Trump’s leadership, this FBI will continue relentlessly pursuing the criminals and cartels poisoning our communities and threatening American lives.”.

    In a recent development, “Homeland Security Investigations is proud of the exceptional work of our special agents and personnel across our domestic and international offices whose determination, expertise, and coordination through the HSTF helped bring Chapo Isidro to justice,” said HSI Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon. “Working alongside our HSTF partners, HSI investigated this dangerous cartel leader and helped dismantle the criminal enterprise he allegedly used to poison American communities and fuel brutal violence. This arrest demonstrates the reach of HSI’s global investigative authorities and the strength of the HSTF as partners work together to take coordinated and relentless action against transnational criminal organizations that threaten our homeland.”.

    Meza Flores is charged in a six-count superseding indictment filed in the District of Columbia with leading a continuing criminal enterprise, conspiracy to manufacture and distribute cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and fentanyl for importation into the United States, international money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to provide material support to a terrorist organization, narcoterrorism, and using a firearm including a machinegun and a destructive device.

    If convicted of these charges, Meza Flores faces the death penalty or a mandatory term of life in prison.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Department of State is offering a reward of up to $5 million for information that led to the arrest and/or will lead to the conviction of Chapo Isidro. If you have any information concerning Chapo Isidro, please contact your local FBI office or the nearest American Embassy or Consulate or call the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324). You can also submit a tip online at tips.fbi.gov  See: https://www.state.gov/fausto-isidro-meza-flores.

    The HSTF including FBI Washington and San Diego Field Offices and HSI San Diego investigated the case with significant assistance from DEA, ATF, and the U.S. Marshals Service.

    According to recent reports, deputy Chief James Hepburn and Trial Attorney Jayce Born of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF) and Assistant U.S. Attorney Joshua Mellor of the Southern District of California are prosecuting the case. The Justice Department's National Security Division, Office of International Affairs and Capital Case Section provided significant assistance.

    The Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section’s (MNF) mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations.

    MNF’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Unit investigates and prosecutes the top command and control elements of international drug cartels, drug trafficking organizations, and related transnational criminal organizations.

    This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of U.S. law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Berlin, November 26, 2026) – The German government’s decision to discontinue funding for dozens of civil society projects, following budget cuts, undermines Germany’s efforts to address racism, discrimination, and antisemitism and protect human rights, Human Rights Watch mentioned today. The German government and Bundestag should release further funds to guarantee the continuation of dozens of essential civil society projects. The Bundestag is due to vote on the federal budget on November 27, 2026.

    “The German government’s cuts undermine critical civil society work and networks that directly protect human rights and combat the threats from the far-right,” said Almaz Teffera, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The German government and Bundestag should remedy the cuts in the federal budget by providing funds to save trusted anti-discrimination and anti-extremism work that directly protects and empowers people at this critical time.”.

    On November 12, the Bundestag’s budgetary committee approved the government’s proposed cuts of about €20 million to the federal civil society democracy fund, “Live Democracy!” (“Demokratie Leben!”). On November 13, the government sent funding rejections to dozens of trusted civil society projects that monitor and document discrimination and hate crimes, foster civic engagement and education, and support victims and those at risk amid alarming levels of hate crimes.

    Recent findings suggest that in March, the government confirmed that it intended to restructure the Live Democracy! program and required all funded initiatives and projects to reapply. The government introduced new criteria and objectives, which the education and family affairs minister, Karin Prien, mentioned would mean funded initiatives “reach the silent majority [in society], which is in danger of turning away from democracy.” The cuts undermine the work of civil society groups that advocate for human rights, diversity, and democracy.

    Industry observers note that live Democracy! began in 2015 as a response to racially motivated right-wing extremist terror cases in Germany in the early 2000s and subsequent institutional failures. The program had supported civil society groups, initiatives, and structures to push back against extremism, racism, and antisemitism, aiming to strengthen Germany’s democracy, promote diversity, and prevent extremism. Prien removed the goal of promoting diversity, claiming that it was “not a sufficient funding objective” on its own. Projects on racism, antisemitism, or other hostility against a group fall under the category of preventing extremism, with a restricted list of potentially fundable activities.

    Industry observers note that according to media reports, the government invited only 150 out of 1,200 applicants who expressed interest in funding to submit a full funding application. The program had previously funded about 600 projects. Several applications for projects on anti-Black and anti-Muslim racism as well as antisemitism and right-wing extremism received partial or full rejections.

    Previous funding from Live Democracy! was used by civil society groups like CLAIM, which works to combat anti-Muslim racism and hatred, to partially finance vital civil society monitoring and documentation infrastructure to track anti-Muslim discrimination and hate incidents. The group said that discontinuing their funding puts Muslim people in Germany at risk at a time when anti-Muslim incidents are at a record high.

    Sources indicate that project funding for Each One Teach One, a group that empowers Black people in Germany and conducts surveys of anti-Black racism, was also rejected. Funding was cut 60 percent for other projects countering right-wing extremism. Groups said the funding cuts demonstrated a lack of political will to defend democracy.

    In January, Prien had spoken about education as a key driver to counter antisemitism, yet educational projects on antisemitism that had been funded also received negative decisions. Unexpectedly, on November 20, three projects on antisemitism that had initially received rejections were told they would be funded.

    It has been revealed that while civil society groups have no guarantee of public funding, governments should create clear, transparent, and nondiscriminatory funding criteria and processes that prevent arbitrary funding decisions, Human Rights Watch remarked. Governments should not use funding decisions to sanction groups for their legitimate advocacy and criticism of government policies.

    In February 2025, the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union, of which Prien is a member, had sought to delegitimize more than a dozen nongovernmental organizations after they criticized the bloc’s willingness to pass a parliamentary motion on migration with votes of the far-right political party, Alternative for Germany. The bloc alleged that these groups violated so-called “political neutrality,” falsely suggesting that groups that receive public funds should not engage in political debates or advocacy.

    Civil society groups are essential for monitoring human rights and holding states to account to meet their obligations under international and regional human rights law, including the elimination of racial discrimination. In line with the right to freedom of association, groups have a right of access to funding on a fair and nondiscriminatory basis, Human Rights Watch stated.

    “Cutting funds for essential civil society work when it is needed most sends the wrong message,” Teffera noted. “Germany’s federal government and Bundestag should recognize that funding civil society work is an essential investment in the defense of human rights, rule of law, and democracy.

    ICC: Promote, Protect International Justice

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (The Hague) – Member countries of the International Criminal Court (ICC) should prioritize measures to promote and protect the court and those cooperating with it, Human Rights Watch mentioned in a report released today.
    • Industry observers note that this year’s session takes place as the court and the broader international justice system face unrelenting pressure from the United States.
    • Sources indicate that “The start of the Duterte trial at the same time as the annual ICC Assembly session should remind member countries of the court’s critical importance,” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (The Hague) – Member countries of the International Criminal Court (ICC) should prioritize measures to promote and protect the court and those cooperating with it, Human Rights Watch mentioned in a report released today. The 24-page report makes detailed recommendations for the annual session of the ICC’s Assembly of States Parties, which will convene in The Hague from November 30 to December 7, 2026.

    Industry observers note that this year’s session takes place as the court and the broader international justice system face unrelenting pressure from the United States. On October 9, the US government escalated its campaign to destroy the ICC “brick by brick” by imposing sanctions on the whole court under a February 2025 executive order. This followed the sanctioning of ICC judges and prosecutors, a United Nations human rights expert, and three leading Palestinian rights organizations. Yet, the ICC continues to advance its critical work for justice. The landmark trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is scheduled to begin on November 30.

    Sources indicate that “The start of the Duterte trial at the same time as the annual ICC Assembly session should remind member countries of the court’s critical importance,” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “At the session, member countries should stand firmly by the court and not take steps that could curtail victims’ access to justice.”.

    In his October 9 announcement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza.

    After a China-Russia-US summit––at which the three countries’ leaders adopted a declaration that included expressing concern for state consent and the immunity of state officials, and that the ICC and other similar bodies should not “abuse their jurisdiction”––US President Donald Trump on November 20 remarked that Russian President Vladimir Putin “especially is not happy with” the ICC. Putin faces war crimes charges before the ICC for the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia.

    The US government has pitched the court-wide sanctions as “structured ... to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address” its “concerns.” The authorization of certain transactions with the court for a six-month period, which otherwise would have been immediately affected by the court-wide sanctions, is an ultimatum to member countries to meet the US government’s demands; but these demands effectively allow the Trump administration to determine whom the court can prosecute, Human Rights Watch stated.

    In the lead-up to the Assembly session, media reports referred to concerning proposals by some countries to meet US demands, including curbing the court’s jurisdiction over nationals of nonmember countries or exempting heads of state from the court’s reach. Offering the US government solutions that would hollow out the court’s mandate and guarantee impunity for certain powerful individuals would severely undermine the legitimacy and credibility of the ICC and the international justice system, Human Rights Watch said.

    In a recent development, at the Assembly session, ICC member countries should focus on safeguarding the court’s independence and taking concrete actions to protect the ICC and those cooperating with it. This should include calling on the European Union to urgently activate its Blocking Statute, which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions, Human Rights Watch said.

    Seven lawsuits have been brought in US federal court over the US sanctions targeting the ICC and those supporting its work. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed one of these lawsuits on August 11, seeking to have the sanctions regime struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit.

    The United States is also stepping up diplomatic pressure on ICC member countries to leave the court. Over the past year, seven countries—Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Venezuela, Chad, Naoero and Tajikistan—decided to withdraw from the ICC. While not all of these withdrawals can be linked to US pressure, they undermine efforts to achieve the global adoption of the court’s founding treaty, the Rome Statute. Tajikistan’s notification of withdrawal on November 20 followed its failure, for a second time, to arrest Putin when he was visiting the country and surrender him to the court, as required by its obligations as an ICC member. The Tajik parliament had adopted legislation on withdrawal in October.

    According to recent reports, “US efforts to press countries to withdraw from the Rome Statute are both an attack on states that have chosen to become ICC members and on international justice itself,” Evenson said. “The Trump administration has little standing with respect to either.”.

    According to recent reports, at the upcoming session, ICC members should call on the countries that have withdrawn to reconsider their decisions and remain part of the court. They should also engage with other ICC members to develop strategies to counter US pressure and promote a unified community of member countries, Human Rights Watch noted.

    Other issues on the Assembly’s agenda include electing 6 of the court’s 18 judges and making decisions on the process for the election of the court’s next prosecutor, expected to be held in December 2027. On July 24, 2026, the Assembly removed ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan from office for serious misconduct and serious breach of duty. Member countries should focus on merit and the most qualified candidates as they make decisions about elections that will shape the future of the court, Human Rights Watch said.

    Sources indicate that “The ICC’s daily work as grave abuses continue around the world is proof of the urgent need to protect the global rule of law,” Evenson said. “Member countries should demonstrate that they reject the idea of a world where might makes right and use their annual meeting to stand for ensuring no one is above the law.”.

    Upcoming UN Report Investigates Attacks on Aid Workers During Sri Lanka’s Civil War

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (438 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that on August 4, 2006, 17 Sri Lankan staff members of the Paris-based humanitarian organization Action Contre la Faim (Action Against Hunger) were summarily executed at their office in Muttur, Sri Lanka.
    • A newly introduced report by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, “I Died Many Times”; Attacks on Humanitarian Assistance in Sri Lanka, documents the numerous threats aid workers faced during the final years of Sri Lanka’s civil war with the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.
    • The report finds that the government purposefully shut down humanitarian space “as a slow, deliberate strangulation” that effectively cordoned civilians into government-held areas, preventing independent observers from witnessing war crimes by the warring parties.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that on August 4, 2006, 17 Sri Lankan staff members of the Paris-based humanitarian organization Action Contre la Faim (Action Against Hunger) were summarily executed at their office in Muttur, Sri Lanka. Over 20 years later, this unresolved case is emblematic of attacks on humanitarian workers during the country’s brutal civil war that ended in 2009.

    A newly introduced report by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, “I Died Many Times”; Attacks on Humanitarian Assistance in Sri Lanka, documents the numerous threats aid workers faced during the final years of Sri Lanka’s civil war with the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.

    The report finds that the government purposefully shut down humanitarian space “as a slow, deliberate strangulation” that effectively cordoned civilians into government-held areas, preventing independent observers from witnessing war crimes by the warring parties. The report, which is the latest from the UN’s Sri Lanka Accountability Project to gather evidence of international crimes in Sri Lanka, also finds “that impunity has resulted not from isolated failures, but from mutually reinforcing practices that have repeatedly frustrated accountability.”.

    The UN identifies four causes of impunity. First, it notes the state’s denial of responsibility. Second, the persistent failure of domestic investigations and prosecutions to deliver accountability. Third, it documents threats to victims, witnesses, and experts and the lack of effective witness protection in Sri Lanka. Lastly, it notes the appointment of presidential commissions of inquiry by successive governments instead of pursuing effective prosecutions.

    Recent findings suggest that sri Lanka’s 26-year civil war was marked by serious human rights abuses and war crimes by both sides. Despite numerous domestic, international, and UN investigations, there has been no justice.

    In a recent development, while President Anura Kumara Dissanayake took office in September 2024 promising justice for past rights abuses, most victims remain without answers or accountability because of the government’s failure to bring legal and structural reforms, including the promised independent public prosecutor’s office. The government has also refused to accept the Sri Lanka Accountability Project, which was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021 to collect evidence of serious rights abuses for use in possible future trials. This report shows why the UN’s evidence collection in Sri Lanka is as important as ever.

    #135952. Breaking: Slow Horses has been renewed well into the future

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (513 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Slow Horses has been renewed well into the future

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone.
    • Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed.
    • But the series has been renewed even further than that.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone.

    Yes. Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed. Season 6 just aired this fall, on its home network of Apple TV+, and work on the 7th season has begun.

    But the series has been renewed even further than that. When Season 6 aired, we learned that the show had been renewed for an 8th season. This was great news.

    And now, Apple has revealed that the series will continue through Season 10! Yes, Seasons 9 and 10 have been announced! This means we have four more seasons to look forward to. That’s four more years of Jackson Lamb and his crew of misfits. That’s a whole American presidential term’s worth of Slow Horses.

    It has been revealed that until Season 6, each season of the show has adapted a single one of Heron’s novels, all in chronological order. Season 6 broke the mold by adapting two: the sequential volumes Joe Country and Slough House. This means there are two extant novels left to adapt, Bad Actors and Clown Town, and early reports have confirmed that seasons 7 and 8 will undertake each of those novels, respectively. This means that Heron’s next novel will also be guaranteed a season, as will the next.

    Will he indeed write more? Yes, it certainly seems so, though there have been no announcements about a upcoming installment. The most recent novel, Clown Town, was released in 2025, and Heron’s novels typically have a 1-3 year gap in between them. But there’s still plenty of relevant Slough House material rife for adaptation; Heron has also published five Slough House novellas, none of which have been adapted yet. (Interested readers should note that all the novellas thus far have been collected in a volume called Standing By the Wall.).

    The series Slow Horses stars Gary Oldman as the irascible, perpetually-disheveled, foul-mouthed, flatulent and yet thoroughly lovable MI5 agent Jackson Lamb, who oversees a notorious departmental backwater of the Secret Service called Slough House, an institutional repository for agents who have badly messed up (or pissed off somebody vital). Time and time again Lamb and his team of oddballs, including Jack Lowden’s put-in-Slough-House-by-sabotage River Cartwright, wind up using their special skills, disregard for the rules, and occasional desire to prove themselves/not be messed with to save the day, often. It’s the best.

    • He can go anywhere in the world except his homeland.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When I was choosing the setting for my new book, The Mark of Moriarty, which re-imagines the titular Professor survived his last battle with Sherlock Holmes, I found myself genuinely spoiled for choice.

    Holmes, for all his fantastical adventures, rarely travelled beyond London, glimpsing the wider world only when it came to his doorstep. Professor Moriarty, presumed dead post-Reichenbach and presumably still notorious in the UK, is in the exact opposite position.

    He can go anywhere in the world except his homeland.

    While I was scouring the globe for an interesting place to send the master criminal, I kept coming back to a recurring theme in Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s books. Indeed, even as a child, reading the classic Holmes adventures, one thought kept jumping out at me….

    “Wow, this guy really likes the USA.”.

    As I grew up, I discovered just how true this is. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s enthusiasm with the United States was a matter of public record. He took great inspiration from this newfound nation, recovering from a civil war and forging its future before his eyes.

    In the process of looking into this transatlantic fascination, I thought I’d share some weird and wonderful findings about Doyle’s brushes with the states, his encounters with citizens of that nation…  and one confrontation with a visitor from Atlantis.

    Recent findings suggest that even before he set foot in the States, Doyle devoured news from America. In fact, factions and societies from the USA featured prominently throughout his work and across the Sherlock Holmes canon.

    Sources indicate that when he was just twenty-one years old, Doyle anonymously published “An American’s Tale”, a short story in which an Englishman is accused of murdering a rival in Arizona. Taking the Englishman to “Flytrap Gulch” to hang him for his crime, the supposed victim is unexpectedly discovered inside… a giant man-eating plant.

    One of Doyle’s more fantastical tales, it certainly paints the USA as a strange and undiscovered country.

    As he embarked on the Holmes canon, Doyle still injected America into his stories, with a particular interest in the factions and societies across the pond.

    It has been revealed that his story, “The Five Orange Pips” features allusions to the infamous KKK. His final of the Sherlock Holmes novels, The Valley of Fear, was born out of his fascination with the Molly Maguires, a secret society that engaged in radical industrial action against Pennsylvanian mining companies, and the Pinkertons, the brutal detective agency who were hired to stop them.

    Doyle’s enthusiasm for American goings-on did sometimes outpace his knowledge, however, particularly due to his reliance on secondary sources which filtered to the UK.

    Holmes’ very first appearance, A Study In Scarlet, featured an organisation called the Danites, an avenging division of the Mormon Church’s mysterious “Council of Four”.

    While the Danites certainly existed, historians consider them a short-lived faction based in mid-century Missouri, and far from the organised assassin squad from the book, with Doyle’s own daughter explaining that her father “would be the first to admit that his first Sherlock Holmes novel was full of errors about the Mormons”.

    For the record, there’s no evidence that he believed in man-eating plants.

    Eventually, shortly after Sherlock met his end at the Reichenbach Falls, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle finally visited America for the first time.

    Recent findings suggest that the Sherlock Holmes stories had proceeded him. He was met with an incredible reception from his already prominent U.S. fanbase, with the Boston Globe reporting him as; well proportioned, attractive and with a handsome face.

    In his journeys, Arthur Conan Doyle only grew fonder of America; reporting an incredible time spent on an elevator in Manhattan’s Woolworth Building, whose speed he compared to an artillery weapon, and defending the USA against nitpicking critics by saying;.

    “Every globe-trotter has paragraphs about the number of spittoons in a hotel bar (as if it matters!)”.

    Doyle also fell in love with the sport of baseball, to the point of committing a cardinal sin for any Brit; suggesting British football teams should adopt the sport.

    “I will venture to say, that if this was done, we should in a few years have as many to see a baseball final between Tottenham Hotspur and Preston North End as come now to the football.

    As to the furore which a decent British team, could we evolve one, would create in America, it is impossible to exaggerate it.”.

    Sadly, the United Kingdom has failed to assemble Doyle’s dream team.

    Despite the international success of his books, it was his forays into Spiritualism which brought Doyle back to the United States in the 1920’s, and which brought him in contact with his most prominent trans-atlantic friendship.

    One of the dramas that marked Doyle’s later American travels was his fractious friendship with magician Harry Houdini.

    Recent findings suggest that admirers of each other’s work, Doyle and Houdini held the opposite opinions on the supernatural that one might expect. Doyle, the creator of super-logician Sherlock Holmes, had become a devout spiritualist, while the magician Houdini was an ardent sceptic.

    Strangely enough, so strong was Doyle’s belief, that he insisted Houdini’s escapist tricks involved some form of magic, refusing to budge when Houdini himself told him otherwise.

    “My dear chap.” Doyle wrote in a letter to his friend. “Why do you go around the world seeking a demonstration of the occult when you are giving one all the time?”.

    Houdini even invited Doyle to the annual dinner at the Society of American Magicians. As a prank, and to prove Magicians could be fooled as much as they claimed Spiritualists were, Doyle screened footage of “live dinosaurs” to an astounded audience.

    These live dinosaurs would prove to be stop-motion animations, taken from the upcoming film adaptation of Doyle’s novel; The Lost World.

    Despite their spirited back and forth, tensions between the pair came to a head during a 1922 visit to Atlantic City, where Doyle’s wife Jean, channelled Houdini’s mother at a séance. The incident forced Houdini to publicly denounce the events in question, placing Doyle & Houdini publicly at odds.

    It was on his Spiritualism tour that Doyle had the strangest encounter Doyle he would perhaps have in America, when Doyle met one of his fans, an old Colonel from the South.

    While in Cleveland, described unflatteringly by Doyle as “a grim city of iron and shipping”, Doyle was advancing his lectures on Spiritualism, when he was confronted by an old Southern Colonel with an incredible story to tell.

    “The Colonel thought he was an Atlantean by origin,” Doyle reported, with the Colonel continuing to explain that his mother was the former Atlantean Queen.

    Though the author tolerated this eccentric visitor in the daytime, when the Colonel showed up at his hotel room at night, with a message from the former Queen, Doyle was forced to confront the more troubling side of fandom.

    In the end, long after Doyle’s love-affair with the USA began, Sherlock Holmes himself finally set foot in the States.

    It was in 1917, in “The Final Bow”, the last story in the Sherlock Holmes canon, that the detective confirmed he had crossed the Atlantic, travelling to Chicago and beyond.

    It’s a fitting end to a canon which, despite taking place primarily in London, is so deeply suffused with Doyle’s love for the States.

    The more I’ve learned about it, the more of a privilege it has seemed, to get the chance to send the iconic Professor to 1890’s Fresh York.

    A place full of the societies, mysticism and people his creator adored so much, where he’ll pull in to the same dock that Sir Arthur Conan Doyle did when he first set foot in America.

    Jack Anderson is a UK-based writer of horror and mystery fiction. Jack got his start writing for the internet, penning the viral serial "Has Anyone Heard of the Left/Right Game?," which he wrote in a caffeine-fueled haze. It has since been adapted into a hit QCODE podcast starring Tessa Thompson in the leading role of Alice. His debut thriller, The Grief Doctor, was published by Raven Books in June 2024. Jack is also developing a number of original television and film ideas across the horror genre. He lives with his wife in Sheffield. Lifelong fans of games and puzzles, together they’re burning through every escape room in the North of England.

    #135949. Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1590 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing.
    • Recent findings suggest that until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a).
    • Industry observers note that under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that on Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

    Recent findings suggest that until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a). According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado.

    Industry observers note that under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. Partly due to this policy, ICE’s overall detained population, which also includes people held on other grounds, hit a reported record of roughly 73,000 in mid-January 2026.

    In a recent development, section 1225(a)(1) deems any noncitizen “present in the United States who has not been admitted [to the country]” to be an “applicant for admission.” The detention command then provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained.” The courts of appeals agree that long-term residents who entered the U.S. unlawfully are deemed “applicant[s] for admission.” The dispute is whether that deemed status also means they are “seeking admission,” and would thus fall within Section 1225 and be detainable without bond.

    Eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) have now answered. Nine hold that Section 1226, not Section 1225(b)(2)(A), governs people arrested in the interior: the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits. Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.

    For the majority of circuits, “seeking admission” is an ordinary phrase Congress left undefined, and as the 1st Circuit put it, “means seeking lawful entry.” A person who crossed the border years ago is not seeking entry; he already entered. The deeming clause in Section 1225(a)(1) may make a long-term resident an applicant for admission, Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the 7th Circuit, but it does not “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission.” Structure points the same way: in the Laken Riley Act of January 2025, Congress expanded Section 1226(c)’s mandatory detention categories to reach certain unlawful entrants accused or convicted of specified offenses, a needless step if Section 1225 had always reached them. The majority of circuits add that five administrations over three decades read the statute their way, and that Congress would not silently have required detaining some two million people.

    Sources indicate that for the 5th and 8th Circuits, however, ordinary meaning cuts differently. To apply for something is to seek it, Judge Edith Jones wrote for the 5th Circuit; for example, a college applicant does not stop seeking admission once the application is filed. Several dissenters elsewhere go further and rest on the deeming clause itself, arguing that a legal fiction carries the attributes of the thing it deems. As 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa wrote in dissent, in a line later adopted by a 1st Circuit dissenter: “If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.”.

    According to recent reports, as for the government’s long contrary practice: “Years of consistent practice,” Jones wrote, “cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute’s plain text.” Government-side judges answer the Laken Riley point, too: Section 1226(c) also reaches admitted noncitizens and bars parole, and in January 2025 DHS still treated unlawful entrants as bond-eligible. Both sides now also cite the justices’ own June decision in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, which read “arrives in the United States” to mean crossing the border, noted fears of encouraging illegal entry “cannot defeat the best reading of the text,” and called the rule that every word must do work “not an iron rule.”.

    It has been revealed that the Supreme Court will soon have its say. On Oct. 1, the justices agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the government’s challenge to a unanimous 2nd Circuit panel ruling for a Brazilian man who has lived here more than 20 years, was detained in 2025 under Section 1225(b)(2)(A), and which that circuit court found to be inapplicable. No argument date is set yet; proposed merits briefing runs into February, pointing to argument in late winter or spring and a decision by term’s end.

    But a related constitutional question is also pending at the court. This is whether, even if under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detainees do not have a statutory right to a bond hearing, they have a right to one under the due process clause. On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.

    Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority: “Because Petitioners have never been admitted to the United States, due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal.” Seven judges dissented. Judge Leslie Southwick countered that the court “has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents,” who by the record had each lived here for more than a decade.

    For now, in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, noncitizens who entered without inspection thus have no ordinary path to a bond hearing; discretionary parole and a few claims the majority reserved remain, but those are narrow exits. The 8th Circuit’s ruling closes the statutory route across its seven states as well.

    In a recent development, the 3rd and 6th Circuits, on the other hand, have held that detaining long-present noncitizens under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) without a bond hearing does indeed violate due process. In these circuits, which cover Delaware, Newly introduced Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (the 3rd Circuit), and Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee (the 6th Circuit), long-term residents can point to circuit precedent recognizing a due process right to a bond hearing. One’s geographical location thus makes all the difference.

    Recent findings suggest that if the court affirms in Rhoney, subject to specific exceptions, noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later arrested in the interior could again ask for bond everywhere, as they could before July 2025. A hearing does not guarantee release, and the burden is generally on the detainee, but the right to ask for bond would be the same in every circuit. If the court reverses in Rhoney, mandatory detention becomes the statutory rule everywhere, yet geography, as noted, would still matter: the 3rd and 6th Circuits have held that a constitutional right to due process requires bond hearings for long-resident detainees like those before them, and the 5th has held it does not.

    Industry observers note that that is where the case of Putra v. Lopez-Campos comes in. The government’s petition from its loss in the 6th Circuit in that case raises both the statutory and constitutional questions, and the solicitor general urged the justices to take it for that reason. The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided. If the government wins in Rhoney, the split between the 3rd and 6th Circuits, which found a due process right to a bond hearing, and the 5th, which did not, would matter far more, and the justices would likely have to take up Putra to settle the due process issue. But if the detainees win in Rhoney, that constitutional question may never need an answer.

    Recent findings suggest that rhoney should be decided before the term ends next summer. Based on this decision, we will see if the constitutional dispute follows. In the meantime, tens of thousands of people remain detained.

    Kemal Hepsen is the managing attorney of Hepsen Law Firm, a federal litigation firm that represents noncitizens nationwide in habeas corpus, mandamus, and Administrative Procedure Act cases.

    Recommended Citation: Kemal Hepsen, Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 17, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/mandatory-detention-arrives-at-the-supreme-court-though-not-all-at-once/.
