    #135948. Breaking: Quinn Connor on body horror, queerness, academia, and southern gothic novels

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3667 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Quinn Connor on body horror, queerness, academia, and southern gothic novels

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Your Beloved Remains is the third novel by Quinn Connor, and sits alongside their other Southern gothic stories.
    • After discovering the school might be closing, Celia finds a lost manuscript by the school’s founder, a feminist writer and heiress whose life and work has cast a long shadow over the school and its reputation.
    • The book is part mystery, part gothic horror, part dark academia, part dysfunctional romance, though that doesn’t do justice to the strangeness of the book, the atmosphere, the ideas around literature and the university that are thrown around—and just how much fun it all is.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Your Beloved Remains is the third novel by Quinn Connor, and sits alongside their other Southern gothic stories. This novel is set at Basin College, a small school in a remote part of Arkansas where Celia Kiel, the school’s archivist, has spent her whole life.

    After discovering the school might be closing, Celia finds a lost manuscript by the school’s founder, a feminist writer and heiress whose life and work has cast a long shadow over the school and its reputation. Working from a partial manuscript she found pickled in formaldehyde, she teams up with Joan Harriot, a literature postdoc, who is not just a gifted mimic but Celia’s academic nemesis, to forge and reconstruct the book in an effort to save the school.

    The book is part mystery, part gothic horror, part dark academia, part dysfunctional romance, though that doesn’t do justice to the strangeness of the book, the atmosphere, the ideas around literature and the university that are thrown around—and just how much fun it all is.

    The book tells the story of a very dysfunctional pair writing a manuscript, and so we reached out to Dr. Robyn Barrow and Alex Cronin, the writing duo behind Quinn Connor to ask about how they write together without trying to kill each other, academia, queer Southern stories, body horror, and how their writing surprises the people who know them.

    In a recent development, AD: I really enjoyed Your Beloved Remains, which was so much fun. Maybe fun is the wrong word?

    AD: From the beginning of your writing career, I’m sure people have asked, how do the two of you work together? Here you have written a book that is explicitly about a literary partnership. Was this kind of inevitable?

    AC: It probably was a little bit inevitable, because it’s always been interesting to us. Just quickly on the way we work: We’ve been doing this for thirteen years now. The way it works is that I have a character, Robyn has a character, and then we bring them in conversation. We are often literally passing the laptop back and forth, line by line, switching who writes it. So it ends up being super seamless.

    Recent findings suggest that of course, over thirteen years, I think we have learned enough about it to know how bad it could be if we did not truly like each other. We have strong boundaries with co-writing. We get along. We have a lot of the same tastes. We love each other. These are the things that make co-writing safe.

    But because it’s so safe for us, it was really fun to explore [the question], “but what if it wasn’t safe?” Because it is so vulnerable to be co-writing and sharing a creative project. To share that can feel really scary. So what if the worst thing happened? What if all of those hurt feelings that could exist grew into something wild and terrifying?

    Industry observers note that AD: There is a scene where, not to spoil too much, but Celia gets those first pages back and she goes, this is horrible. Because she can’t give or take criticism well. But she’s also in pain because it’s so good and she knows she could never have written it, so she’s overwhelmed by anger and jealousy.

    AC: Robyn and I are very lucky because we have similar standards and we have similar but different talents. We’re very compatible, but co-writing with someone who is not compatible would be really difficult. Celia finds herself in this position where she just is struggling to keep up and that is a horror for her because she wants to be the keeper of Beatrice. The keeper of this archive and of her voice. And she can’t do it. The way that Harriot describes it is Celia is “a high priestess who can’t hear the voice of god.”.

    AD: Which is such a great phrase, but the book resembles a lot of different genres. It’s gothic, it’s dark academia. Robyn, I know you work in academia, so I’m sure you have thoughts on the genre.

    RB: We have always loved Donna Tartt and The Secret History. We loved it and around 2017, 2018, it felt like suddenly the internet discovered it. It was everywhere and it sort of ballooned into this whole genre, “dark academia.”.

    It’s great that there are so many people enjoying reading and writing this genre, but it has gone quite far from The Secret History. Now there’s dark academic fantasy and all these versions that, to me, have nothing to do with academia. They’re not really exploring the themes of the university that I find interesting.

    According to recent reports, when I pitched the idea for Your Beloved Remains to Alex, I was like, “We’re gonna make this call from inside the house.” This is about academic frustration. The kind of rage that can build up in an eternal grad program.

    Sources indicate that when I came up with the pitch, I was in the sixth year of an eight-year grad program. A lot of Harriot’s struggles with her career and the feelings that she has about being a postdoc, was cathartic for me to write through. Hopefully it gets back to some of the roots of dark academia. We’re re-coining this book as “academic horror.”.

    AC: I’m just going to parrot what I’ve heard Robyn say before, which is that often these books focus on the students, but in our book, the students are not really a part of it. It’s about the institution. The students can leave on holiday break. They get to go home. This is about the people that don’t leave. Where the university is their life. Which, for Robyn, has been a really good thing.

    Recent findings suggest that RB: It’s funny because since I wrote the book, I have gone on to finish my PhD and get a tenure-track job, which is like winning the lottery. That was never in the cards for Harriot. Harriot was never destined for tenure. [laughs].

    AC: It’s kind of the same thing as the collaboration question. It’s an exploration of the dark side and the horrible “what if things had gone a different way.”.

    AD: There’s an exchange in the book. “What does it mean to want something so much you end up destroying it?” Harriot answers “it sounds like doing a PhD in the humanities.”.

    It has been revealed that RB: [laughs] Exactly! Sometimes you make the thing that you love your job, which I would say is true both in academia and as an author. You make writing that you love the thing that you make money off of, and then you spend so long grinding that you actually ruin it. Harriot is so burnt out. She clearly came to being a literary scholar because she loved reading, and now she’s so cynical and so lost because of all the years of struggle with that.

    AD: You remarked that students are kind of the point of academia, but they’re only there for a few years, but there are people who spend their whole lives there.

    RB: Since most people who write books about academia have only ever been undergraduate students, they see themselves as the center of the system. But they’re really the compensatory engine of a system that is producing something that is actually not their education. I think that is fascinating. I truly care so much about my students. My students are the reason I want to be in academia, but for many researchers and faculty members, students are not the reason that they are doing their job.

    Industry observers note that AC: Also, the people who run the college, the board and the President, they’re looking at the bottom line. There’s this question that’s the propulsive engine of the first act: Is Basin College going to close? Celia cares because of the archive and because it’s her home. But there’s also the question of what about all of these students that are presently there. What’s going to happen to them?

    There is this unspoken understanding that the board doesn’t care about them. It’s not about them. They’re a part of this system and nobody is thinking about them at all.

    AD: They’re running a business.

    RB: The book was coming out of a moment when it felt like universities were operating as these hedge funds for the wealthy. We started writing this book in 2023. Now higher education is under threat. I think that the university is a really good and important thing in our society. I want to defend it and I want to be a good voice in the university.

    Industry observers note that AC: I think there’s a big question in the book, “how do you love something?” Celia’s version of loving it is excusing any of its wrongs and pretending it’s perfect. Harriot’s version is critiquing it almost to the point of picking it apart.

    I think that’s how we feel about the university. Yes, it’s wonderful. It’s something that we need. It also is worthy of critique and could be improved and made better. There are these questions of how you engage with something that you love, and because you love it you are frustrated by it greatly.

    Sources indicate that AD: Historically most universities were set apart from cities to let people study and work. And there’s a way that attracts people like Celia who use it as a place to hide from the larger world.

    Industry observers note that RB: It’s got a monastic quality. That can also go into a cult-like quality. Harriot is really running from her past by arriving at Basin College, which is a very particularly isolated and spooky version.

    AD: It is very remote, but also, there are a lot of colleges in the middle of nowhere.

    AC: Beatrice Donahue created it specifically for that reason. She said, “my husband is finally dead, I have money, I am free. I want to go do exactly what I want to do.”.

    What she wanted to do was find some place remote where she and the women in her life and her lover could be themselves in all of their weird, witchy, queer glory. A lot of universities were not created for that reason, but it was fun to think about this university that was and how these things can start from such a seed and still become so institutionalized and twisted and different from the starting place.

    RB: I do like that point that Basin College in its foundational message, was meant to be a safe place for women and a safe place for queer people to live as their true selves. I feel like the university can be that way. The ivory tower is a place where you see many different kinds of people getting to ask the kinds of questions they’re interested in. I feel like that is a beautiful thing about college. But it all depends on who’s in charge.

    Sources indicate that AD: It does get at that, which is so important for people. Also it touches on how a lot of schools that may have become institutions, but were started by people who were strange or even crazy.

    AC: [laughs] Beatrice is, but she’s gloriously powerful. She’s dead but she has cast such a long shadow. She brought these women who did not fit in society. One of our inspirations was Victorian tea rooms, which was one of the few jobs back then that women could have. So Beatrice had a tea room. Women were finding ways to exist and to be free under incredible constraints. That’s what Basin College was for her.

    AD: It’s a queer book about how queer spaces have always existed just as queer people have always existed. And that these spaces and institutions have existed through time.

    RB: This is our third novel and in our previous work we’ve had queer storylines that have been a reclaiming of queer joy, which has been really wonderful. In this book we wanted to just have freaky scary lesbians doing bad things and not apologizing for it. Just ripping the world down.

    In a recent development, AC: There’s all sorts of different ways that queer people can be portrayed. Because they’re people. You almost have to start with a portrayal where they are good, because there are a lot of people that may not have knowingly met a queer person. You almost have to start with, guess what, you can love a queer character. The more these stories come out, the more freedom you have to add grittiness and reality into that portrayal.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s wonderful to be able to have queer characters that behave badly and it doesn’t feel like a condemnation on queerness as an entire experience. For us, being able to write through queer joy gave us the freedom to write queer messiness as well.

    RB: This is coming from our background as Southern women, as well. I feel like up in these parts it can feel that queer pain is a distant memory for many people, but for us, coming out in 2018 was a completely different world. Writing Southern stories about queer people means a lot to people in Arkansas and these places.

    Industry observers note that AC: There’s people that would have you believe that queerness doesn’t exist there. Or that it needs to be kept very quiet, or regulated extremely heavily. Or made illegal. But there have always been queer people in Arkansas.

    In a recent development, there’s also the idea that the North is the home of the ivory tower. That New England is where you’ve got all these schools, but there’s always been incredible intelligence like in Arkansas. These things, that they would have you believe don’t exist, have always been there. These people, that they tell you don’t exist or don’t deserve to exist, have always been there and been a part of it.

    AD: As you were talking about the messiness, I keep thinking about how the book takes place over a few months. It opens with the fall semester and the school is functioning as it has been, and by the Christmas holiday, everything unravels and descends into chaos.

    RB: We have Beatrice Donahue’s dark secret at the center of the novel. You don’t find out right away, which has made it hard for me at times to know how to pitch the novel. I feel like this is a key element that you don’t want to spoil. Beatrice lost her lover and the aftermath of that grief and where she goes with that is super kinky and interesting and transgressive and queer.

    Then you have these women in the 1980s that are excavating that and discovering within themselves how they feel about that and how they feel about each other. It’s fun to surprise the reader with that part way through. It’s good to highlight for readers that the book is spicy and bizarre. And a great time, hopefully.

    In a recent development, AC:  We’re thinking about all of these highfalutin ideas, but we’re also playing a game of chicken with each other. We’re trying to freak each other out a little bit when we’re writing. We’re trying to make it fun.

    Sources indicate that sometimes I write something and then I’m sitting there waiting for Robin to get to it so I can get her reaction. There’s a lot about the book that is intentionally fun because we were having fun. Everything that the reader feels, we felt as we were writing it and surprising each other and grossing each other out and delighting each other.

    AD: I’m sure. Going, what if she cuts her foot, what if it gets infected, what if we have this body horror scene.

    AC: What’s weird is that we wrote all of that, but it grosses me out to think about it. One of my friends was reminding me about a particular scene with the foot. I remember us writing that, and I have not gone back and read it again because it grosses me out! [laughs].

    AD: I’m pretty sure I know the exact scene you’re talking about.

    AC: [laughs] It’s a weird way to feel about something you wrote.

    AD: At the center of the book is this lost manuscript of Beatrice’s, and in writing the book you had to figure out how much of that book to write, how much to include so it doesn’t overwhelm the story.

    Sources indicate that AC: A couple people have asked about this, actually. One friend said, “you should do Dreams of the Rose, the entire book from Beatrice Donahue.” Our answer has consistently been, “no!” My gosh, that was so hard to do.

    Industry observers note that RB: One of the substantial influences in the book that I don’t think we’ve talked about before is Possession by A.S. Byatt. I love that novel. It’s absolutely amazing. In that book there’s a lot of the writing of the authors in the book.

    With Beatrice Donahue we wanted the kind of unreachability of her to be center stage. What’s on the page is all of the writings of Beatrice Donahue that there is. There’s no additional pages. We found it extremely tiresome to do.

    Harriot has this power of mimicry where she can hear the writing of someone else and then produce it. That came from my own perception of my own writing. I feel like I can really get the sound of someone else’s writing and copy that or produce that, in a sense. Beatrice Donahue is a shared character, but I would read Mary Shelley and Poe and nineteenth-century work and then I would write these passages of Donahue.

    Industry observers note that I’m very attuned to word choice. I feel like it’s so easy to get taken out of that kind of writing with a misplaced word or something that just doesn’t hit quite right. This is just someone in the present pretending to write about the past. I wanted it to have a strong truth claim. Starting with the note from the editors and then all the writing, I wanted it to feel really immersive. This could have been true.

    According to recent reports, AD: You mentioned before that each were the primary writer of one of the characters. Who did you write?

    AC: I wrote Celia. To the great surprise of most people, I wrote Celia.

    RB: For some reason, Alex’s friends were like, “she couldn’t have done that.”.

    AC: I think because the wildness of Celia and where we go in her perspective is pretty stark. I think that a lot of people that know me are just surprised because I’m an introvert. There’s a lot that comes out in Celia’s perspective that people maybe didn’t think we were capable of, who have read our other books or know us personally.

    AD: I think Celia would have to be written by an introvert.

    Recent findings suggest that AC: That’s how I feel! She’s got a very rich inner world, and it’s twisted in there.

    AD: It’s also funny that you wrote the foot scene and then went, this is disgusting, I can’t read it again.

    RB: Alex writes way grosser stuff than I do.

    AD: That is interesting. Do people have a somewhat misunderstood sense of what you write or how you write?

    RB: I think there’s definitely a pattern between the three books. Alex’s characters are always extremely vulnerable and very emotionally open. Which is interesting because between the two of us, she’s definitely more emotionally unavailable in the real world. My characters are a bit more closed off and they’re usually cool. [laughs] I’m the least cool person, but then I write these cool characters. To my best friends, it’s pretty obvious that Harriot is me. She’s like my shadow side.

    Sources indicate that people do have a good time guessing. We go back and forth, should we tell people who wrote what? Should we keep it a secret? Because obviously we want the experience to be seamless.

    According to recent reports, AD: You mentioned one struggle has been finding a way to talk about the book without spoiling too much. Which I understand.

    RB: I’ve been thinking about the pitch for the book and if we’re pitching it correctly. I think what it’s really about is that Celia longs for more than anything, the love of this Victorian author that she’s always admired. In her desperate reaching for that, she recruits her academic nemesis who has this talent for mimicry to go with her on this journey that leads to a total shit show descent into complete chaos in this snowy remote college.

    In a recent development, that’s what I think the book is about. There’s many, many bizarre and spicy surprises along the way. [laughs].

    It has been revealed that AD: It’s true, and a lot of what we’ve been talking about, the gothic elements and academia and the two falling for each other, that’s the first half. The second half, just buckle up for the ride.

    RB: Someone asked us, do you provide aftercare for your readers at the end of the book? I was like, we don’t. I feel like the book is just like a rock and roll roller coaster and you get spat out at the end. I hope that you’re sitting there, staring at the book going, what did I just read? [laughs].

    Alex Dueben has written for The Believer, Vulture, The Millions, The Los Angeles Review of Books, The Brooklyn Rail, and many other publications. He is the writer and editor of the artist monograph Hurricane Nancy, and his debut novel is forthcoming.

    Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on fresh petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks.
    • Sources indicate that the federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec.
    • Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on fresh petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

    Sources indicate that the federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

    In United States v. Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

    In the government’s petition for review, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”.

    The challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. And in any event, they added, the ruling is correct, because the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers was motivated by hostility to transgender people rather than “military judgments.”.

    It has been revealed that in another case to be considered, Trump and the federal government have each filed petitions for review in connection with Trump’s challenge to the $83.3 million verdict entered against him in a lawsuit brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a Newly introduced York department store and that Trump in 2019 had defamed her by calling her a liar.

    In a recent development, trump’s petition for review points to the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office. Trump’s private attorney, Robert Giuffra, wrote that “[t]he threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”.

    The federal government’s petition for review asks the Supreme Court to also decide whether the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case because Trump made the statements at the center of the dispute as part of his role as president.

    And in United States v. Jackson and United States v. Office of the Upcoming York State Attorney General, the justices will decide whether to weigh in on the legality of Trump’s appointments of acting U.S. attorneys in Nevada and New York.

    Industry observers note that under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Sigal Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

    Sources indicate that with only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi remarked, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

    Sources indicate that bondi followed a similar path for John Sarcone in the Northern District of Upcoming York, naming him first as the interim U.S. Attorney and then, when his interim term expired, naming him as the first assistant U.S. attorney and a “special attorney,” effectively designating him as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.”.

    When challenges to the legitimacy of Chattah’s and Sarcone’s appointments followed, lower courts agreed that neither had been validly appointed. Sauer then came to the Supreme Court, where he told the justices that Chattah’s appointment was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.” He urged the court to take up that case, and to hold the Upcoming York case until the Nevada case is resolved.

    Sources indicate that in addition to those disputes, the justices will consider three other noteworthy petitions for review on Dec. 4:.

    According to recent reports, one thing to keep in mind: although the justices are slated to vote on these cases for the first time on Dec. 4, they may not act on any of them right away. In particular, for several years, the court has had a general practice of not granting a petition for review until the justices have considered it at two conferences. After the Dec. 4 conference, the justices will meet again on Dec. 11.

    Industry observers note that finally, yet another high-profile petition for review is likely to be before the justices soon: Trump v. Clinton, in which Trump is seeking to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.” Clinton originally waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition, but the court called for a response, which she filed on Nov. 13. In her response, Clinton contends that “President Donald Trump and his attorneys” “attempt to frame a routine opinion disposing of a frivolous lawsuit as a threat to ‘the Presidency.’”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    #135945. David Brandon Hodge on occult murders and the origins of Ouija boards

    David Brandon Hodge on occult murders and the origins of Ouija boards

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, at the time of the Upcoming Planchette article’s circulation in 1886, Charles Kennard was a real estate agent who owned a fertilizer business in Chestertown, Maryland, just across the wide expanse of the Chesapeake Bay from the state’s industrial center of Baltimore. Kennard was born in Delaware on Christmas Eve, 1857, and was eleven years old when he witnessed the “wonderful workings of Planchette” during its ﬁrst great craze. By 1876, he had begun “an investigation of psychical phenomenon” while living in Philadelphia, and his table-rapping experiments continued after he moved to Chestertown that same year.

    While Kennard never acknowledged any inﬂuence of the Ohio talking-board reports that appeared in 1886, it was that same year he claimed he envisioned an identical breakthrough, imagining he could receive communications quicker than raps or automatic writing “if words could be spelled by the alphabet.” He struck on what he believed was an original idea: “In 1886 I made a crude board, using a cake board and a table with four legs and a pointer, marking the alphabet and numerals in pencil,” and used the pairing to autonomously spell out messages letter by letter, joining the ranks of Armstrong, Damon, and Long as one of the earliest- known talking-board creators.

    To reﬁne his primitive eﬀorts, Kennard claimed, he visited local cabinetmaker and undertaker Ernest Christian “E. C.” Reiche, a Prussian immigrant whose workshop was adjacent to Kennard’s oﬃce in Chestertown’s Voshell House. He commissioned “about a dozen boards a little neater in appearance than the cake board,” which he then oﬀered for sale locally. He claimed his boards were “always being borrowed by neighbors, and those who purchased the few wanted more,” echoing similar stirrings of interest in Ohio that same year.

    According to recent reports, by his own account, he petitioned Reiche to continue the productive partnership, but as Kennard later recalled, “I asked him to continue making them for me and we would put the board on the market. This he stated he would not do. He was too busy to make any more. I would have to get someone else.” Left without a craftsman to manufacture the boards, Kennard’s commercial ambitions sat temporarily idle.

    According to recent reports, three years later, a competitive marketplace took its toll on Kennard’s fertilizer business, and in February 1890, he relocated his family to Baltimore. There, he opened a new real estate oﬃce in the Barnum Building and established new headquarters for his fertilizer company at 220 S. Charles Street. Kennard also rekindled his ambition to commercialize a talking board.10 In an account that echoes Cyrus H. Farley’s attempts to pitch planchettes in Boston, Kennard “showed the board to several who could see nothing of the future in it.”.

    In a recent development, but a fortuitous meeting came with local attorney and fellow Freemason Elijah Jeﬀerson Bond, who took an intense interest in what he called Kennard’s “witch board.” Bond recounted in later years how he made “important improvements” to Kennard’s design to get it into “marketable shape,” which included a round planchette with a sharply pointed extension that served as an indicator, setting it far apart from the heart-shaped planchettes of yesteryear. He paired the new planchette with a board that included two arched rows of the alphabet with a straight line of numbers below, closely matching newspaper illustrations from 1886.

    Bond added embellishments, including a black dot representing the full moon in one upper corner and a crescent moon in the other, and black stars in the bottom corners. An illustration at the bottom center depicting two men shaking hands—an important symbol of fraternity among Freemasons—ﬂanked on each side with the conjunction “Good Bye.”.

    The pair partnered with the goal of patenting and manufacturing the idea, with Bond ﬁnancing their earliest eﬀorts with a $500 investment.

    According to recent reports, the duo’s upcoming talking board had not yet been christened with its iconic name. As the two ironed out the details of the patent design in April 1890, they assembled at Bond’s home with some of his family members. Not satisﬁed with the initial name they had chosen, Charles Kennard proposed they ask the board what it would like to be called, as he later recounted:.

    The name Ouija was adopted by Mr. Bond and myself. We called this board by another name until we could secure a better one. One evening about April 1890, while trying the board with a Miss Peters, Mr. Bond’s sister-in-law, in the large boarding house at that time on the corner of Charles and Centre streets, where Mr. Bond boarded, I remarked that we had not yet settled upon a name, and as the board had helped us in other ways, we would ask it to propose one. It spelled out O-U-I-J-A. When I asked the meaning of the word it said “Good Luck.”.

    Industry observers note that miss Peters there upon drew upon her neck a chain which had at the end a locket, on it a ﬁgure of a woman and at the top the word “Ouija.” We asked her if she had thought of the name, and she stated she had not. We then adopted the word.

    According to recent reports, ouija was a strange word seemingly without precedent, and its fascinating combination of consonants and vowels, fabricated through Peters’s mediumship, added to the board’s mystique, even as unlikely as it was to have appeared on a locket. Yet her locket is an key clue that her role in Ouija’s naming may have direct ties to the Spiritualist movement.

    Peters had no known connection to Spiritualism in her upbringing, but such influence was deeply rooted in her future husband and then suitor Ernest Herbert Donisthorpe Nosworthy. An immigrant from the UK who arrived in January 1888 to work as a traveling salesman, Nosworthy was the seventh child of Frederick Arthur and Eliza Louisa Spry Nosworthy, née Thompson, of Manchester, England, the latter of whom was a talented trance medium who “often attracted large and refined public audiences at Birkenhead by her dramatic powers.”.

    In a recent development, she was the daughter of George Thompson, himself a prominent Spiritualist who sat with Leah Fox in the United States, and had served on the Council of the British National Association of Spiritualists. The younger Nosworthy’s sister, Beatrice, was also regarded as “one of the youngest and one of the best of trance mediums” in England.

    The Nosworthy family’s close bonds with one of the most famous mediums of the era may have directly influenced Ouija’s name. The family hosted famous medium Cora Hatch when she visited England, living with them for months at a time on multiple occasions during Nosworthy’s formative school years. Eliza Nosworthy was considered Hatch’s herald and was so close to the family that when Eliza’s prominent father died, the medium adopted him as a upcoming spirit guide with the blessing of the Nosworthy clan.

    However, it was another of Hatch’s spirit guides who might have inspired Ouija’s name: the specter of a woman named Ouina, Cora Scott’s most famous contact for her trance mediumship, and Spiritualists considered her a generous spirit who acted as “a messenger of peace and love between the two worlds.” Exposure to Ouina was most certainly in the environment of Ernest Nosworthy’s upbringing, and it may explain the mysterious locket with a woman’s figure and name described by Kennard in his remembrance of Ouija’s naming.

    Whatever the case, Bond and Kennard adopted the enigmatic moniker and turned toward securing a patent for their newly named product.

    During the mid-1930s, more stories of deaths involving messages received through Ouija made the headlines of American newspapers. The first involved the Turley family of Arizona, when fifteen-year-old Mattie shot her father, Ernes, twice in the back with a shotgun, which resulted in his death a few weeks later.

    The news spread far beyond local publications when reports revealed that it was Ouija’s messages that had commanded Mattie to murder her father. The story was further sensationalized by news that her mother and Ernest’s wife, Dorothea, was once voted “the most beautiful girl in America.”.

    It has been revealed that widely reprinted articles revealed how Dorothea had become obsessed with a local “handsome cowboy” named Kent Pearce and used the Ouija to manipulate her daughter into murdering her own father so that Dorothea would be free to marry Pearce. All three were charged, although Pearce denied any involvement and was ultimately found not guilty. Mattie pled guilty in juvenile court and was sentenced to an Arizona reform school, while her mother was found guilty and sentenced to prison but was freed three years later.

    Another sensational Ouija murder involved the Hurd family of Kansas City in 1935. Family matriarch Nellie received messages through her Ouija that her seventy-seven-year-old husband, Herbert, was “too fond of another woman” and that he had given his secret lover “$15,000 of a hidden fortune.”.

    According to recent reports, after receiving the messages, Nellie and her daughter Bertha ambushed Herbert and chained him to his bed before subjecting him to all manner of tortures, including beating him with a revolver, burning the soles of his feet with matches, and stabbing his legs with a dagger. Bertha also set to killing “the children”—three dogs and a cat—with carbon monoxide, which Nellie had commanded.

    These horrible acts led to Herbert signing a forced confession admitting to his affair, which the two women signed as “witnesses.” But a few hours later, Nellie momentarily left her gun within Herbert’s reach, and he seized it and shot his wife four times before making his escape.

    Police afterward discovered Herbert “running along the street clad only in his pajamas and carrying a still smoking revolver,” and he confessed to police immediately. Nellie died from her wounds, and the courts deter-mined her death to be a “justifiable homicide.” Bertha remained free after Herbert refused to press charges.

    As in prior decades, these Ouija-inspired murders sparked a flurry of sensational headlines like “The Ouija Again Spelled Death!” even if Herbert’s actions were an act of self-defense, and helped contribute to the growing chorus of Ouija’s malign and diabolical associations in the media.

    David Brandon Hodge is the author ofSupernatural Machines: The History of Spirit Communication Devices. Hodge is a historian, collector, and author specializing in the history of spirit communication devices. Founder of MysteriousPlanchette.com and curator of the world’s largest archive of séance artifacts, his research has appeared in Smithsonian Magazine and Paranormal Review, and has served as a consultant for museums and exhibitions worldwide, including the acclaimed Supernatural America exhibit at the Minneapolis Institute of Art and the Peabody Essex Museum’s Conjuring the Spirit World exhibit. Hodge has also appeared in many prominent programs as an expert on the occult, including Oddities, Mysteries at the Museum, and Expedition Files, and served as historical consultant and provided séance artifacts for Rick Alverson’s film The Mountain and Lasse Hellström’s biopic Hilma. Hodge is also a respected game designer and lecturer, known for his horror-themed scenarios and his work with Atlas Obscura and Coast to Coast AM. He owns and operates Monkey See, Monkey Do! toy store and Substantial Top Candy Shop in Austin, Texas, where he lives with his two children, Jack and Elliot, and the ghosts of several cats.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that here are five newly translated works of crime fiction, featuring selfish tourists, corrupt cops, desperate horse racers, antiquities smugglers, and amateur sleuths. Enjoy!

    Yves Ravey, Taormina Translated by Alyson Waters (New York Review of Books).

    Recent findings suggest that taormina is a ruthless condemnation of our selfish modern era, a road trip novel in which a married couple on vacation in Italy run over a migrant child, then proceed to do….nothing. They do not check on the body. They do not go to the police. They do not accept any form of responsibility. They don’t even bother to cover up their crimes (or at least, they cover for themselves only lazily and ineptly). The only action available to either spouse, by dint of their warped world view, is to blame others for their problems. A vicious gem that wouldn’t feel out of place in mid-century noir, although the story’s catalysts are firmly grounded in the 21st century.

    Gustavo Eduardo Abrevaya, The Bullet Inside Me Translated by Andrea G Labinger ( Schaffner Press).

    The Bullet Inside Me takes places at the height of Argentina’s Secret War; in this hard-boiled thriller of compromise and conspiracy, the young daughter of a fascist functionary is kidnapped, in a case that threatens the entire dictatorial order. By the same author as the impressive Sanctuary, this one’s just as compelling, and just as vicious.

    Genki Kawamura, The Horse and I Translated by Chikako Kobayashi (Flatiron).

    A beautiful tale of the lengths we go to for love. In The Horse and Me, a shy clerk forges a deep bond with a racing horse, one coveted by a wealthy rider who seems poised to destroy the stallion’s spirit. Without means of her own, the clerk begins stealing from her own union’s coffers in order to purchase, then maintain, her newfound soulmate. When her colleagues begin to catch on to the thefts, Kawamura’s heroine finds herself backed into a corner and desperate to turn her horse into a champion.

    Sacha Naspini, The Witch’s Mouth Translated by Clarissa Botsford  (Europa).

    Grave robbing in Tuscany from ancient Etruscan graves has been big business since before the war, but with new regulations cracking down on antiquities smuggling elsewhere in Italy, the little band of thieves at the center of the novel face new gangs trying to muscle into their territory, renewed inquiries from weary local authorities, and internal divisions that threaten to dissolve their operation entirely.

    Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press).

    Hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

    Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to The Fashion Police, a column where we spotlight some of the best fashion in crime film and TV.

    Industry observers note that it’s true. The United States navy is retiring a its signature peacoat. Yes, its signature peacoat! “The double-breasted, hip-length wool peacoat that is synonymous with the romance of the sea.” They’re retiring an iconic garment, a staple not only of military fashion, but also of fashion in general.

    They are replacing it with a black, synthetic, all-weather parka. Why are they doing this? A statement from the Navy’s Uniform Board remarked that it was due to the Navy’s “commitment to eliminating unnecessary costs while ensuring sailors have the cold-weather protection they need to accomplish their missions.” The U.S. Naval Institute News revealed that it was chosen was chosen for its “modern appearance,” and “its versatility in being able to be worn with service and dress uniforms and civilian clothing.” But it has NO personality. This is like tearing down a historic 18th century townhouse to put up a glass and steel high rise.

    In her piece on this landmark decision, Vanessa Friedman at The Fresh York Times noted the history and symbolic associations of the garment, writing.

    Recent findings suggest that first designed for Dutch sailors in the 18th century, the pijakker was particularly well-suited for life at sea: roomy enough to accommodate warm inner layers but streamlined enough not to get caught in a ship’s rigging. Its collar could be turned up to shield the face against wind, and side pockets kept the coat closer to the body in cold weather.

    Adopted by the Royal Navy in 1857, the peacoat made the leap to the U.S. Navy shortly thereafter, becoming standard problem in 1886. And though small details may have been tweaked, the general style has remained the same.

    Industry observers note that in 1962, Friedman notes, Yves Saint-Laurent included a peacoat in his womenswear Rive-Gauche show, launching the coat as as style staple for women. According to the brand,.

    It has been revealed that the simple shape of this practical garment sculpted the silhouette. The fact that it was not fitted and covered the hips made it ideal for women who did not yet feel daring enough to wear pants, which accentuated the female form.

    Recent findings suggest that saint Laurent’s 1962 fashion show opened with the pea coat, which was the first piece he presented under his own name. The model wore it with white shantung pants and mules. This ensemble paved the way for Yves Saint Laurent’s signature style, which borrowed from menswear in order to make women feel comfortable and confident.

    Recent findings suggest that but, for our purposes, the most iconic use of the peacoat is Robert Redford’s look in Three Days of the Condor, Sydney Pollack’s 1975 political espionage thriller, based on James Grady’s novel Six Days of the Condor). Redford plays a low-level CIA employee in Fresh York City who is the sole survivor of an attack on his small office branch, and then goes on the run, attempting to untangle what appears to be an enormous intra-bureau conspiracy. The peacoat is a nice choice for this character; as Valerie Steele, the director of the Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology told The New York Times, “the peacoat doesn’t have the associations with violence and warfare often attached to camouflage and Army greatcoats. Rather, the peacoat more often represents bravery against the elements and the romance of voyages to places unknown.”.

    In a recent development, an investigation last week by the Washington Post reported that Tate Weston, a graduate of Tulane University, was admitted to the law school after accusations of sexual assault of a fellow student. He pleaded guilty this month of felony second-degree battery and misdemeanor sexual battery.

    Despite the university president and the board of trustees knowing about the situation, Weston was not put on leave until last month.

    According to recent reports, now, 38 law students are calling for the immediate resignation of law dean Melanie D. Wilson—along with the associate dean of law student affairs, community and belonging; the assistant dean of law admissions; and the Title IX coordinator.

    #135940. Jessica Hamilton on possession, menopause, and the horrors of middle age

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1180 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Jessica Hamilton on possession, menopause, and the horrors of middle age

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Demonic possession or plain old menopause?
    • Sources indicate that in my novel, The Woods, my protagonist, Alice, is in the throes of middle age.
    • Industry observers note that scalding flames spread rapidly up the chest, wrapping a burning hand around the neck, moving onto the face causing a sheen of sweat on the forehead and upper lip that only intensifies the burn—no escape is possible from the fire within.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Demonic possession or plain old menopause? It can be hard to tell, which is why the horrors of middle age for women lend themselves so well to the horror genre. There are the physical horrors, when our bodies betray us. There are the psychological ones, when our minds betray us. And there are the sociological ones, perhaps the most insidious of them all, when our own communities betray us.

    Sources indicate that in my novel, The Woods, my protagonist, Alice, is in the throes of middle age. So, while she’s sure something sinister is in the woods, which seems to be targeting her family, she also questions herself at every turn, is constantly doubted by those around, her all while powering through the many physical hurdles of menopause.

    Industry observers note that scalding flames spread rapidly up the chest, wrapping a burning hand around the neck, moving onto the face causing a sheen of sweat on the forehead and upper lip that only intensifies the burn—no escape is possible from the fire within. A description of an everyday hot flash and yet it reads like a scene in a horror novel of a person being burned alive. The same can be done for the rivers of blood that may run unabated, the headaches that feel like a metal stake being driven into the scalp, the withering of the skin, the clumps of hair found in the drain after showering, the crack and creak of joints that ache.

    Recent findings suggest that these physical symptoms sound like well-known body horror tropes but are in fact real life experiences for many women going through menopause. In combination these symptoms can easily make a woman feel as though her body has been possessed by some evil force.

    Industry observers note that in his novel, Mary, Nat Cassidy describes the physical struggles of his middle-aged protagonist, Mary, in such a visceral way that it is in itself the horror. Making the reader forget that this is a stage of life that all women go through and not just the fiction of a very adept horror author.

    Then there are the psychological impacts of middle age for women. Extreme fatigue, anxiety, unprovoked anger, incessant mental chatter, dark thoughts, disrupted sleep, sudden surges of unmanageable rage, untreatable depression, gaps in memory—I have heard many women complain of one or more of these symptoms due to menopause.

    And yet, this list is what comes up when you google the symptoms of demonic possession. Clearly making the point that middle age lends itself well to the horror novel. It is one thing to feel that your body is turning on you, it’s another to feel that your mind is as well. And if you can’t trust yourself, then who can you trust?

    In the novel, Death in Her Hands by Ottessa Moshfegh the protagonist Vesta becomes obsessed with a note that she finds in the woods around her house and the mystery that it presents. Very rapidly the lines of reality become blurred for Vesta due to her confused state and her inability to decipher what is real and what is her own paranoia and delusion. She can’t trust herself which means she’s locked in an inescapable cycle of discovering something and then mistrusting that discovery.

    My own protagonist, Alice, senses that there is something sinister in the woods around their latest home but is prone to second guessing her own intuition because she no longer feels as sure of her memory or perception as she once did, before middle age. She wants to assert herself and what she believes is happening but lacks the confidence to do so under the influence of menopause.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re unable to trust your memory, if you’re prone to paranoia and anxiety, irrational mood swings and brain fog you’re also ripe to be gaslit by those around you. Women being gaslit is not a latest concept. The diagnosis of hysteria, which women were given until it was removed from the DSM in1980, was perhaps the most powerful tool of gaslighting.

    It has been revealed that these days it’s a little less obvious but happens just the same. It’s easy to dismiss a middle-aged women’s feelings by claiming that they are caused my menopausal hormones. But, if the paranoia, anxiety, depression grief etc. are in fact rooted in something other than hormonal changes this leaves a woman without the support she actually needs.

    In the case of my protagonist, her concerns about the safety of her family and the threat of the woods are dismissed by her husband, mother and best friend as the ramblings of a paranoid, anxiety riddled, grief stricken menopausal woman. Add to this the fact that women often feel invisible in society after reaching middle age and it results in lack of credibility, power and presence. What could be worse than the horror of not being believed, not having any authority and not being seen?

    Why did I choose to write about a middle-aged woman experiencing menopause in my latest novel? I’m fifty-one years old and have begun to experience a lot of what my protagonist, Alice, experiences. I wanted to give a voice to this stage in life and hopefully create some empathy for it in readers.

    Recent findings suggest that mostly though, it was because the things that Alice was experiencing at this stage of life were great tools to ramp up the tension of the horror in my writing. A character filled with paranoia, anxiety, and sleeplessness from the very start of the novel. One who questions herself and is questioned by those around her and who causes the reader to question whether something is real or simply a paranoid delusion. Set this character in a house with a tragic history, surrounded by ancient woods and I was off to the races.

    The simple truth is that often real life is the scariest of all and in the case of middle age for women, I’m sad to say, that is most certainly the case. Demonic possession or menopause? My bet is that it’s menopause. I don’t believe in demons, despite being a writer of horror.

    Recent findings suggest that fortunately, there’s hormone replacement therapy, an increase in information about it and the horror does, apparently, have an end at some point. In the meantime, may there be many more novels that have the menopausal hero saving the day, despite the hot flashes, brain fog, sleepless nights and gaslighting.

    Jessica Hamilton was born in Australia but grew up in Canada. She has lived and worked in the Czech Republic, Taiwan, India and Japan. She studied writing at the Humber School for Writers as well as George Brown College. She lives in Ontario, Canada with her husband, son and daughter. Her debut novel is titled What You Never Knew, her second novel is titled, Don't You Dare, and both are thrillers published by Crooked Lane Books.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This month’s recommendations feature Zhang Yimou’s sumptuous story of organized crime in 1930s Shanghai; Sergei Loznitsa’s disturbing satire set in Russian-occupied Ukraine; and Manuella Martinelli’s quietly haunting depiction of Augusto Pinochet’s Chile.

    Glamorous, criminal underworld,1930s Shanghai.

    It has been revealed that with Gong Li (Memoirs of A Geisha, Farewell My Concubine) in the lead role as Bijou, a nightclub singer and the mistress of an underworld boss (Li Boatian), Zhang Yimou’s Shanghai Triad features opulent period sets and a propulsive narrative. The story unfolds from the perspective of 14-year old Shuisheng (Wang Xiao Xiao) who has been sent from the countryside by his uncle to work for the Boss, who in turn makes him a personal servant to Bijou. “This is Shanghai,” Shuisheng is told. “There are hidden rules in everything you do or say.”.

    Over the course of seven days, Shuisheng learns about those rules as he witnesses gangland shootouts, discovers that Bijou is having an affair, and watches as Bijou’s relationship with the Boss unravels in intrigue and betrayal.

    Before making Shanghai Triad, Yimou and Li had previously collaborated on several classic films including Ju-Dou (1990) and Raise the Red Lantern (1991)—which is being re-released in theaters across North America for its thirty-fifth Anniversary.

    Directed by Zhang Yimou, 108 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    It has been revealed that composed of a series of several loosely linked vignettes that take place in Russian-occupied territory in Ukraine, and based on real-life amateur videos, Ukrainian director Sergei Loznitsa’s (The Two Prosecutors) Donbass makes you question everything you’re seeing. Up is down and right is wrong as actors get dressed to film what is supposed to be real news; a police chief explains to a man why his car no longer belongs to him; a bureaucrat at a maternity hospital shows staff a huge stock of food that they say they haven’t received.

    Loznitsa’s skills are on full display as he dips in and out of incidents with minimal set-up—you really don’t know where you’re headed, or what anyone will say or do—which is perhaps a good summary of what life was and is like in these zones.

    Sources indicate that filmed after Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and its covert operations in the eastern Donbass region, but before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Donbass keeps you transfixed with its bewildering and inexorable logic. In that sense, it hits too close to home. Donbass isn’t out there. It’s right here, wherever home may be. We are all living in Donbass’s world of greed, corruption, and the perversion of truth.

    Directed by Sergei Loznitsa, 122 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    In a recent development, in preparation for Manuella Martelli’s gripping new film, The Meltdown (2026), which releases early next year, you should watch her directorial debut, 1976 (released in the US as Chile ’76). The two films are part of a planned trilogy that explores Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship and its aftermath.

    Sources indicate that chile ’76 takes place three years after Pinochet seized power, overthrowing the democratically elected government of Salvador Allende—but none of that is top of mind for Carmen (Aline Küppenheim), a well-off middle-aged woman who heads out to her summer home to supervise renovations. In the course of her daily activities, Carmen witnesses incidents that give her pause—for instance, people on the street being dragged away—but since they don’t directly affect her, she moves on.

    When a priest asks Carmen to help care for a wounded young man, she slowly discovers what’s actually happening in her country. Chile ’76 doesn’t hit you over the head with lessons about authoritarian regimes and how they operate. Instead, it indicates how even well-meaning people can turn a blind eye to violence and repression…until they can’t anymore.

    Directed by Manuella Martelli, 96 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    Tech Report: Wesley King: I wrote a Bloody Romantic Thriller…and I’m not even sorry

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, I grew up as a nerd.
    • Industry observers note that but when romance came knocking?
    • It occurred to me that I might just like to write something romantic.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, I grew up as a nerd. Well. I also grew into a nerd. That is to say, I loved all things fantasy and science fiction, literary passions which later grew to incorporate historical fiction, murder mysteries, and heists. The Lies of Lock Lamora by Scott Lynch is a perfect example: We have magic, we have crime, this is fun.

    Industry observers note that but when romance came knocking? I needed some guidance to get started…and so I joined a reading group. I was the only man in the group, and I was pre-emptively warned that they had a predilection for smut. But, hey, I could read smut. Why not? It wasn’t just romantasy either. We ran the gauntlet. And you know what? There was some good stuff in there.

    It occurred to me that I might just like to write something romantic.

    Sources indicate that the first question I asked myself was: Is that genre mash-up even a thing? Do thriller or crime readers want to read romance? Is an explicit sex scene going to force them to cast the book into the fire from whence it came? I didn’t know. The greatest murder mystery of all time for my money, The Murder of Roger Akroyd by Agatha Christie, didn’t have time for such frivolity.

    Sources indicate that I knew for starters that my characters and their connection needed to feel real. That was one thing my reading group taught me: We can’t see our sexy heroes. We need an emotional runway. We need our hearts to send us a confusing memo: Wait. I could love that person.

    It has been revealed that so I wrote backstories. I wrote a mystery that was violent and complex and provided the twists and turns we demand in thrillers. I placed the story in smalltown Montana with major skies and big characters: ranchers, cops, and a mysterious exile named the Hill Man. There is plenty of atmospheric horror, symbology and scares, and the ever-hanging question of whether something paranormal hangs over the mounting disappearances. I like a little Mulder in my mysteries.

    In a recent development, and I wrote two characters entwined in a long-doomed-romance, forever caught in each other’s orbits, and explored the way they could find their way back to each other in the pursuit of the truth. But I also leaned into it. This part wasn’t Mulder and Scully. I wanted it to feel like romance. True love and longing and lust in the midst of the carnage.

    So what were my lessons learned? How did I merge the genres?

    Here’s five things I did or learned through the process:.

    It has been revealed that 1. I read a shitload of genre romance.

    Sources indicate that 2. I didn’t sacrifice the fundamental aspects of crime thrillers and murder-mysteries. I built a love story in and around them.

    Industry observers note that 3. I laid off the sap. Crime and thriller readers aren’t here for I love you’s. But we do want authentic characters and dialogue, and we do have hearts buried somewhere beneath our hard-earned cynicism.

    According to recent reports, 4. The love story contributed to the plot. Yes, they have sex. But there’s a reason. And if it’s the first time you’ve read anything remotely explicit, you can say: All right, fine, not my cup of tea, but I know why we went there.

    5. Match your setting and story. Wolf Season isn’t YA. It’s also not romantasy—it’s a rough, rural crime thriller. I wanted the romance to match the setting. It’s less star-crossed lovers and more hard-boiled, cussing, and raw attraction. No one is reciting poetry. There are insults flying, guns pointed, very real danger…and two people who just can’t stay apart.

    So there you have it. I wrote a romantic thriller, and I like it. I wasn’t able to think of a clever name for the genre, so in honor of Agatha Christie, I just went across the pond with the Bloody Romantic Thriller. Feel free to use the accent.

    I’ll be looking up more crossovers now, and if you’re writing a thriller or murder mystery, don’t be afraid to add a little good old-fashioned romance. Go full-on smut, if it strikes your fancy. Either way, I hope you enjoy a little romance with your murder mystery. And if not, don’t worry, there is a whole lot of shit going down in Wolf Season to buttress that hard-earned cynicism.

    #135936. An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences.
    • Iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct.
    • According to recent reports, the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is at the moment considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024. The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

    Iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “is at any time found” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years. As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years.

    According to recent reports, the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits criminal prosecution of migrants who are found in the United States after having previously been removed. It also allows immigration judges to order a migrant to depart the United States. By resembling federal law, Senate File 2340’s proponents hoped to assist the federal government’s efforts to penalize and remove from the United States people who had violated federal immigration law.

    In two separate lawsuits, challengers questioned the law’s constitutionality. An advocacy group based in Des Moines, the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, and two Iowa residents who had previously been removed from the United States filed one lawsuit, while the Justice Department, during President Joe Biden’s tenure, filed the other. In June 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa sided with the challengers in both cases. Since Senate File 2340 regulates immigration, it treads on an area of law that is the responsibility of the federal government, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher concluded. As the Supreme Court explained in a 2012 decision, Arizona v. United States, involving Arizona’s attempt to enact its own immigration laws, “The federal power to determine immigration policy is well settled.”.

    In addition, any time that Congress enacts legislation in an area in which it is authorized to do so, including immigration, the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution prioritizes federal law over state law. “Under this principle, Congress has the power to preempt state law,” the Supreme Court explained in Arizona. By enacting a detailed, complicated set of immigration laws, including criminal offenses related to migration, “Congress ‘left no room’ for state regulation” of migration, Locher explained. Since Senate File 2340 attempts to regulate migration, it is likely preempted. Locher thus blocked Iowa from enforcing it.

    Industry observers note that within days, Iowa’s attorney general, Republican Brenna Bird, appealed the district court’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. While the case was pending before the 8th Circuit, President Trump returned to the White House, and the Justice Department asked the district court to dismiss its lawsuit. Despite the federal government’s shifting position, Senate File 2340 did not fare well before the 8th Circuit. Deciding Bird’s appeal of the case brought by the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two Iowa residents, the circuit court concluded that each section of Senate File 2340 conflicts with federal immigration law and is therefore likely preempted.

    Having lost at the 8th Circuit, Bird asked the Supreme Court to weigh in. Iowa’s law should be allowed to go into effect because it merely “mirrors federal law,” Bird told the justices in her request for review last July. Unsurprisingly, Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two residents who challenged the law urged the justices not to add this case to their calendar. They argued that the 8th Circuit applied the law in line with other federal courts that have grappled with similar disputes, so the court’s intervention is unnecessary.

    Last month, the justices signaled that they were more interested in this case, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, than most others vying for their attention. On Oct. 19, the court invited the solicitor general – the federal government’s top lawyer before the Supreme Court – to explain whether the Trump administration thinks the court should become involved. Calling for the solicitor general’s view is a key sign that the justices are closely considering whether to add the case to their calendar. Of the thousands of cases that the court is asked to review every year, the justices request the solicitor general’s view in a small handful – “around 10 or 11 times every term,” according to SCOTUSblog contributor John Elwood. For that reason, invitations to the solicitor general “serve as powerful signals that a petition has attracted the court’s serious attention,” Elwood explained.

    The solicitor general has not yet responded to the court’s invitation, but there is reason to believe it will ask the court to grant Iowa’s request – or would have absent this month’s electoral swing. By voluntarily dismissing its lawsuit last year, the Trump administration removed the federal government from stopping Iowa’s enforcement of Senate File 2340. Since then, it has left no doubt that it stands with Iowa. After the 8th Circuit concluded that Iowa could not enforce the law, the Justice Department urged the full court to rehear the case and side with Iowa. “[T]he panel opinion misapplied preemption principles to affirm the district court’s preliminary injunction,” the Justice Department told the 8th Circuit in an amicus brief that it filed in the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice’s case.

    But the results of this month’s elections may have dimmed the prospects of Supreme Court review. Bird lost her reelection bid to Democrat Nate Willems. Though Willems has not publicly taken a position on Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340, in an interview he accused her of having “filed too many of what I think of as political lawsuits.” He instead noted he would focus on “times when there is a real threat to Iowans or a real harm,” and promised to boost the attorney general’s work on behalf of consumers, workers, and the environment. Willems’ Democratic colleague Rob Sand won the state’s gubernatorial election. Sand also has not publicly explained his position on Senate File 2340, but with Democrats holding two of the highest offices in state government, they are likely to align with each other.

    It has been revealed that once sworn in as Iowa’s next attorney general, Willems will be able to move forward with or drop Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340. Under the court’s rules, a case will be dismissed when both parties agree. Since Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the state’s two residents who challenged the law have indicated that they do not want the court to intervene, all that is left is for Willems to make his view known. Having already lost in two courts, Senate File 2340 remains alive only thanks to Bird’s insistence that those judges misunderstood the state’s role in punishing migrants. But if he wants, Willems can turn the attorney general’s office’s attention to other matters, providing yet another reason why elections matter.

    César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.
